summary: Adversarially verify the 20 finding clusters from the pulse-flood audits: re-run each reproducer, check mechanism, realism and fix, then independent skeptic review

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers with conforming equipment, on every local connect. The window is the words plus SETTLE, about 32 ms. A claim that lands in it is always refused, never taken. That is roughly 0.1-0.4% of incoming claims at 150-400 connects an hour. The outcome is graceful: the caller hears 03 and nothing stays held. The same claims would be refused by the simplest fix too, so the only loss is against the spec's stated intent (marker.md 4.8 and 5, network.md 3.6: 'a claim waits out a watch').
findings.ran: Rebuilt the auditor's work/audit/cableb/tb_attw.v on the pure snapshot (work/RTL.list), scale 8: work/verify/C01-watch-late-refusal/attw_snap_scen1.log matches run_attw_scen1.log. New real-timer bench work/verify/C01-watch-late-refusal/tb_c01r.v (site_net default timers, 10 pps 60/40, 720 ms pauses; the claim is aligned by event to land 10 ms into B's WATCH), +scen=1: r_snap_s1.log.
findings.evidence: Reading: mini_marker.v:282 exempts only S_WATCH. WATCH ends with r_release<=1 and state<=S_IDLE (550-552) or S_DRAIN (542-548). pulse_reg.v:117-118 clears busy on the edge after it sees release_it. So on tick T+1 att_refuse is true (r_busy still 1, state not WATCH) and att_take is false. Real timers, r_snap_s1.log: WATCH 2660..2692, att 2670, 'REFUSED the claim on 11' at 2692 (the WATCH-exit tick), then 'B wr dst 11 src 03 bsy 1 clm 1'. A20 hears 03 and B22 is never connected. Everything is idle 3 s after hang-up.
findings.notes: The mechanism is exactly as stated. I rate it low, not medium, because the outcome is graceful and the minimal safe fix refuses the same claims anyway. It is one half of the cluster's single root cause. The class marker has the same code: rtl/marker.v:273, with reg_release registered and r_busy off the pulse_reg card in top_max.

findings.real_timing: Reproduced at REAL timers two ways. (1) With a FAULT: the owner's local line chatters (4 ms break / 12 ms make: never a pulse, never steady) through the WATCH, and the far caller abandons. A dirty hook switch or an intermittent loop does this: plausible but uncommon. Given that fault and a claim landing in its WATCH, the stuck state is likely, because the far caller then hears silence for up to NODIG (10 s) and gives up. (2) With CONFORMING equipment: the claim lands in the ~33 ms WATCH, the far caller hangs up, then the local caller hangs up, all inside SETTLE and in that order. The rate is negligible (order 1e-11 per claim). The damage is permanent and cumulative: each occurrence holds a trunk at both ends plus a monitor cell at the neighbour (of NMON=2).
findings.ran: Scale 8, pure snapshot: attw_snap_scen2.log matches the auditor's run_attw_scen2.log. Real timers, tb_c01r on the snapshot: r_snap_s3.log (chatter fault, +scen=3) and r_snap_s2.log (conforming double abandon, +scen=2 xa=2 xb=10). All logs are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C01-watch-late-refusal/.
findings.evidence: r_snap_s3.log: WATCH 2660..3347, att 2670, A20 on-hook 2671. 'B11 releases itself' at 2928 (A20 + T_REL). At 3347 B's gone ends WATCH, the claim is REFUSED and B writes dst 11 src 03 bsy 1 clm 1. At 3349 A writes dst 11 src 00 bsy 1: the phantom hold. 3 s later: B11 03/bsy/clm BUSY, A11 BUSY, A monitors 01, A n_nofwd 1 (4 FAIL). r_snap_s2.log is the same with WATCH 2660..2937 (B20 on-hook at 2679, 8 ms after A20). B11 releases at 2928, the refusal lands at 2937, the phantom at 2939, and the same held state remains 3 s later. The chain checks out in the RTL: port.v:176-193 clears only on a fall of fM/fE, and on the released B11 M=0, fm=0 and E=M(03)=0. port.v:153 then drives backward A = clm = 1 for good. A11 is free with st cleared in the gap, so net_unit.v:283/609-621 holds it as a seizure whose M never falls.
findings.notes: Duplicate of late-refusal-no-edge-hold: same mechanism, same fix. The auditor calls it high; I rate it medium because the realistic trigger is a line fault at the owner combined with a far abandon. The transit spread (a phantom forwarded, holding a trunk, monitor and resolver per hop) is reasoned but not simulated here: A had no onward direction, hence n_nofwd 1. It is consistent with the resolver's R_GONE needing the incoming port's BUSY to fall, which never happens.

findings.real_timing: Same as att-watch-late-refusal-stuck-clm: real at real timers with a chattering-line fault at the owner, or with a vanishingly rare conforming double abandon inside the 32 ms SETTLE. A conforming dial cannot keep WATCH open by dialling on: the 720 ms minimum pause against the ~160 ms from the last digit to the end of WATCH rules it out. The auditor's '20 pps dial dialling on' example is therefore not a conforming trigger.
findings.ran: Read the auditor's work/audit/origin/run_s6.log and run_fix2.log. The real-timer reproductions are the same as for the previous finding: r_snap_s2.log and r_snap_s3.log.
findings.evidence: run_s6.log: [544.004] REFUSED after B11 had released itself about 428 ms; [546.562] A holds the phantom; the idle check FAILs. My real-timer runs show the same sequence (r_snap_s2 and r_snap_s3, above). The monitor cell is freed at w_claim (net_unit.v:666-668), and CL_ACK (674) waits only for att_ack, so nothing watches the claimed trunk during the wait.
findings.notes: Same finding as att-watch-late-refusal-stuck-clm. The origin auditor's fix (rtl_fix: !r_release plus a 9-bit att_wait bound at CLR/2) works at real timers (below). Their note that '!r_release alone moves the hazard' is right. A take writes nothing to the trunk, so the stuck state vanishes, but an unbounded wait then gives C02's late attach.

verifier.root_cause: One root cause with two parts, at mini_marker.v:282 (and identically at rtl/marker.v:273). (1) A claim in S_WATCH is always answered on the stale r_busy. r_release is a register (550-552, 542-548) and pulse_reg.v:117-118 drops busy one edge later, so the waited claim is always refused and never taken as intended. (2) The wait is unbounded (WATCH lasts until settled, gone or nodig) and nobody watches the claimed trunk meanwhile (net_unit.v:666-668 frees the monitor cell). So the refusal's 03/BSY/CLM write (320-327) can land on a trunk that has already released itself. On that trunk no detector edge will ever come (port.v:176-193), so it stays BUSY with CLAIM for good, and the neighbour holds it as a phantom seizure.
verifier.best_fix:
Recommended: a hook-gated wait, two gate inputs and no counter (tested). In mini_marker.v:282: `wire att_refuse = u_att && !att_ack && r_busy && !rd_done && !r_release && ((state != S_WATCH) || !r_hook);`. r_hook is pulse_reg's hook, already on the register ribbon and unused in mini_marker. If the watched line stays off-hook, WATCH ends at SETTLE (<= ~33 ms) and the claim is TAKEN, as the spec intends. The first break (hang-up or chatter, the only things that make WATCH long) refuses it at once, while its trunk is still up. The wait is bounded by SETTLE+1 ms, well before the far caller's h (>= ~590 ms later).

Alternatives:
- Deleting '(state != S_WATCH)' is the simplest (one gate input fewer). It is tested by cableb at scale 8 and by C02's tb_net (88/88). It refuses claims that land in the ~33 ms WATCH, as the RTL effectively does today, but the spec text (marker.md 4.8/5, network.md 3.6) must change.
- The origin auditor's '!r_release' plus a 9-bit att_wait bound (CLR/2) also works, but costs a counter.
- '!r_release' alone is not enough: the stuck state goes, but an unbounded wait then late-attaches (C02).

Whichever fix is chosen must also go into rtl/marker.v:273. For the hook gate there, top_max.v:179 already has r_hook on the register card; it needs one ribbon wire into marker.v. The auditor's suggested unit-side gate on the trunk's M is not needed, and it races: a hang-up can only be told from a dial break at CLR, which is also when T_REL releases the port.

verifier.summary:
All three findings are one defect in mini_marker.v:282, which is duplicated in rtl/marker.v:273. att-watch-late-refusal-stuck-clm and late-refusal-no-edge-hold are the same finding written by two auditors.

The one-tick r_busy lag is real: every claim that waits out a WATCH is refused on the WATCH-exit tick instead of taken, which I reproduced at real timers (r_snap_s1). On its own that is graceful, so I rate it low. Because the wait is also unbounded and unsupervised, the refusal can land on a trunk that has released itself. That trunk then stays BUSY with CLAIM for good, and the neighbour holds a phantom seizure with a monitor cell. I reproduced this at real timers with a chattering-line fault (r_snap_s3) and with a conforming double abandon inside the 32 ms SETTLE (r_snap_s2). The conforming route is vanishingly rare; the realistic trigger is a chattering line at the owner plus a far caller who abandons. The damage is permanent and cumulative, so medium rather than the auditors' high. The auditors' benches and logs hold up: tb_attw rebuilt on the pure snapshot gives identical logs.

The cheapest complete fix is two gate inputs: `&& !r_release && ((state != S_WATCH) || !r_hook)`. It keeps the spec's 'a claim waits out a watch' for a steady line, refuses at the first break, and bounds the wait to SETTLE with no counter. It passes my real-timer bench in all three scenarios and tb_net 88/88. Deleting the exemption is simpler still (tb_net 88/88 per C02) but means changing the spec. The origin auditor's counter-bounded fix also passes but costs more hardware.

Everything is under /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C01-watch-late-refusal/: the bench (tb_c01r.v), the fix copy (rtl_hk/mini_marker.v), the logs, and NOTES.md.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: I re-derived each mechanism from the snapshot RTL, looked for any condition that blocks it, and looked for a second path the auditors and the verifier missed.

per_finding.reason: Re-derived; the outcome is fixed, with no escape. S_WATCH leaves only when bus_idle holds (mini_marker.v:541). So on the exit tick the queue holds at most two words, and at T+1 room is at least 6. u_local, u_done and u_nogo cannot pulse, because the origin bank is idle while the register holds a local or claimed caller. rd_done cannot be high outside S_READ. So at T+1, att_refuse (282) always fires on the stale r_busy (pulse_reg.v:117-118 clears busy only at the T+1 edge), and att_take (273) never gets its T+2 tick. The only other states where a claim neither is taken nor refused are S_READ with r_busy=0 (a caller candidate's word read, at most about 2 ms, ending in S_TAKE where att_take fires) and one tick of COLLECT after attach. Both are harmless, so S_WATCH is the only unbounded wait. Low is right: the extra blocking is about 33 ms per local connect, against a one-register marker that is already busy for whole seconds of dialling on every call. I found one more graceful effect. At the end of a ring (network.md 7) the direct copy claims first, waits out WATCH and is refused. The queued long-way copy is then claimed with the register free and is TAKEN, but the origin has already dropped the long way. The caller hears 03, and the register sits on a dead trunk until gone (about 256 ms).

The chain checks out link by link, and nothing blocks it. (1) net_unit.v:666-668 frees the monitor cell at w_claim, and CL_ACK (674) waits only for att_ack, so nothing supervises the trunk during the WATCH wait. (2) B11 clears itself when fM falls, T_REL after the far caller hangs up (port.v:176-193). (3) The late refusal writes 03/BSY/CLM (320-327). After that m=0, fm=0 and e=M(03)=0 (site_net NG a=0), so no detector can ever fall again. (4) A trunk card ties /ANS low (baseband_card.v:158, local_trunk.v:193), so on=0 and a_rx=e||clm=1 steady, with no ring-cadence chop that could ever release A11. (5) A's st bit clears on the M-low samples in the gap (net_unit.v:566-567), and cls_seen (283) takes A11 as a fresh seizure whose M never falls. Variant: if the refusal lands less than one pass after B11's release, A keeps st=1. Then there is no phantom at A, but both trunk ends are still dead. The verifier left out one realism point, and it makes the fault trigger rarer. Any make of 32 ms settles WATCH, and chatter during dialling stops ID so digits never complete. So the chatter must START within about 33 ms of the connect words, not just exist on the line. Given that onset and a claim in the WATCH, the far caller sits in silence for up to NODIG, so 'likely' holds. The conforming route (claim, far abandon, local abandon, all inside SETTLE) is negligible, as stated. The damage goes further than simulated: with ring straps the unstrapped links form a tree, so a phantom at A is forwarded down A's whole subtree. That permanently holds a trunk per link, one of NMON=2 monitors at each exchange, and one of NRES=2 resolvers at each transit. Two events end claiming and transit there. Medium is right: the damage is permanent and spreads, but the trigger is a fault whose onset must fall in a narrow window.

This is the same defect as att-watch-late-refusal-stuck-clm, and my re-derivation above covers it. The auditor's conforming example ('a 20 pps dial dialling on') does not hold up. Any make of 32 ms or more settles WATCH, so pulsing can keep WATCH open only if a new pulse train starts within about 160 ms of s completing (ID 128 plus the connect). That needs an inter-digit pause far below the 720 ms minimum. Their other trigger (a chattering hook or jack) is the real one, with the onset-window qualifier noted above. run_s6.log and the verifier's real-timer r_snap_s2 and r_snap_s3 logs match the sequence the RTL predicts: B11 releases, then the refusal lands 9 ms later, then A holds the phantom 2 ms after that. The auditor's suggested unit-side gate on the trunk's M is correctly rejected. The unit can tell a hang-up from a dial break only at CLR, and T_REL releases the port at the same moment, so the gate would race.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's hook-gated fix is correct: `att_refuse = u_att && !att_ack && r_busy && !rd_done && !r_release && ((state != S_WATCH) || !r_hook)`. I checked how it works.

**The `!r_release` term.**
- At T+1 neither branch fires: refuse is blocked by r_release, and take by r_busy. S_IDLE cannot start a read, also because of r_busy.
- At T+2, att_take fires in IDLE or DRAIN.
- It also turns into a take the rare claim that lands on the tick after any other r_release.

**The hook term.**
- The claim waits only while the watched line is made. The wait ends at the first sampled break (refused) or at settled (taken, at most SETTLE after the claim plus the bus delay for the connect words).
- At w_claim the trunk is still live, because the cell is still held and d_clr would have freed it after 256 ms of break. The trunk cannot release until about 256 ms after that.
- So every answer lands on a live trunk.
- A take writes nothing to the trunk. If the far caller hung up during the 33 ms, the register's later gone-write (SILENCE, BSY 0, CLM 0) lands on an idle port and does no harm.

**Alternatives.**
- Deleting `(state != S_WATCH)` is equally safe and one input simpler. It fits "simplest mechanism first". It only refuses the claims that land in the 33 ms WATCH, which the snapshot refuses anyway, but network.md §3 ("A claim waits out a watch after a connect") and marker.md §5 must change.
- The origin auditor's counter-bounded fix works but costs a counter.
- `!r_release` alone is not enough (C02).

**Either fix.**
- It must also go into marker.v:273. For the hook gate, add a ribbon wire for r_hook from top_max.v:179. The same lag applies there, because reg_release is registered.
- It leaves a pre-existing, unrelated race of about 1-2 ms. The port's T_REL is counted directly, but the monitor's d_clr and the register's CLR come through the probe and lag by up to one pass. A queued w_claim (C02), or a nodig NOGO write, that lands in that gap re-busies a released port. This is negligible, and it belongs to C02, not C01.

I ran no simulations. Notes are at /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C01-skeptic-mechanism/NOTES.md.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier on all three findings. They share one root cause at mini_marker.v:282, which is duplicated at marker.v:273.

- **watch-exit-refusal:** It happens every time. Leaving S_WATCH needs an idle bus, and the unit's one-tick signals cannot fire in WATCH, so a claim that waits out WATCH is always refused on the stale r_busy. The outcome is graceful. Low.
- **The two stuck-state findings:** They are the same finding. I re-derived the chain gate by gate, and no condition blocks it. A trunk card ties /ANS low, so the backward A that CLAIM drives is steady and nothing ever releases the phantom.
- **Two things the verifier did not say:**
  - The fault trigger is narrower than "a chattering line". Any 32 ms make settles WATCH, and chatter while dialling stops digits completing, so the chatter must start within about 33 ms of the connect.
  - The damage is wider than what was simulated. A phantom at A is forwarded over the whole unstrapped tree, permanently holding a trunk per link, one of two monitors at each exchange and one of two resolvers at each transit.
- **Severity:** On balance medium stands.
- **A new graceful side effect:** at a ring end the direct claim is refused, and the doomed long-way copy then gets the register.

The hook-gated fix is sound and bounds the wait to SETTLE while the claimed trunk is still up. Deleting the exemption is an equally safe, simpler alternative, but it needs a spec change. Either fix must also go into marker.v.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity: real timers, real telephones and line cards, plausible faults; rate per exchange per busy hour; what the subscriber hears; whether the fix suits 74HC hardware and is complete

per_finding.reason: The mechanism is exactly as stated. mini_marker.v:282 exempts only S_WATCH. WATCH exits set r_release, a register (550-552 and 542-548), and pulse_reg.v:117-118 clears busy one edge later. So on the first IDLE or DRAIN tick att_refuse is true and att_take is false. r_snap_s1.log shows the refusal at 2692, the WATCH-exit tick. It happens on every local connect, at real timers, with conforming equipment. The window is the words plus SETTLE, about 33 ms. Rate: refused claims per busy hour = C x L x 0.033/3600, where C is incoming claims per hour and L is local connects per hour. With C=30 and L=60 that is about 0.017 per busy hour, one every ~60 busy hours. The verifier's 150-400 connects an hour is high for a 64-port exchange with one register, but the order of magnitude holds. What the subscriber hears: the origin connects the caller only at the last digit, so the caller dials all of 1 e b h s, hears 03, and redials. The failure is clean. It is marginal next to C15: the one register already refuses every claim that arrives while any call is dialling, about C x 7% (~2 per busy hour at the same load). This adds ~1% to that. The deletion fix refuses the same claims. Low is right; info could be argued.

The mechanism is real and I agree with the label, but the fault route is much rarer than the verifier's wording ('dirty hook switch or intermittent loop... likely') suggests. Stuck needs the refusal at WATCH end to land after t_a + T_REL, where t_a is the far hang-up. (a) The bench's 4 ms break / 12 ms make chatter goes straight onto M, because site_net has no detector. The real line card's hook RC (cvsd_line_card.v:110-135, tau 4 ms: ~7.6 ms before a break shows, +6.1 ms on a make) swallows it. A realisable chatter needs raw breaks of at least ~8 ms, less than ~34 ms apart, for seconds: close to continuous 30 pps pulsing. (b) Any break sample resets the ID timer, so a line that is already chattering cannot complete a digit. The chatter must therefore start within ~35 ms after s's digit strobe. tb_c01r lines this up on an event (wait mks_b==7). (c) The far caller hears silence from the key until the connect at h s (network.md 4.1). A real caller therefore dials h s (2-4 s) and then waits before giving up, so the chatter must last seconds, towards NODIG. A20 hanging up 2 ms after att, before dialling h, is the least likely behaviour. A dirty hook switch bounces for milliseconds at a transition, which only reaches the conforming case (~1e-11 per claim). My estimate: about 0 on a healthy plant, and 1e-5 to 1e-3 per busy hour with a severe sustained-chatter fault. No subscriber is misrouted and nobody hears anything wrong at the time. The damage is permanent, silent and cumulative: a trunk at both ends plus one of NMON=2 monitors at the neighbour. Because the unit has no timeout anywhere (C08), the phantom would also be forwarded through transits (reasoned, not simulated). Only a reset recovers it; a lit BUSY lamp shows it. That keeps it at medium, low end of medium. The auditors' high is overstated.

This is a duplicate of att-watch-late-refusal-stuck-clm: same mechanism, same fix, same realism limits. run_s6.log holds: REFUSED at 544.004 after B11 released itself, then the phantom hold at A at 546.562. The auditor's conforming-sounding trigger, 'a 20 pps dial dialling on', does not survive. With the 720 ms minimum pause, WATCH ends about 165 ms after the last pulse. A 10 pps make (~46 ms after the detector) settles WATCH anyway. Only a 20 pps dial with a 128-165 ms inter-digit pause keeps WATCH open, and then for at most one digit (<=500 ms). That is non-conforming and would nearly merge digits. The network-wide consequence ('after two, the exchanges on that path can no longer claim') is C08's mechanism and was reasoned, not simulated here. Medium, for the same reasons as the duplicate.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's hook-gated fix, `att_refuse = u_att && !att_ack && r_busy && !rd_done && !r_release && ((state != S_WATCH) || !r_hook)`, is correct and complete for mini_marker. With it the only way WATCH can end with a claim still waiting is `settled`. `!r_release` covers the one-tick lag, so the take lands at t+2. The first break sample refuses at once, at most ~33 ms after att. The trunk cannot release until at least ~223 ms after that, so the refusal always finds it up. A take lands at most ~34 ms after att, and h is at least ~590 ms away, so there is no C02 late attach. It passed at real timers (r_hk_s1/2/3) and tb_net 88/88. It costs two gate inputs (Q-bar of r_release, and an OR with !r_hook).

It is not the minimal fix, and its argued advantage is weak. Keeping 'a claim waits out a watch' still needs a spec edit ('...unless the caller breaks'). Deleting `(state != S_WATCH)` removes a gate input instead of adding two, and is safe by construction because every claim is answered at once while its trunk is up. It refuses only claims the snapshot already refuses, so there is no service regression. That is ~0.05-0.3% of claims, far below C15's one-register refusals. In the class marker it needs no new ribbon wire, whereas the hook gate needs r_hook carried from top_max's register card. Deletion is tested at scale 8 (cableb fixwatch) and by tb_net 88/88 (C02 run_net_fix.log). Its refusal happens at att whatever the timers, so scale does not matter. Joel's rule is breadboard first: the simplest mechanism wins, speed up later. By that rule I would take the deletion now and keep the hook gate as a later refinement.

Either fix must also go into rtl/marker.v:273. That edit is untested: run tb_max. The class marker also watches CO lines and call nails, whose M is not a telephone's hook. The origin auditor's 9-bit counter is correct but spends a counter for nothing. The unit-side gate on the trunk's M is not needed: the monitor cell is freed at w_claim, and the gate races T_REL. `!r_release` alone is incomplete, because the wait stays unbounded (C02).

Outside this cluster but recommended as defence in depth: a monitor/hold timeout (C08). Without it, any source of a stuck backward A (this bug, a card fault, C09) becomes a permanent phantom.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier on all three findings: all confirmed and overstated by the auditors. watch-exit-refusal is low. The two stuck-state findings are one duplicate defect, rated medium.

**The refusal (low).** The one-tick r_busy lag refuses every claim that waits out a WATCH. The window is ~33 ms per local connect, at real timers, with any equipment. That is about 0.02 refusals per busy hour at C=30 claims and L=60 local connects an hour. The caller hears 03 after dialling h s. It is clean, and small next to C15's one-register refusals.

**The stuck state (medium).** Here I think the verifier makes the realistic trigger sound more likely than it is:
- The bench's 4/12 ms chatter goes straight onto M. The real line card's 4 ms RC hook detector would swallow it. A chatter that gets through needs breaks of at least ~8 ms under ~34 ms apart, kept up for seconds.
- A line already chattering cannot complete a digit, so the chatter must begin within ~35 ms after the last digit.
- A real far caller hears silence until h s, so dials h s before giving up. The chatter must therefore outlast several seconds of dialling and waiting, not the 2 ms the bench uses.
- The conforming double abandon is ~1e-11 per claim.

So a healthy plant sees essentially none. With a severe sustained-chatter fault I estimate 1e-5 to 1e-3 per busy hour. I keep medium, at the low end, only because the damage is silent, permanent and cumulative: a trunk at both ends and half the neighbour's monitor pool. Through C08's missing timeout it could spread (reasoned, not simulated).

**The fix.** The verifier's hook gate is correct and complete for mini_marker, and bounds the wait to SETTLE. For 74HC I would take the simpler one first: delete `(state != S_WATCH)`. It adds no gates and needs no ribbon wire in top_max. It refuses only claims the snapshot already refuses, and the spec needs editing under either fix. Whichever is chosen must also go into marker.v:273, which is untested there (tb_max).

findings.real_timing: It reproduces at real timers, but only when a local line has a fault. per_finding.reason: I re-derived every step from the snapshot RTL and it holds. net_unit.v:487: w_claim needs cl_st==CL_IDLE. :673-674: att is held in CL_ACK with no bound. :641: at M_DONE the cell ignores digits but stays held. It is freed at w_claim (:666-668) and is still cleared by d_clr (:647-649), so a queued claim is withdrawn only if its trunk breaks for 256 ms. mini_marker.v:282: att_refuse exempts S_WATCH; :273-274: att_take is only in IDLE/TAKE/DRAIN with !r_busy. WATCH exits at :541-553, and pulse_reg busy drops one edge after release (pulse_reg.v:117-118), so claim 1 is refused on the stale r_busy (C01) and claim 2's att then finds the register free. Counting starts at the attach: pulse_reg.v:86 (arm = busy && seen), :106-107, and pulse_rx.v:72-76. The auditor's 'pulse_rx.v:244-249' cites a 105-line file; those are the right lines. The verifier's snapshot re-run is byte-identical to the auditor's log (I diffed it), and the real-timer log (attach 96 ms into h, count 2 2, B22 rings) matches the RTL. Low, not high, and reachability is narrower than the verifier says. (1) The bench drives port M straight from hook (site_net.v:121, s_a = hook), bypassing the line card. The real cvsd_line_card.v:110-130 hook RC (tau 4 ms, thresholds 0.85/0.70) needs about 7.6 ms of open loop to show a break and stretches every make by about 6 ms. The 1 ms break / 2 ms make chatter would read as a steady make, so WATCH would end at about 33 ms. A fault that reaches the marker needs line breaks of about 8 to 260 ms and line makes under about 26 ms. It must start in the roughly 35 ms between the connect and settled, and last more than about 0.6 s: an intermittent short or chattering hook contact that begins right at a hang-up. That is rarer than 'a human can't do it'. (2) The 'claim 2 needs seconds of WATCH' condition holds only for two sites. With three or more exchanges the two claims can come from different origins within one WATCH. (3) The wrong number needs the WATCH to end inside claim 2's h pulse train. Before h the call completes, late but correct. After h, s is read as h and the call ends in NODIG, then cannot-complete. It is still a wrong number the caller cannot see, but it needs a fault and a coincidence, so low.

The unbounded wait is real: the S_WATCH exemption, plus CL_ACK with no timeout, plus WATCH ending only on settled, gone or nodig. NODIG (10 s) is the ceiling because nd_t is not reset in WATCH: dig_stb needs a make of ID, and SETTLE ends WATCH first. The stated consequence for a lone claim is wrong in the snapshot, and I checked that it cannot happen. Every WATCH exit needs bus_idle, so the marker queue has room 8 on the refusal tick. No read is in flight, and the unit cannot pulse local/done/nogo then. So the stale-r_busy refusal ALWAYS fires on the tick after the exit, and a lone waiting claim is always refused and never late-attached. A late attach needs a queued second claim, or C01's +fixatt. Two smaller errors: its 'at most 256 ms' normal wait should be about 290-320 ms (hang-up inside SETTLE then CLR, or flash then SETTLE). Its '640 ms less ID' margin should be 720 less 128, about 590 (ES 201 187; network.md 4.2). Its proposed per-att counter bound stacks: k queued claims can wait k x W. A tap on nd_t, counted from the connect, bounds every claim at once.

A second path the auditors and verifier missed, which needs NO fault. I reasoned it from the RTL and did not run it. In a ring or mesh the owner can hear one call on two paths (C18's ring case). The digits are relayed live, so both cells decide b within a few ms of each other, and the second always queues behind the first on cl_st. If the owner is in an ordinary WATCH, about 33 ms or up to about 290 ms after a hang-up, when claim 1's att rises: the origin (or transit) keeps path 1 and drops path 2 at claim 1's CLAIM (net_unit.v:795-804). At the WATCH exit, claim 1 (the kept path) is refused on the stale r_busy, and claim 2 is TAKEN on the dropped path, which now shows a break. The register sits on a dead trunk until CLR (256 ms), and the caller gets cannot-complete. The second CLAIM goes out a WATCH later than normal, so C18's late-claim race is more likely lost: a phantom seizure where path 2 was dropped. No wrong number, because the attach is before h. It matters for choosing the fix: +fixatt alone would take claim 1 correctly here but still delay the second CLAIM, while the deletion restores normal timing.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
I agree with the verifier's fix: delete `&& (state != S_WATCH)` from att_refuse at mini_marker.v:282 and marker.v:273.
- It is correct and minimal: a pure deletion with no gate cost.
- It is complete for both C02 findings. Every claim is answered within one read (S_READ with a free register) plus a queue drain, a few ms. The queue behind cl_st then also lasts ms, far inside the roughly 590 ms before the far caller's h.
- It also closes C01, because no claim is pending across a WATCH exit. In the ring case it returns the second CLAIM to its normal timing, about 1 ms after the first, where +fixatt with or without a bound leaves it delayed by the WATCH.
- Side effects checked: a refusal preempts one tick of S_WATCH. Its word briefly holds the r_restart hold (about 0.3 ms), and WATCH's exits are all levels, so nothing is lost.
- Cost against the snapshot: none, since the snapshot already refuses these claims, only late. Against the spec's intent: claims landing in a WATCH of about 34 ms are refused. At C15's roughly 22% register occupancy that is about 0.1% more claims refused, which is negligible.

Caveats:
- The marker.v half is untested, and no bench exercises the class marker with a unit, though top_max.v:183 fits one (tb_max.v:47 says it does not cover a unit). By inspection the edit is a no-op unless u_att is high.

If Joel keeps take-after-watch, use C01's `&& !r_release` plus a bound taken from pulse_reg's nd_t, which counts from the connect's words. Do not use a per-claim att counter, because queued claims stack k x W. Any tap up to 512 answers before h: 512 keeps every conforming WATCH (at most about 320 ms) a take, while 128 or 256 are safe but refuse the hang-up tail. This needs a new pulse_reg output and a ribbon line for the class marker's register, and it is untested. The auditor's extra suggestion (keep the claiming cell until att_ack and refuse on brk_stb) is not needed with the deletion.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity

per_finding.reason:
The mechanism is real and the verifier explains it correctly. mini_marker.v:282 exempts S_WATCH from att_refuse. net_unit.v:487 and :673-674 allow one claim at a time, with no bound in CL_ACK. The claiming cell stops counting at M_DONE (:641) and is freed at the CLAIM write, and pulse_rx only arms at attach. C01's stale r_busy then refuses claim 1 and hands the register to claim 2 mid-h. run_att2r_snap.log matches the verifier's account: a real-timer attach 96 ms into h, counts 2 2, and B22 rings.

REALISM. With conforming equipment WATCH ends about 33 ms after the words go out (settled). The worst case is about 290 ms (the caller hangs up inside SETTLE, then CLR) or about 320 ms (a hook flash, then off-hook). That is far inside the time from claim-want to h. So a wrong number needs a fault. The M of the local caller, or of a claimed-trunk caller, must chatter with every make under 32 ms and every break under 256 ms, and the chatter must START within about 36 ms after s's dig_stb. A line that is already chattering never completes s (its makes never reach ID), so it never connects and never reaches WATCH. The start therefore has to be a coincidence, or be caused by the connect itself. One speculative example: ringing starting about 16 ms after the connect (T_ARM) and disturbing the feed of a marginal analog loop.

The bench's 1 ms break / 2 ms make chatter goes straight onto M (site_net has no detector RC). The CVSD line card's detector would swallow it: 4 ms RC, 7.6 ms to assert on-hook. That detector also reads random bits as steady off-hook, so a fault on a digital line is unlikely to chatter at all. The plausible sources are an analog FXS loop, a loose connection or a faulty set. A realisable equivalent chatter is raw breaks of at least ~8 ms with raw makes under ~26 ms. The mechanism does not depend on the shape, so the reproduction stands.

Two more limits. T_CLAIM (2 s from b at the origin) caps the window: WATCH must end inside claim 2's h pulse train and within about 1.9 s of claim 2's want, otherwise the origin has already dropped the call cleanly. In a two-site net, claim 2 needs A's single register to be freed and a second caller to dial 1 e b, so D must be at least ~5 s (and at most NODIG, 10 s).

RATE. On a healthy exchange it is effectively zero. On an exchange with such a faulted line, with about 30 claims per busy hour, I estimate roughly 1e-7 to 1e-4 per busy hour.

WHAT SUBSCRIBERS EXPERIENCE. The far caller gets a silent wrong number: the wrong person answers. Claim 1's caller hears silence for seconds, then cannot-complete. The fault is on a third party's line, which makes it hard to diagnose.

SEVERITY. Low for the snapshot is right. It is a wrong number, but it needs a fault plus a two-claim coincidence. Because the fix is free, it should be applied anyway.

One correction to the margin. The verifier's 590 ms floor comes from ES 201 187's 720 ms minimum pause, which binds automatic senders. A fast human on a rotary dial may pause less than 720 ms, perhaps around 500 ms, which leaves a margin of roughly 350-450 ms. That is still above the ~320 ms conforming WATCH, so the verdict does not change. It does make C01's +fixatt-alone fix look worse: that fix would late-attach a lone claim with a thin conforming margin.

The unbounded wait is real. S_WATCH is exempt at mini_marker.v:282, CL_ACK has no timeout at net_unit.v:673-674, and WATCH exits only on settled, gone or nodig (mini_marker.v:541-553). pulse_reg's nd_t is reset only by attach, release, restart or dig_stb, and chatter never produces a dig_stb, so a chattering line can hold WATCH until NODIG.

The auditor's stated consequence for a lone claim is wrong for the snapshot. On the tick after WATCH ends, the stale r_busy (C01) turns the claim into a refusal, as both verifier runs show. The only way that refusal could become a take is if the queue has no room on that one tick, or if a u_local/u_done/u_nogo tick coincides with it; both are negligible. The real outcome is a late but clean cannot-complete: the far caller dials h s into a trunk with no register attached, hears silence for up to about 10 s, then gets cannot-complete.

The auditor's 'normally at most 256 ms' should be about 290-320 ms (the SETTLE window plus CLR, or a flash plus SETTLE). That is still well inside the time before the far caller's next digit. A long wait is fault-only, as in the first finding. Low is right. It is the same root cause, and it only matters as the reason a +fixatt-only fix for C01 would turn this into a lone-claim wrong number.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The recommended fix is correct, minimal and complete: delete `&& (state != S_WATCH)` from att_refuse at mini_marker.v:282 and marker.v:273, and change the docs.

- **Cost on 74HC hardware.** It costs nothing. It removes one decode input from the refuse gating and adds no state, timer or ribbon wire. That fits the breadboard-first, simplest-mechanism rule.
- **What still delays a claim.** After the edit, att waits only in these cases, all bounded to about a millisecond or two against a margin of 350-590 ms:
  - S_READ with a free register, until the read's rd_done (about 2 ms);
  - a full queue (room < 1), at most 8 words (about 1 ms);
  - the single tick of u_local, u_done or u_nogo.
- **The class marker.** Its S_NAIL lasts one tick and it takes claims only in S_IDLE or S_DRAIN, so the same deletion closes it there too. C01 becomes moot, because no claim now waits through a release. What remains is a one-tick stale-r_busy refusal, which is clean.
- **Side effect inside WATCH.** A refusal in WATCH pushes a word, and !bus_idle then re-asserts r_restart. That restarts nd_t and lengthens that WATCH by up to about 32 ms. This is harmless: WATCH only protects the called port's release. WATCH's exits are levels and its gone/nodig exit needs room >= 2 of 8, so nothing is lost.
- **Service cost.** The verifier says it costs no service against the snapshot. That is true except for the vanishing case of two claims inside one ~33 ms normal WATCH, where the snapshot takes claim 2 correctly and the fix refuses it. Against the spec's intent it loses only claims that arrive during about 33 ms per connect, which is negligible next to the seconds the single register is held by dialling.
- **Fault anchors.** faults.py has no anchor on att_refuse (F37 and F48 anchor elsewhere), so fault injection is unaffected.
- **Untested and still to do.**
  - The marker.v edit has not been run. It needs tb_max (top_max is the only class-marker top), since tb_lnet, tb_lfull and tb_lchain do not exercise it.
  - The doc text to change: exchange/network.md:189 ('A claim waits out a watch after a connect'), exchange/marker.md §4.8 ('never during a watch (§5), which a claim waits out') and §5 ('A claim arriving during a watch waits for it to end'), plus the comments at mini_marker.v:276-281 and marker.v:268-270. Changing that rule is Joel's decision.
- **Alternatives.**
  - The bounded wait (C01's !r_release plus a refusal once nd_t passes 128 ms) would also work. It costs a ribbon wire on the class build and saves nothing worth having.
  - The auditor's defence-in-depth idea (keep the claiming cell until att_ack and refuse on brk_stb) is unnecessary once the wait is bounded to milliseconds.
  - Fixing C01 with +fixatt alone must not be done, as the verifier says: it turns a lone claim into a late attach and a possible wrong number.

With conforming equipment WATCH lasts about 33 ms, and at worst about 290-320 ms, well inside the far caller's pause.

A mid-h attach needs a faulted M: every make under 32 ms and every break under 256 ms, and the chatter must start within about 36 ms after s completes. A line that was already chattering could never have completed s, so this is a coincidence or a fault triggered by the connect. The snapshot also needs two claims inside that window. In a two-site net that means D of at least ~5 s, and T_CLAIM still caps the window at about 1.9 s after claim 2's want.

The bench's 1/2 ms chatter could not get through a real CVSD detector; a realisable equivalent chatter (breaks of about 8 ms or more, makes under about 26 ms) gives the same result. My estimate is effectively zero on a healthy exchange and about 1e-7 to 1e-4 per busy hour with a chattering line. When it does happen it is a silent wrong number for an innocent far caller, while claim 1's caller hears silence and then cannot-complete. In the snapshot a lone waiting claim gets a late but clean refusal (C01), not a wrong number.

The margin is not a hard 590 ms floor for human rotary dialling: 720 ms binds automatic senders, and a fast human may pause around 500 ms. That does not change the verdict, but it makes a +fixatt-only fix for C01 riskier.

The recommended deletion is right: zero gates, and complete, because every remaining wait is a millisecond or two. marker.v needs the same edit plus a tb_max run, which has not been done, and the three doc passages in network.md and marker.md need rewording, which is Joel's call. findings.real_timing: Yes, at the board's timers and with conforming equipment only. I built a new bench, tb_c03g, from two real exchanges. Origin A keys 1 with ordinary timing. The far exchange Y seizes A12 2 ms after A does, which is ordinary glare. A takes that as its claim and drops A11 after 2 ms, so X (code 13) sees a seizure of about 2 ms. Y then sends an unrelated flood to A on A13, and A's forwarder puts it on A11 again 72 ms later. Y's caller dials 3 2 2 1 at 60/40 ms with 800 ms pauses. The trigger chain is: a short seizure (glare taken as a claim by an origin or a resolver, or a caller hanging up in a window of about 13 ms), then the same channel re-seized within 256 ms (a transit forward under load; the auditor's origin route needs a caller who keys within about 40 ms of dial tone), then a code match. verifier.root_cause: One root cause. A monitor cell's only signal that its seizure has ended is 256 ms of break (CLR, pulse_rx.v:93 into net_unit.v:647-649), and the trunk can be seized again sooner. There are two ways in. (1) C_UNHOLD (net_unit.v:590-594) writes a hold away inside T_ARM but leaves the cell given at 611-615. Because neither end's detector armed (port.v:147), both ports are free at once and a re-seizure is classified again. (2) The dropping end's RC fE detector may release before the far cell's digital CLR. In both cases the stale cell counts the gap as one pulse and the new seizure's make as a digit 1 (pulse_rx.v:84-99), and it claims at net_unit.v:656-671.
verifier.best_fix: Take the auditor's fix as work/audit/monclaim/fix.patch, with one simplification. (a) One flip-flop per cell, cls_cell, set at the w_cls that gives the cell and used to free that cell in the C_UNHOLD write. The auditor's extra m_port == cls_port compare is redundant. While cst is C_HOLD no other w_cls can happen, and within T_ARM+2 ms the cell cannot be freed or given away again (a digit needs ID of make, and CLR needs 256 ms). So it costs 1 FF per cell and no comparator. (b) longbrk = arm & !m_d & (t >= ID), one gate per cell off the existing timer, freeing the cell on a break no dial makes. Fix (a) completely closes findings 1 and 2 on the snapshot. Fix (b) closes finding 3's wrong number unless the dropping end's RC is under about 50% of nominal; the port-level lost call stays with C20. Total cost is about one package. CAVEAT: C03's fix and C04's proposed fix conflict. C04 makes the watch go to C_LOW and write nothing until M has been low for CLR (or ID). With both applied, a re-seizure 72 ms after a short seizure looks like the make after a dial break. C_UNHOLD never fires, the break is shorter than ID, and the stale cell claims again. I tested this and it fails with either C_LOWT. Whoever merges must choose one of two routes. Either keep the immediate C_UNHOLD and fix C04 another way, or add a release guard at the seizing end so that a trunk the unit dropped before its fE armed is not swept again for at least CLR (origin dmo and N_DROP, resolver leg drops). X cannot tell a fast re-seizure from a dial break by itself.

verifier.summary:
All three findings hold and share one root cause: a monitor cell learns that its seizure has ended only after 256 ms of break, and the trunk can be seized again sooner.

- **stale-cell-after-unhold (confirmed, high).** I reproduced it at the board's timers with conforming equipment only, in a new two-exchange bench (tb_c03g). Origin A takes glare as its claim and drops its east leg after 2 ms. X (code 13) keeps the cell it gave that 2 ms seizure. A forwards an unrelated flood onto the same channel 72 ms later. The stale cell reads the gap as a 1, then the caller's 3 as X's b, and claims. X22 rings for a call dialled 1 3 2 2 1.
  - The exposed exchanges are those with e = 1, which numbering.md 5 reserves for the backbone by convention.
  - The auditor's second variant, where the stale cell miscounts e itself, needs a non-conforming fast dialler; that part is overstated.
- **stale-cell-starves-monitors (overstated, low).** It reproduces at real timers. A stale cell blocks a monitor for 256 ms, but every normal flood already holds one at every exchange for about 1 s.
- **rc-tolerance-reseize (understated, medium).** The auditor rated it speculative. I reproduced it (tb_c03r) with the dropping exchange's release RC 22% short and a caller hanging up inside the guard. At nominal the RTL is safe by only about 13 ms of sweep time, so any RC about 5% short opens it.

The auditor's two-part fix works on the snapshot: free the classifier's cell when the hold is written away, and drop a cell on any break of 128 ms or more. The address compare in the first part is redundant, so it costs one flip-flop per cell. Two caveats:
- The port-level lost call in the third finding remains; that belongs to C20.
- The fix conflicts with C04's proposed fix. With both merged, the same glare bench gives the wrong number again under either C04 setting. Whoever merges must either keep the immediate write-away or add a release guard at the seizing end.

One of the auditor's fix-run failures ('A21 is not talking to X22') is a fault in the check itself, not in the fix.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: I re-derived each mechanism from the snapshot RTL, looked for a condition that blocks it, and looked for a second path the auditors and the verifier missed. I made one short run (tb_c03b) to settle a disagreement.

per_finding.reason: The mechanism is exactly as claimed. The cell is given at net_unit.v:611-615. C_UNHOLD (590-594) never touches m_held, m_armed or m_st. The cell is freed only at 635-639, 666-668, or 647-649 (CLR, pulse_rx.v:93). I looked for something that blocks it and found nothing. C_READ and C_ACT never re-check M, so a single sample of M earns a cell (a 1 ms noise glitch on a trunk's M takes the same path). The cell arms at its first probe sample (629-632) with m_d=m. So whether M is still up or already down, pulse_rx counts cnt=1 at HIT (84-90), and a make of at least ID gives digit 1 (96-99). port.v:147 frees both ends at once because neither detector armed. st is cleared by the M-low sample (566-567), so the re-seizure is classified again. Even if the re-seizure lands before the unhold write, the stale cell still counts it; only the fresh cell is lost. Two rare side paths the audit did not list, both closed by fix (a): (1) If the gap is under HIT, no pulse is counted and the stale cell counts the new call exactly like the fresh cell. At the true destination both cells then want on the same tick. w_claim serves one, and after att_ack it fires a second CLAIM on the same port, which mini_marker.v:282/320-327 (att_refuse, r_busy) writes to NOGO. (2) k short seizures on one channel inside CLR make the oldest cell hear k, so an exchange with OWN_E=k is exposed. I agree with the verifier that the (e+1,b) variant needs a non-conforming fast dialler. I also agree the auditor's 'A21 is not talking to X22' FAIL in run_fix_mc2.log is a bench artefact: tb_mc2.v:169 tests busy_x[P22] after X22 was taken off-hook, and the printed samples show 0 both times.

The mechanism is the same and correct. A seizure that finds m_free1 empty at w_cls never gets a cell (612), and nothing gives it one later. I agree with the verifier's comparison: an ordinary flood holds a cell at every exchange for about 1 s, and a stale cell holds one for 256 ms. The result is monitor.md 4's accepted 'unwatched here' loss, a lost call and not a wrong one. Fix (a) frees these cells within a couple of ms.

I agree it is real and understated. I disagree with the verifier's scope and severity, and I settled the scope with one run. (1) The verifier says a wrong number needs an OWN_E = 1 exchange. That is true only for the C_UNHOLD path, where a seizure shorter than T_ARM carries no digits. On the RC path the flood was abandoned after T_ARM, and the stale cell keeps whatever state the abandon left. If the caller hangs up in the pause after an e that matched, the cell is in M_WANT_B with done=1. The break counts cnt=1 (pulse_rx.v:88, done ? 1). The re-seizure's make then gives digit 1 = b, and the cell claims ID after the re-seizure, before the new caller has dialled anything. Every exchange 'e1' is exposed, and the call goes to its line e' b' whatever was dialled. A hang-up in the middle of a digit gives a phantom k+1 at any OWN_E. Reproduced by tb_c03b on the snapshot at real timers: A is a transit whose ports have T_REL 200, and X is code 21 with nominal timers. Flood 1 is dialled 2 and abandoned 300 ms into the pause. Flood 2 is forwarded onto A11 214 ms later while X11 is still BUSY. X claims at 1586 ms, 130 ms after the re-seizure with no digit dialled, its register attaches, and X25 rings for a flood dialled 1 2 5 3 4. That is 3 SAFETY FAILs (work/verify/C03-stale-monitor-cell/skeptic-mechanism/run_b_snap200.log). (2) The nominal margin is not about 13 ms, and 5% short is not what it takes. The 13 ms was the bench's case: a fresh sweep, port 11. With a sweep already running that visits the freed port late (stride 9, port 70 is step 63), the re-seizure takes about 1.3 ms: read, 1 ms CONFIRM, WAIT and the word. The cell sees the fall and the rise with the same probe phase, so the nominal slack is under 1 ms. C20 release-margin-thin gives 0.13-0.29 ms at port level. So any dropping-end fE shorter than the monitor's 256 ms counter by about 1-2 ms opens a window of (256 - RC - s) ms. fabric.md 8 lists the '14 threshold spread as not measured, and it alone is about ±20%. There is no designed margin, so about half of all dropping ends qualify. The trigger is an ordinary abandon, far more common than finding 1's glare, and the consequence is the same silent wrong number or worse. I rate it high, level with finding 1.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The auditor's fix is correct and minimal for the RTL.

(a) One flip-flop per cell, cls_cell, set at the w_cls that gives a cell and used to free that cell in the C_UNHOLD write. It closes stale-cell-after-unhold and stale-cell-starves-monitors, and also the twin-cell double claim and the k-short-seizure variants. The verifier is right that the m_port == cls_port compare is redundant. While cst is C_HOLD or C_UNHOLD no other w_cls can occur, and a cell cannot be freed within about 18 ms: a digit needs ID of make and CLR needs 256 ms.

(b) longbrk = arm & !m_d & t >= ID frees the cell after 128 ms of break. It closes the RC-path wrong number, including the any-number M_WANT_B variant I reproduced. In the tb_c03b trace the cell would free at about 1371 ms, before A11 frees at 1443. I did not simulate the fix on tb_c03b because of the one-run limit, so this is from reading the code. (b) is also better grounded than the snapshot. monitor.md 6's monitor has only the Q3 and Q7 taps, so the RTL's 256 ms CLR has no circuit behind it, and (b) uses the Q7 tap that is there. It also turns C07's 128-256 ms link hits from phantom pulses into lost calls. Side effect: a flash of 128-256 ms during dialling now loses the call instead of counting a pulse. That is lost, not wrong, which is acceptable.

Caveats:
1. I agree with the verifier's conflict with C04's C_LOW fix. X cannot tell a fast re-seizure from a dial break, so if C_LOW is kept, the seizing end needs a hold-off: do not sweep a trunk you dropped before its fE armed for at least ID plus a margin. That hold-off should be a counter, not an RC.
2. After (b), a lost call remains at port level: X11 is held by its fM while A11 is free again. That is a race between two RCs, reachable at ordinary tolerance. C20 release-margin-thin rates it 'not reachable with baseband or local trunk' because it counts only A-path delay asymmetry, so C20 should be re-rated.
3. There is an adjacent race with the same root that neither fix covers. A drop write can land on a trunk that has already freed itself on a short fE and been re-seized by the forwarder: the origin's N_DROP comes at the register's digital CLR (a hang-up after the guard), and the resolver's R_GONE comes when its incoming port's RC releases. The write kills the new leg and makes a short seizure downstream. It should get its own finding.
4. new network.md 3.4 says '256 ms of break (the trunk released) frees the cell'. That treats 256 ms of break as the trunk's release, and that assumption is the defect. It should read: a hold written away frees its cell, and 128 ms of break frees it.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity (real timers, real telephones, 74HC RC detectors, plausible faults; rate per exchange per busy hour; subscriber experience; is the fix right for 74HC and complete)

per_finding.reason: The code reading holds. net_unit.v:590-594 writes the hold away, and the cell given at 611-615 survives until mismatch, claim or d_clr (CLR 256 ms). I read tb_c03g and run_g_snap.log: the stale cell claims at 1693 and X22 rings. The stimulus is a fair stand-in, but the bench's glare on A12 while A13 was free would not occur with opposite-order hunting. Real glare needs the last free channel; the re-seizure can come from any direction, so the chain stands. This is the RARER of the cluster's two routes. It needs a seizure that dies within about 20 ms of its rise (glare on the last free channel, ~1e-4 per call only when links are near full per C13; a hang-up in that window; or a glitch or intermittent A conductor). Then the same channel must be re-seized within 256 ms (~1e-2) and the (1,e) code must match (~0.03: X coded 1b, the new call's e = b). That is roughly 2e-7 per call, ~1e-5 per exchange per busy hour in a 10-exchange tree at 500 floods/BH. The RC detectors widen the trigger somewhat: a seizure of ~16-60 ms charges the RC only partly, so both ports release early (~110-240 ms) while the cell's digital CLR still runs. The result is a fresh classification alongside a stale cell at nominal parts; still rare. Subscriber experience: the caller is connected to a stranger's line at X (rung, answered). No event is raised anywhere (the claim comes after the guard, so it is not counted as glare). To the caller it is indistinguishable from a misdial, and a redial works. High is right on consequence: a silent wrong number with conforming equipment. On frequency alone it would be medium. The (e+1,b) part is overstated, as the verifier says (it needs a first break within ID of the re-seizure).

This reproduces (rerun_real13_sc3.log), but the added blocking is tiny. A stale cell holds 256 ms, while every normal flood already holds a cell at every exchange for about 1 s. The only plausible way to keep both cells stale is a fault: an intermittent A conductor bouncing an idle channel with blips shorter than T_ARM. Then X cannot own calls, which is a clean cannot-complete after T_CLAIM. Calls through X are still held and forwarded. Low. Fix (a) closes it at no extra cost.

I agree it is real, and the verifier was right to upgrade it from speculative. But medium still understates it: in hardware this is the MAIN route to C03's wrong number. (1) The trigger is ordinary. Any flood dropped before b (caller hang-up, T_KEY, the guard) leaves unresolved cells on every tree link it crossed. The dropping end's fE is an RC into a '14 (fabric.md 3.5), while the far cell's CLR is an exact '4040 tap. At nominal the only margin is the dropping end's free-to-rewrite time. The verifier's own control run_r_snap256.log shows A11 and X11 both free at 936 and the cell's CLR at 938. The margin depends on the trunk's place in the stride-9 sweep (visit k = 57(p-1) mod 64): about 10-13 ms for A11 (step 8), about 1-2 ms for a trunk at 13 (step 58). '14 threshold spread plus C tolerance puts RC times at roughly +-20-35%, so about half of all ports open a window that averages tens of ms. (2) Exposure is wider than 'needs an OWN_E = 1 exchange'. After an abandon AFTER e, the cells at exchanges with that e sit in M_WANT_B; the drop's break becomes digit 1, and any exchange with b = 1 (21, 31, ...) then claims the re-seizing flood ~130 ms after it arrives, whatever the new caller dials. My one run proves this: work/verify/C03-skeptic-realism/tb_c03b.v and run_b_snap200.log (snapshot, real timers, A's T_REL 200, X = 31, A's T_KEY 2000 only to shorten the sim). A's origin drops at 2630 with X's cell in M_WANT_B. A re-seizes A11 at 2844 for Y's flood, and X claims at 2974, before any digit of Y's. X's register reads Y's e b (2 4) as h s and X24 rings: 3 SAFETY FAILs. (3) Rate is about 2e-4 wrong numbers per exchange per busy hour (~4e-6 per call) in a 10-exchange tree at 500 floods/BH, about 20x finding 1's. It grows as roughly lambda^2 times size: a 20-exchange net at twice the traffic gives a few a week network-wide. The consequence is the same silent wrong number, with conforming subscribers and in-tolerance parts, so its severity should be at least finding 1's: high. The RTL's exact 256 = 256 is why no tree bench met it.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The auditor's two-part fix is right for 74HC and minimal. I agree with the verifier's simplification.

(a) cls_cell is one flip-flop per cell, loaded from m_free1 at w_cls, plus a gate that frees the cell on the C_UNHOLD write. The m_port == cls_port compare is redundant: no w_cls can occur during C_HOLD or C_UNHOLD, and no cell can be freed within about 20 ms.

(b) longbrk = '4040 Q7 (128 ms) AND the '74's M-low, ORed into the cell's existing clear, one gate per cell. It is safe against dialling: the longest conforming break is about 93 ms (7.5 pps at 70%). It closes finding 3's wrong number, including the M_WANT_B variant I ran (the cell would free at drop+128, before the re-seizure at +214; code reading, not re-run on the fix), unless the dropping end's RC is under about 50% of nominal (a gross fault or an aged electrolytic). (a) is still needed, because a re-seizure can follow a C_UNHOLD within 10-128 ms. Cost is about one package, as claimed.

Gaps (none of them should block adopting the fix):
1. Port level (C20). X's port may still hold the old hold when A re-seizes, so the new flood's copy is swallowed at X and relayed down X's old resolver legs. This is a lost call, not a wrong number. The robust cure is at the seizing end: a re-hunt guard for dropped trunks, or an fE RC deliberately slower than fM by more than the spread.
2. RC partial charge. A seizure that dies about 20-35 ms after its rise (past the digital watch, before the RC is fully charged) can release both ports in about 110-195 ms, just before (b)'s 128 ms. That leaves a narrow residual of a fresh classification plus a stale cell. Its rate is negligible.
3. Conflict with C04. The verifier is right that X cannot tell a fast re-seizure from a dial break. C04's own verifier found its trigger needs a non-conforming dial (first break within guard+18 ms). So merge C03's immediate write-away with (a) and (b), do not adopt C04's C_LOW, and count the 18 ms watch in the guard's reach (network.md 6 already lists about 17 ms for a hop delayed by an earlier hold's watch). Fixing both would need per-port re-hunt state at the unit, which costs more than a package.
4. Adjacent issue, outside this cluster and not simulated. The origin's N_DROP at r_gone (the register's digital CLR) and a resolver's R_GONE write can hit a trunk that its own short RC has already released and the forwarder has re-seized (the sweep ignores `mine`), cutting an unrelated flood's leg.
5. The classifier's digital watch (about 20 ms from the rise) should cover the slowest RC arming time. Otherwise a seizure that dies in between leaves a stuck hold until the next seizure's release. That loses one flood copy; low.
skeptics.summary:
All three findings share one real root cause: a monitor cell learns that its seizure has ended only from a digital 256 ms break, while the trunk can be seized again sooner. The two routes are finding 1's short seizure (C_UNHOLD) and finding 3's short release RC at the dropping end.

My main disagreement with the verifier is about realism. On real 74HC hardware, rc-tolerance-reseize is the COMMON route to the wrong number, not the rare one. Any flood dropped before b (hang-up, T_KEY, the guard) crosses every tree link. About half of all ports release before the far cell's exact CLR, because at nominal the margin is only the free-to-rewrite time: about 1-13 ms depending on the trunk's place in the stride-9 sweep. The '14 plus capacitor spread is +-20-35%.

It also reaches more exchanges than the verifier said. I ran one bench (tb_c03b, snapshot, real timers). After an abandon after e, an exchange whose b is 1 (here 31) claimed the next flood re-seizing the channel 130 ms after it arrived, before its caller dialled anything, and rang X24.

Rough rates for a 10-exchange tree at 500 floods per busy hour:
- finding 3: about 2e-4 wrong numbers per exchange per busy hour
- finding 1: about 1e-5 (it needs glare on the last free channel, or a hang-up or glitch within about 20 ms of the seizure)

Both grow steeply with traffic and network size. The subscriber is silently connected to a stranger's line at the wrong exchange; no event is raised anywhere, and it looks like a misdial.

Severities I give:
- finding 1: high (agree)
- finding 2: low (agree; a stale cell costs 256 ms of monitor time against about 1 s for every normal flood)
- finding 3: high (the verifier said medium)

The auditor's fix is right, cheap (about one package) and complete for the wrong number: (a) a flip-flop per cell, the port compare redundant; (b) free the cell on a break of 128 ms or more, one gate per cell. The remaining gaps are:
- the port-level lost call (C20)
- a negligible residual for seizures of about 20-35 ms, where the partly charged RC releases early
- the conflict with C04: keep C03's immediate write-away and fold C04 into the guard budget, since C04 needs a non-conforming dial

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C03-skeptic-realism/: NOTES.md, tb_c03b.v, run1.sh, run_b_snap200.log and vl_b.log.

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real protocol timers, but only with a non-conforming fast dialler. The watch covers T_ARM+2 ms (about 18 ms) after the hold. The failure needs the caller's first break of e to reach an exchange 2-17 ms after that exchange held its incoming trunk. The guard puts that break at least T_GUARD0 after the origin's seizure write, so the exposed exchange is one that holds in the last ~18 ms of the guard. At the 128 ms tap and a ~12-14 ms hop that is hop ~9-10, which is inside new network.md §6's '128 ms covers ~10 typical hops', or ~4-5 hops when loaded (slow hop 22-30 ms). It is outside the old 8-hop rule when hops are unloaded: hop 8 holds at ~100 ms and its watch ends at ~118. Breaks arriving from 128 to ~146 ms after the seizure mean a key-1-to-e pause of ~267-285 ms (651-669 at the 512 tap). ES 201 187 requires at least 720 ms, so a conforming dial's first break comes at least ~580 ms after the seizure. The exchange that would then be exposed holds at 562-578 ms, which is ~45 typical or ~20 slow hops and beyond the documented reach of every tap up to 512. So conforming equipment cannot trigger it in a network sized to its guard. Frequency is the product of (a) a pause inside an ~18 ms band just above the guard's cutoff, (b) an exchange at the edge of the reach, and (c) for a wrong number, (e-1, b) being that exchange's code (a wrong number comes from the second cell's count of e-1; otherwise the call is only lost). The auditor's 'medium' comes from scale 8, where 3 of 4 offsets fail because the unscaled sweep puts hop 2 at the guard's edge. In effect the bug shrinks the guard's reach by ~18 ms, as the auditor's 'realistic' note says.

(2) tb_brk_rt.v, which is tb_brk with REAL timers: T_ARM 16, T_REL 256, HIT 8, ID 128, CLR 256, NODIG 10000, T_KEY 5000, T_CLAIM 2000, dial 60/40, 800 ms pauses, wait for the register before dialling. Only the guard is lowered to 16 ms, so that C (hop 2) is the exchange at the guard's edge; C's local timing is the same as hop ~9-10's at the 128 tap. Offsets 2, 10, 17, 26, 60 ms.
