findings.evidence: The mechanism holds line by line in the snapshot. net_unit.v:584-588: C_HOLD goes to C_UNHOLD on any sample of M low while cls_ms <= T_ARM+1, with no test of how long it stays low. 566-567: st[port] is cleared by any M-low sample. 590-594: the unhold writes bsy=0 and sets f_cancel. port.v:147: BUSY = bsy|fe|(fm&!m), so at the make BUSY=0 with M=1, and cls_seen (283-284) takes the port again. That gives a second hold and a second cell (612-615). The unhold does not release the first cell. No guard stops any of this. At REAL timers on the snapshot (run_brkrt_snap.log), off 2 and off 10 are wrong numbers. off 10: '[6586] C HOLD 11 (tmr 17)', '[6597] C UNHOLD 11 (tmr 28)', '[6658] C HOLD 11 (tmr 89)', 'cell 0 counts 3', 'cell 1 counts 2', 'cell 1 counts 4', 'C CLAIMS 11', 'C21 hi 142'. off 17 (the break reaches C at the end of its watch), 26 and 60 are clean. Result: 'wrong-number attempts 2 of 5', FAIL. The run also shows a mode the auditor did not report. At off 2, B (hop 1, still in its own watch at the lowered guard) unheld too ('[570] B UNHOLD 11'). Its resolver sees the incoming port BUSY-clear at the make (R_GONE, net_unit.v:688-689) and drops the leg to C. B's re-classification then floods C again after pulse 1 ('C HOLD tmr 94', 16 ms after the make), and C claims on e-1. So a mid-path exchange inside the band re-floods downstream late, or kills the flood if its forwarder is busy. This changes how the call fails, not who is exposed: downstream exchanges hold later still, so they are already in the band or past the guard. The bench stimulus is legitimate: a live dial break on a trunk that was just seized. The only artificial part is the lowered guard, which moves the edge to hop 2 for a 3-site bench.
findings.notes: One root cause. The watch cannot tell a dial break from a death. new network.md §6's guard budget ('every transit's hop, the last exchange's monitor attaching') leaves out the last exchange's own T_ARM watch, so the RTL does not honour the documented reach. Unverified lead: a single 1 ms A dropout (link noise or bit error) inside a watch also unholds. The re-hold then sees a rise before e, so both cells count correctly, and a double CLAIM/att on one trunk could follow at the owner. Not run.

verifier.root_cause: The classifier cannot tell a dial break from a dead seizure. net_unit.v:584-588 (C_HOLD) writes the hold away on any M-low sample within T_ARM+2 ms of the hold. That clears bsy (590-594), and st[port] is cleared on any M-low sample (566-567). At the make M=1 and BUSY=0 (port.v:147), so cls_seen (283-284) takes it as a new seizure and attaches a second cell after pulse 1, which counts e-1. At a transit, the same BUSY-clear make also trips the resolver (688-689) and makes it re-flood late. On the document side, network.md §6's guard budget stops at the last monitor attaching and leaves out the last exchange's ~18 ms watch.
verifier.best_fix: The auditor's C_LOW state, with two changes. Tested on work/verify/C04-hold-watch-dial-break/fix/net_unit.v; diff in fix/net_unit.diff. (1) When M comes back up in C_LOW, go back to C_HOLD with cls_ms reset, not to C_IDLE. The watch then restarts from the make, so a short make followed by a real death is still caught. It costs nothing extra. (2) Call it a death at CLR (256 ms) rather than ID. network.md lets a carrier lengthen a break up to the 256 ms that means hang-up, CLR matches the port's own T_REL and the monitor's 256 ms release, and ID is enough only for breaks that are not lengthened (+lowid knob, not run). The cost is one state and a compare on the existing cls_ms. The classifier is held for up to CLR only when a hold's M falls inside its watch: a dial break (~60 ms, then 18 ms more) or a real death (glare, a guard abandonment). Rises seen meanwhile stay in st and are read later, which only matters to callers who dial faster than the standard allows. Bigger alternative: the cls auditor's fix (work/audit/cls/fix/net_unit.v) moves the watch onto 4 watchers with a CLR low-streak test and does not hold up the classifier. It also closes C04 (tb_brk 7/7) but is far larger. Cheapest option, with no hardware: add T_ARM+2 (~18 ms) to network.md §6's guard budget, i.e. reach = (tap - ~21 ms)/hop, about 8-9 typical or 3-4 slow hops at 128 ms. That makes the band unreachable in a network sized to its guard, but the RTL change is small and keeps the documented reach.
verifier.fix_tested: On the C_LOW fix copy (CLR threshold): tb_brk passed 7/7 with 0 of 5 wrong numbers, C unholds 0 and one cell per attempt (was 3 of 5 and FAIL on the snapshot). tb_net passed 88/88; scenario 7 (a seizure that dies inside the watch has its hold cleared) still passes. tb_chain passed 32/32, the same as base-chain. Logs: work/verify/C04-hold-watch-dial-break/run_brk_fix.log, run_net_fix.log, run_chain_fix.log. The cls auditor's fix also passes tb_brk 7/7 (run_brk_clsfix.log). The fix has not been run at real timers, where B's mid-path unhold happens. That run was queued and got no slot. By RTL reading the fix covers it, because the hold stays BUSY through the break so the resolver's R_GONE never fires.
verifier.summary: The finding is real and reproduces at real protocol timers, but it is overstated. On the snapshot RTL, a dial break that reaches an exchange within ~2-17 ms of its hold is written away as a death. The make is then taken as a new seizure, and a second monitor counts e-1 and can claim a wrong number: 2 of 5 offsets at real T_ARM, with C21 rung for 1 3 4 2 1. At a transit the same event also drops and re-floods the forward late, which the auditor did not report. The trigger needs a caller whose pause from key 1 to e is ~267-285 ms at the 128 ms tap, below ES 201 187's 720 ms minimum, and an exchange holding in the last ~18 ms of the guard (hop ~9-10 unloaded, 4-5 loaded). Conforming dials cannot reach it in a network sized to its guard. The guard's real reach is ~18 ms shorter than network.md §6 claims. Severity is low rather than medium. There is one root cause. A C_LOW state that waits out a break before writing the hold away closes it at one state's cost; tested on tb_brk, tb_net and tb_chain.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: re-derive each step from the snapshot RTL, look for a condition that blocks it, and look for a second path the auditor and verifier missed. One short run was used for the second path.

per_finding.reason: MECHANISM, re-derived line by line on the snapshot. Nothing blocks it. (1) net_unit.v:584-588: C_HOLD goes to C_UNHOLD on one probe sample of M low while cls_ms<=T_ARM+1. There is no filtering at all, unlike every other consumer of M (pulse_rx HIT 8 ms; the port's T_ARM/T_REL detectors). exchange/network.md §3.3 specifies exactly that ('if M falls writes the hold away'), so the flaw is in the rule itself, not only in the RTL. (2) 590-594: the unhold writes ent(port,P00,0,0) and sets f_cancel only if the forwarder is busy with this port. It does NOT release the port's monitor cell. (3) 566-567: any M-low sample clears st[port]. (4) port.v:147: BUSY=bsy|fe|(fm&!m) is 0 at the make whether or not fm had risen: with fm=0 all terms are 0, and with fm=1 the fm&!m term is 0 once M is up. So cls_seen (283-284) takes the port again, and a second cell (612-615) attaches after pulse 1. The auditor's '(e-1,b)' is wrong for e=1: pulse_rx never strobes a zero count (dig_stb needs cnt!=0), so the late cell reads b as e and h as b, and the wrong claim needs (b,h)=own code. REAL-TIMER REPRODUCTION: I agree with the verifier's run_brkrt_snap.log (wrong number at off 2 and off 10, clean from off 17 on). DETAIL THE VERIFIER GOT SLIGHTLY WRONG: in the mid-path mode, R_GONE (688-689) tests only !sp_busy. If the transit's fm has not risen yet, BUSY is already 0 during the break, once the unhold lands, so the leg is dropped in the break rather than at the make. The outcome is the same. REACH, SMALL REFINEMENT: the guard abandons on 'guarding && r_brk' (862), and r_brk is the register's count at HIT. So a break that starts up to ~8 ms before t_guard passes the guard. The early side of the band widens by ~HIT: pauses of ~259-285 ms, not 267-285. The break's own ~1 ms-per-hop lag roughly offsets this at hop 8, so the conclusion stands. SEVERITY FOR THE CLAIM AS STATED: low. With conforming dials (720 ms or more), the first break comes 580 ms or more after the seizure, and no exchange in a network sized to its guard holds that late. SECOND PATH THE AUDITOR AND VERIFIER MISSED, reached with conforming equipment and one plausible fault. A single ~1 ms A dropout on a link (a bit error or a link hiccup at the port's sampling instant) inside a transit's watch goes through the same C_HOLD code. I ran it once: skeptic-mech/tb_drop.v on plain work/RTL.list, with real timers, the real 128 ms guard and 800 ms pauses; log skeptic-mech/run_drop.log. Dropout 2 ms into B's watch: 'B UNHOLD tmr 6', then 'B HOLD tmr 8 (fst 2)', B n_nofwd +1, 'C holds 0', nobody claims. The re-hold finds the forwarder still in F_HUNT, so it does not forward, and f_cancel stays set and kills the first sweep. The flood dies at B: a silent lost call (A gives cannot-complete after its 2 s claim wait). The control on the same bench (no dropout) was claimed by C. A dropout that lands on B's forward write (cls_ms 11) just re-floods 14 ms late and does no harm; C then counted right. By reading only (not reproduced), a dropout in the last ~4 ms of B's watch, after the next hop C has held, would drop and re-seize B's leg ~12 ms later. That gap is at least HIT, so C's held cells would read a spurious digit '1' (wrong claim if C's code is (1,e)). A dropout at the owner would give two good cells and a second CLAIM/att while the register is busy. The consequence confirmed on this path is a lost call, not a wrong number, and it needs a link error inside an ~11-18 ms window, so it does not raise the severity. It does rule out the doc-only fix.

skeptics.fix_assessment: The verifier's C_LOW fix is correct and close to minimal, and I endorse it over both alternatives, with caveats. (a) By reading, it closes both triggers. On a dial break or a single-sample dropout, M-low goes to C_LOW, which writes nothing, cancels nothing and keeps bsy up, so st is set again at the make and R_GONE never fires. M up then returns to C_HOLD with the watch restarted. I did not run it on tb_drop: the one allowed run went on showing the dropout path on the snapshot. (b) Its change (1) over the auditor's version is needed. Going to C_IDLE on the make, as the auditor proposed, leaves a short make followed by a real death with no edge to clear the hold. (c) CLR is the right threshold, better than ID. It matches mini_marker S_WATCH, which waits for r_gone (CLR) on its own watch, and it matches the monitor cell's own CLR. The unhold and the cell's release then fall together, which also removes a sibling in the snapshot: the unhold never frees the cell, so a stale cell can count the gap before a quick re-seizure as a digit '1'. (d) Costs to document. The classifier is stalled for up to 256 ms after a genuine death inside a watch (cls_seen needs C_IDLE). Such deaths need a guard abandonment or a hang-up within ~18 ms of a hold, so they are rare. Seizures arriving meanwhile are delayed, not lost, but that delay is bigger than the whole 128 ms guard budget for any flood passing then. network.md §3.3 ('one each 18 ms') and §6 need a sentence on it. Also, C_LOW takes ANY rise within CLR as the make, including a new seizure after a death. That would be merged, with no fresh cell or forward. The far end's own fe/fm hold-off makes that almost unreachable. (e) The doc-only alternative (add ~18 ms to the §6 guard budget) is NOT sufficient. It does nothing for the single-sample dropout path, which does not depend on the guard and is confirmed to lose the call. So the RTL change is needed, not optional. (f) The cls auditor's multi-watcher fix also works and avoids the stall, but it is much larger. Prefer it only if the stall in (d) is judged unacceptable. (g) Change network.md §3.3's rule to 'M down for CLR'. Separately, §6's 'a break inside the guard' is measured at the count, HIT after the break starts: a small mismatch that belongs to another finding, not a blocker.
skeptics.summary: The finding is real and happens as claimed. On the snapshot, one sample of M low inside the T_ARM+2 watch writes the hold away (net_unit.v:584-594). The make then shows M up with BUSY clear (port.v:147), and the classifier takes the port again (283-284, 566-567), so a second cell attached after pulse 1 counts e-1, or (b,h) when e=1. I agree with the verifier: confirmed, overstated, low. The dial-break trigger needs a non-conforming ~259-285 ms pause and an exchange holding at the edge of the guard, and the verifier's real-timer run reproduces it. Small corrections to the verifier: at a transit, R_GONE can fire during the break rather than at the make, and the guard lets a break start up to HIT before t_guard. Neither changes the verdict. New: the same watch fires on a single ~1 ms A dropout on a link, with conforming dialling. My one run (work/verify/C04-hold-watch-dial-break/skeptic-mech/run_drop.log; bench tb_drop.v, notes NOTES.md) shows a dropout 2 ms into a transit's watch killing the flood: B re-held with its forwarder still sweeping, so it did not forward, n_nofwd +1, and C was never seized, so the call was lost. A wrong-number variant (the next hop reading a spurious '1' from the leg being dropped and re-seized) is plausible by reading but was not reproduced. My run's dropout fell before C had held, and the re-forward was then clean. Severity stays low, since the confirmed conforming path gives a lost call from a rare link fault. But it rules out the doc-only fix. The verifier's C_LOW state (M up returns to C_HOLD, death at CLR) is the right fix. Document its up-to-256 ms classifier stall after a genuine death inside a watch.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity (real timers, real telephones, real cards, plausible faults); fix fitness for 74HC

per_finding.reason:
MECHANISM: real, and the explanation is right. I checked it line by line in the snapshot.
- net_unit.v:584-588: C_HOLD unholds on any single M-low sample.
- 566-567: that sample clears st.
- 590-594: the unhold writes bsy=0.
- port.v:147: BUSY=bsy|fe|(fm&!m) is 0 at the make, whether or not fM had armed.
- cls_seen then gives a second hold and a second cell after pulse 1, and the first cell is never released.
The verifier's real-timer run (run_brkrt_snap.log: off 2 and off 10 ring C21, off 17/26/60 clean) is a fair emulation. Lowering the guard only moves the edge to hop 2; C's local timing is untouched. B's unhold at off 2 is an artefact of the 16 ms guard, which the verifier says.

Small corrections:
- The window runs from the rise, not the hold. A break landing during C_READ/C_ACT is still low at the first C_HOLD sample.
- For e=1 the second cell counts b as e, so the wrong-number condition is (b,h)=X, not (e-1,b). e=0 gives 9 pulses, which is vacant, so it never misroutes.
- With NMON=2 the double hold takes both cells of the exposed exchange for about a second.

REALISM: I agree it is overstated, with one qualification the verifier missed. "Conforming dials cannot reach it" holds for automatic pulse dialers. ES 201 187 requires 720 ms, and Joel's own su-1, hotline card and pulse-gen all use 700 ms, above the 669 ms top of the band at every tap up to 512. A hand-wound rotary dial, however, pauses as long as the user does; no equipment enforces 720. The band is tap+139..tap+156:
- At 128 (267-285 ms) it is at or below a dial's mechanical floor after the digit 1, so essentially never.
- At 256 (395-413) it takes a very fast dialler.
- At 512 (651-669) it is ordinary brisk rotary dialling. But a 512 network is about 40 typical hops deep, and that tap already abandons around 10% of rotary calls. Nobody builds it.

The second condition is an exchange holding in the last ~17 ms before the break reaches it:
- In a network planned to network.md §6's slow case (4-5 hops at 128), this needs nearly every hop at its slow maximum: about 1e-3 to 1e-4.
- In a network built out to the table's '10 typical hops' it is routine.

FREQUENCY: rough, assuming 50 inter-exchange calls/BH per exchange and N=10 codes.
- 128 tap, slow-case plan, any phones: below 1e-5 wrong numbers per exchange per busy hour (never).
- 128 tap built to 10 hops, rotary: about 1e-3/BH, one per roughly 400-1000 busy hours per exchange. At that rate it is dwarfed by the guard's own clean abandonments of slightly faster callers.

SUBSCRIBER: silence until the connect, then ringback and a stranger at h s of (e-1,b), with no warning.
- If the dialled code also exists, both owners claim and the first claim back wins.
- If (e-1,b) has no line h s, that exchange's marker gives a tone.
- If the exposed exchange is a transit, the call is lost (cannot-complete after the 2 s or 5 s rule) or is wrong downstream.

SEVERITY: low is right. It is a genuine silent wrong number, but only 18 ms beyond C05's reach edge (the same failure class) and outside every conforming configuration. The real defect is network.md §6's reach table, which leaves out the destination's own ~18 ms watch.

The auditor's 'medium' is a scale-8 artefact: the unscaled sweep puts hop 2 at the guard's edge.

The verifier's unverified lead (a 1 ms A dropout, hit or bounce inside a watch):
- No wrong number: both cells see the rise.
- At a transit mid-sweep, the re-hold finds fst!=F_IDLE, so it is not forwarded, and f_cancel kills the first forward. The flood dies there: a clean cannot-complete beyond.
- At the owner, two cells claim, giving two att on one trunk; the effect at the marker is unknown.
- Negligible on digital links. The fix covers it.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's C_LOW fix is the right fix for 74HC. It is minimal and correct for the finding.

Why it fits:
- It costs almost nothing. cst's code 6 is unused, the cls_ms counter and its clear already exist, and cls_ms>=256 is cls_ms[8], a wire.
- Restarting the watch at the make is necessary, so that fM arms under the watch and a real death after a short make is still caught.
- CLR is a better threshold than the auditor's ID, because network.md §2 lets a carrier lengthen a break up to just under 256 ms.
- Keeping bsy through the break means no R_GONE and no f_cancel, so the mid-path re-flood mode is closed too. I agree with that by reading the code; I did not run it.
- It also closes the hit, bounce and dropout variants.
- It incidentally sidesteps C09's F_WRITE/f_cancel race for deaths inside the watch: the unhold now comes 256 ms later, when fst is idle.

It is not free of side effects:

(1) The classifier stalls: about 80-120 ms per dial-break event (a whole digit at 20 pps) and 256 ms per real death in the watch (guard abandonments, glare drops, blips). Other calls' seizures wait meanwhile.
- At the 128 and 256 taps this is harmless for 720 ms callers (slack about 450 and 325 ms).
- At 512 the slack is only about 68 ms. A 256 ms stall at a deep exchange can push another conforming call's hold past its first break. So the verifier's 'only matters to callers faster than the standard' holds only up to the 256 tap.
- The stall also runs against C05's recommendation to take the watch off the classifier.

(2) New blind spot: a rise inside C_LOW is taken as the make of the same call.
- The far end can re-seize the channel within CLR when it dropped it before its fE armed: a glare drop, or C03's trigger 2.
- Then the new flood gets no cell and no forward at X, and the old stale cell miscounts it. C03's wrong number persists.
- Rare on rare, but C03 and C04 should be fixed together.

(3) Not covered: a second copy of the same flood that reaches X during the watch is still classified after the break and counts e-1. That is C05.

Better option if C05's direction is taken: put the C_LOW logic in a one-entry watch register beside the classifier, so the classifier never stalls. Or let the attached cell's existing 256 ms CLR write away a hold that never armed, and keep a watch only for seizures that got no cell.

The docs-only alternative (add about 18 ms to §6's guard budget) closes the wrong-number mode in a network sized to the corrected guard, but not the transit, glitch or double-att modes. With the RTL fix that extra budget term is not needed for C04, though C05's re-budget still is.
skeptics.summary:
The finding is real and correctly explained, and I agree with the verifier: confirmed but overstated, severity low. It is a genuine silent wrong number, but in any conforming configuration it amounts to C05's reach edge moved about 18 ms.

The trigger needs two things together:
- The caller's key-1-to-e pause must fall within about 17 ms above the guard's abandonment cutoff: 267-285 ms at 128, 395-413 at 256, 651-669 at 512.
- Some exchange must hold in the last ~17 ms before the break reaches it.

Automatic dialers never reach it: ES 201 187 requires 720 ms, and Joel's su-1, hotline card and pulse-gen use 700 ms. Where I differ from the verifier: hand-wound rotary dials are not bound by 720. At 512 the band is ordinary brisk dialling, but only in a roughly 40-hop network nobody builds; at 128 it is at or below a dial's mechanical floor.

Rough rates: never in a 128 ms network planned to the slow case. About 1e-3 per exchange per busy hour in a network built out to the documented 10 typical hops with rotary users, far below the guard's own clean abandonments. The underlying defect is network.md §6's reach table, which leaves out the destination's own ~18 ms watch.

The C_LOW fix (CLR threshold, watch restarted at the make) is right, almost free in 74HC, and closes the dial-break, hit, dropout and transit re-flood modes. Its caveats:
- The classifier stalls up to 256 ms. That eats the 512 tap's roughly 68 ms slack for other conforming calls.
- A far-end re-seizure inside C_LOW is taken as a make, which interacts with C03; fix the two together.
- It does not cover a second flood copy arriving during the watch (C05).

No simulation was run. My notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C04-hold-watch-dial-break/skeptic-realism/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: The failure happens at real timers, but only with a dialler that does not conform to ES 201 187. For the wrong number, the first break of e has to reach the exchange whose code is (e-1, b) within about 20 ms of the flood's rise there, and the origin allows no break earlier than 120 ms after its seizure. So that exchange has to be at least ~100 ms of flood away: about 9 links on the nominal 12-14 ms hop, or 7-8 with one loaded transit. On the 128 ms tap the caller's key-to-e pause has to fall in a narrow band of about 259-280 ms (387-407 ms on the 256 tap, 643-663 ms on the 512 tap). A conforming pause of 720 ms or more puts the first break at least 581 ms after the seizure, which cannot be reached inside any tap up to 512. The design does expect fast diallers: the guard abandons anyone under about 267 ms and promises never a wrong number. That promise is broken here, silently. Variant (b), the busy classifier, is a different mechanism (finding 2).

verifier.root_cause:
One root cause shows up two ways: the T_ARM hold watch lives inside the classifier.

1. It cannot tell a dial break from a dying seizure. C_HOLD (net_unit.v:584-588) writes the hold away on any M-low sample within 18 ticks of the hold push (590-594). M-low clears st (566-567), and at the make the port shows M with BUSY clear (port.v:147). So cls_seen (net_unit.v:283-284) re-takes the port as a fresh seizure mid-digit: a second cell (612-615), R_GONE (688-689), and a mid-digit re-forward (616-621). This is finding 1, and it is the same root as C04.
2. It blocks the classifier. cls_seen needs cst == C_IDLE (283), so every trunk seizure blocks it for about 18 ms. The result is late pickups and slow hops (finding 2).

Finding 3 is the guard-budget arithmetic that follows from both.
verifier.best_fix:
**Minimal fix, tested: C_LOW.** In C_HOLD an M-low sample moves to a new state C_LOW (value 6 of cst) and writes nothing. In C_LOW:
- M back up returns to C_HOLD with cls_ms reset, so the watch starts again from the make and the hold stands.
- M low for ID (128 ms) goes to C_UNHOLD, as before.

It costs no packages: one more state on cst and a compare on the existing cls_ms. The copy is work/verify/C05-late-flood-guard-reach/rtl_fix/net_unit.v. It closes the watch-misread in both regimes: port already armed (d112) and not yet armed (d124). It also closes the second seizure's watch case (l1 d104). tb_net stays at 88/88, including scenarios 7 and 14, where a seizure dies inside T_ARM.

- **Its cost:** when a seizure really dies inside the watch (a far guard abandon at the flood front, a blip, an outage), the classifier is busy 128 ms before it writes the hold away; the snapshot writes it away at once. That is rare.
- **What it leaves open:** a flood that the busy classifier first sees at the make, after its first break (l1 d112 still FAILS).

**Fuller fix, also tested: the cls slice's.** It moves the watch off the classifier and queues rises with their lateness. That closes l1 d112 as well; the cls slice's own tb_net is 88/88. But it costs 4 watchers, a rise queue and a second 64-stage delay line. A cheaper stopgap for the late pickup is the rule-1 lateness bit alone (8 x '164): a late pickup gets no cell, so the wrong number becomes a lost call.

**Against the auditor's list:**
- Fix 1 (no re-seize for 256 ms, about 3 packages) stops B's wrong number but drops the flood beyond B.
- Fix 2 (time the watch from the rise) only narrows the window; d124 fails anyway.
- Fixes 3 and 4 only give back reach.

**Doc:** with C_LOW, network.md 6's figures stand. Without it, add about 18 ms for the destination watch.

**Warning:** do not apply the monclaim slice's fix (a), which frees the cell at C_UNHOLD, without C_LOW. In this scenario it frees the correct cell.

verifier.summary:
All three findings are real, but overstated. They share one root cause, the T_ARM hold watch living inside the classifier, which is also C04's.

- **Finding 1 (late-flood-truncated-count).** Reproduced exactly: my snapshot re-run matches the auditor's log line for line. It is broader than reported: a flood reaching an exchange only 5 ms before the first break also gives a wrong number, although the documents' model says the monitor, attached at 1.8 ms, saw the rise. The watch takes about 20 ms of the destination's guard budget and re-seizes the trunk mid-digit, both at that exchange and in its re-forward downstream. It needs a dialler that does not conform to ES 201 187: a key-to-e pause of about 259-280 ms on the 128 ms tap, with the exchange whose code is (e-1, b) at least ~9 nominal links away. A conforming dial cannot reach it at any tap up to 512. Severity medium, not high.
- **Finding 2 (classifier-hold-serialises).** The 18 ms-per-seizure serialisation is confirmed, and a busy classifier can produce a wrong number from a late cell. But today's network.md and decisions.md already document it and budget ≈20 ms for it. What stays undocumented is bursts of three or more, and the fact that the snapshot needs about 38 ms for the second seizure rather than 20. Severity low.
- **Finding 3 (guard-reach).** The hop figures are right, but the mismatch it reports is against superseded documents; the rewrite adopted the same numbers. The one gap left is that network.md 6 does not count the destination's own watch, about 18 ms. Severity low.

**Fix.** A zero-package C_LOW state (M low in the watch writes nothing; M back re-arms the watch; M low for 128 ms writes the hold away) closes finding 1 and the second-seizure case, and keeps tb_net at 88/88. It does not close the busy-classifier late pickup. The cls slice's heavier fix, which moves the watch off the classifier, closes that too (tested).

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: I re-derived each mechanism from the snapshot RTL, looked for conditions that block it, and looked for second paths the auditors and verifier missed. I did one sim, to settle a disagreement about the verifier's proposed stopgap.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived it independently and it is exactly as claimed.
- C_HOLD (net_unit.v:584-588) runs 18 tick_1k after the hold push, i.e. about rise+1.8 to rise+19.8 ms. Any M-low sample sends it to C_UNHOLD, which writes bsy 0 (590-594).
- M-low samples clear st (566-567).
- port.v:147: busy = bsy|fe|(fm&!m), with fe=0 because the port listens to unfitted 00. So at the make BUSY is 0. On that same probe sample, cls_seen (283-284) re-takes the port and R_GONE (688-689) drops the first forward.
- The second cell arms after pulse 1 (pulse_rx.v:72-90).
- I checked the verifier's d124 and l1 d104 logs; the timings match (unhold 35.68 / 56.68, forward cancel 42.0 / 61.0, re-seize 96.5 / 117.5).

Things that block it:
- NMON exhausted (no second cell; l1 d104).
- The forwarder busy (no re-forward).
Nothing else does.

What the verifier's victim set misses:
- When e = 1 the re-seized cell arms after e's only break. pulse_rx gives no digit for cnt 0, so the cell counts b as e and h as b. The victim is exchange (b, h), not (e-1, b); the same holds downstream of the mid-digit re-forward. When e = 0 the count is 9, which is isvc, so the call is lost rather than misrouted.
- A misreading transit also loses the true owner beyond it: the first forward is dropped at the make, and the re-forward carries e-1. The C04 verifier noted this; in a tree the victim set is unchanged.

Small point: the bench injects the break at B directly. The fix log shows the relayed break lags about 0.4 ms per transit (47.389 against 47.0), which is immaterial to the depth arithmetic.

The verifier's real-timing envelope is correct:
- A 259-280 ms key-to-e pause on the 128 ms tap.
- The exposed exchange at 100 ms or more of flood.
- A conforming dialler can never reach it: the first break comes 581 ms or more after the seizure.

Medium (not the auditor's high) is right. It is a silent wrong number that breaks the guard's promise to fast diallers, but it needs a non-conforming dial at the network's reach edge.

The serialisation is real: cls_seen needs C_IDLE, and C_HOLD takes 18 ticks. The late-pickup wrong number is real: l1 d112, which C_LOW does not close.

The verifier's model is FIFO ('the k-th seizure waits 19(k-1)'). It is not FIFO.
- C_HOLD always leaves one clock after tick_1k, which is scan 00. The first cls_seen chance after that is port 00, then 01, and so on (the sample of 63 is missed while cst is still C_HOLD).
- So the lowest-numbered waiting port is taken first, and a high-numbered trunk can be overtaken without bound by lower ones that rise later.
- The cls slice measured this at real timers: work/audit/cls/run_c3_sc7.log, where 47 waited 188 ms behind 11-16 and gave a wrong number with POOL8.

The new network.md is not fully cleared either:
- 3.3 says 'a missed rise is read later' with no bound.
- 3.4 rule 1 says 'up to 20 ms'.
- In l1 d112 the port is first taken on the make after a dial break, so its cell counts a seizure whose rise it did not see. Rule 1 is violated as written today.

Severity stays low on the snapshot's NMON=NRES=2 stuffing. A burst of three or more normally exhausts the cells and resolvers, so the harmful case is essentially one seizure ahead plus a fast dialler. The exposure rises with the larger pools network.md 10 contemplates.

The hop figures are right. I re-derived 1.8 + 0-1 + 9 + 1 + 0.3-0.7 + 0-1, about 12-14 ms, and the fix log shows the first leg's far M 12.385 ms after the rise.

The spec complaints are against figures that today's decisions.md (406-415) retires; network.md 6 now says about 12 ms typical and 22-30 slow.

One real gap remains. Section 6 budgets 'the last exchange's monitor attaching' (2-3.5 ms), but on the snapshot the last exchange needs its whole watch: about 20 ms, or about 38 ms behind a busy classifier. So the 128 ms tap covers about 9 or 8 typical hops (6 behind a busy classifier), not 10.

With C_LOW, the destination needs only its first M-up sample (about 1 ms): a cell that arms mid-break still counts that break if HIT of it remains. The documented figures then hold.

The snapshot's own header comment (net_unit.v:52-56, 'at 9 ms it covers about ten') confuses the 9 ms sweep with the ~12 ms hop.

This is budget arithmetic that follows from findings 1 and 2. Low.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
**C_LOW is the right minimal fix for finding 1 (and for C04).**
- It closes the watch misread whether the port is armed (d112) or not (d124), and the second seizure's own watch (l1 d104).
- It costs no packages, and tb_net stays at 88/88.

**Two corrections to it.**
1. Use CLR (256 ms), not ID (128), as the threshold for calling a low a death, as the C04 verifier's copy does. With ID, a 128-256 ms low inside the watch is written away at 128. If fm is armed, the port shows M with BUSY clear when M returns, and the same re-seize happens. Such a low is a C07-class link outage, which every cell and register already counts as one pulse. CLR matches pulse_rx's own boundary between a pulse and a release, and the port's T_REL.
2. Its cost is not simply "rare". A real death inside the watch now keeps the classifier busy for ID or CLR, where the snapshot kept it busy for 0 ms. That happens at every exchange at the flood front of every call the guard abandons, which is the same fast-dialler population. Other floods reaching that exchange then wait up to about 150-275 ms, and in scan order. That widens finding 2's late-pickup exposure for other fast callers. Conforming callers stay safe, since their first break comes at least 581 ms after the seizure. A one-entry low-watch register beside the classifier (about 3 packages) removes this cost.

**The verifier's "cheaper stopgap" is wrong, and my one run settles it.** The stopgap is the rule-1 lateness bit alone ("M at the last visit"; a late pickup gets no cell).
- The run is `work/verify/C05-late-flood-guard-reach/skeptic-mechanism/run_late_sc6_l1_d112.log`: the snapshot plus only that bit, tb_fx sc6 l1 d112, real timers.
- Result: '109.514 SKEPTIC hold 30 late 0 -> cell', CLAIM at 1437, B21 rung, FAIL 2. That is identical to the snapshot.
- Why: the harmful pickup happens at the make's first visit, when M was low at the last visit, so the bit reads it as a fresh rise.
- The bit marks late only the pickups made inside a make that has stood a pass. Those are the harmless initial-make pickups; for example, in l1 d104 E30 is taken 19.8 ms after its rise with M up throughout.
- So it closes nothing, and it takes the cell away from the second seizure of every coincidence. Where that exchange is the owner, the call is lost.
- The auditor's rule-1 half has the same hole. The cls slice's fix closes l1 d112 through its rise queue and its watchers off the classifier, not through its own late bit.

**What would close the late pickup.**
- Move the watch off the classifier: a 2-entry watcher list that times lows with CLR, which also absorbs C_LOW and removes its classifier-blocking cost. A second seizure is then read about 1-2 ms after its rise. The rise queue is optional at the snapshot's burst rates.
- The cls slice's zero-gate F4' (st set on any BUSY sample, including fm·/M; cleared only on M low with BUSY low) turns l1 d112 into a lost copy. It only covers the case where the first break comes at least 16 ms after the rise, because an unarmed fm shows no BUSY during the break.

**Doc.**
- network.md 3.3 ("a missed rise is read later") and 3.4 rule 1 ("up to 20 ms") need the scan-order and burst facts.
- network.md 6 needs the destination's own watch unless the RTL fix goes in.

**Warning.** The same end mechanism (st cleared by a dial break, then the make taken as a fresh seizure) has triggers that are not late floods. None of the fixes above except F4' touch them:
- cls sc3: a hit during the word read leaves the trunk unheld. This can happen at any depth and with conforming dialling.
- The called party hanging up first (cls o6 sc6).
skeptics.summary:
All three findings are real and correctly explained, and I agree with the verifier's verdicts and severities: medium, low, low. I rebuilt finding 1's mechanism line by line from the snapshot RTL. The only things that block it are NMON exhaustion and a busy forwarder.

**What the verifier missed:**
1. **Victim set.** When e = 1, the re-seized cell counts b as e and h as b, so the victim is exchange (b, h), not (e-1, b). The mid-digit re-forward downstream does the same.
2. **The classifier is not first-come-first-served.** C_HOLD always ends at scan 00, so the lowest-numbered waiting port is taken next. A high-numbered trunk can be overtaken without bound; the cls slice measured a 188 ms wait and a wrong number (run_c3_sc7.log). So "the k-th seizure waits 19(k-1) ms" understates the wait, and network.md's new "up to 20 ms" and "a missed rise is read later" are still wrong.
3. **The recommended cheap stopgap does not work.** I tested the rule-1 lateness bit alone with my one run on sc6 l1 d112 (work/verify/C05-late-flood-guard-reach/skeptic-mechanism/run_late_sc6_l1_d112.log). The late pickup happens at the first sample of the make, where M was low at the previous visit, so the bit reads it as a fresh rise. The cell is still given, and the claim and B21 ring happen exactly as on the snapshot (FAIL 2). The bit only denies cells to harmless pickups made inside the first make, which would lose the second seizure of every coincidence as owner.

**The C_LOW fix.** It is the right minimal fix for finding 1 and C04, with two changes:
- Use CLR (256 ms), not ID, as the death threshold. With ID, a 128-256 ms outage inside the watch re-opens the same mechanism.
- Its cost is that on a real death inside the watch the classifier stays busy for ID or CLR, where the snapshot held it for 0 ms. That happens at every flood-front exchange of every call the guard abandons, which widens finding 2 for other fast callers. A small watcher list off the classifier removes that cost and also closes the late pickup.

Notes are in work/verify/C05-late-flood-guard-reach/skeptic-mechanism/NOTES.md.

The mechanism is real. I re-read net_unit.v:283, 566-567, 584-594 and 862 and the verifier's logs: snap d112 and d124 FAIL, d108 PASS; the fix passes d112, d124 and l1 d104; tb_net on the fix is 88/0.

The verifier's arithmetic is right:
- The exchange that misreads needs a flood-processing delay D >= ~100 ms on the 128 ms tap, because the break must land within ~20 ms of its rise and the origin allows no break before push+120.
- Carrier delay does not count toward D (network.md 2).
- A conforming caller (720 ms or more) cannot reach it at any tap up to 512.

Medium is right, not high. The failure is a silent wrong number, and it breaks an invariant the design states in so many words: analysis/monitor-rules.md 5 says 'Both rules: none, at any pause a pulse register can read', and names 'a worn dial, a non-conforming instrument or an operator's practised hand' as the callers the guard exists for. The fix costs nothing. But the verifier leaves out four realism reductions.

(1) Planning. Today's network.md 6 says 'the guard must cover the slow case', which means about 4-5 hops on the 128 tap. The deepest typical D is then about 60 ms. Reaching 100 ms needs two or three independent slow transits on one path.
- At the reference load of about 0.07 floods/s per exchange (0.19 E over a 2.7 s hold, network.md 10), a transit is slow for about 0.13% of floods.
- A convoy waits only once. The second flood then trails by about 20.6 ms and clears the next watches.
- So in a network planned to today's document the rate is effectively zero. It is live only in a network planned on the typical hop (about 10 hops on 128). The net_unit.v:55 comment ('covers about ten') and topology.md's older shapes still invite that plan.

(2) Who dials in the band. The 128-tap band is 259-280 ms after a '1'. A rotary dial's lost motion plus the wind to hole e puts that about at or past the limit of a human hand. Joel's own diallers pause 700 ms and are safe at every tap: the pulse-gen card (pulse-gen.md:64-66) and the hotline card (extensions.md). The 256-tap band, 387-407 ms, is within human reach, but it needs D >= 228 ms, about 18 typical hops, which network.md 6 rules out.

(3) The claim race, which the bench does not model. sc6 has no rightful owner 3 3. Both cells claim at the end of b plus ID, and a claim runs back at about 1-2 ms a hop. So if (e,b) exists and is nearer than the misreading exchange (the usual case, since that exchange must be 8 or more hops out), the right claim wins. The origin drops the other paths before h is dialled, and the wrong register sees CLR: nobody is rung. A wrong ring needs (e,b) to be vacant (a misdial), no nearer, or cut off behind a transit that misread (its re-forward carries e-1).

(4) A dialler with a fixed cadence inside the band would misroute every call from one origin to one code, the same way each time. That makes the failure noticeable rather than random.

Rough rates:
- Conforming callers, or a network planned to today's document: about 0 per exchange per busy hour.
- Planned at the typical reach, using the design's own uniform 140-900 ms pause model (about 2.8% of callers in the band) and about 4 floods originated per exchange per busy hour: on the order of 0.01 per exchange per busy hour.

What the subscriber hears:
- The caller hears silence, then ringback, and a stranger at (e-1, b) h s answers, or the caller hears busy.
- Owners downstream of a transit that misread lose the call cleanly, 2 s after b.
- With e=1 the target is (b, h), and its register gets only one digit, so the call mostly ends in a timeout rather than a ring.

The mechanism is confirmed: net_unit.v:283 plus 584-588, and 2/21/40/59/78 ms rise to hold in run_real13_all.log.

Realism:
- At the reference load (about 0.07 floods/s reaching each exchange), a second seizure falls in the 18 ms before a given flood for only about 0.13% of floods per exchange.
- The cls slice's traffic runs at 70x that rate (5 floods/s) measured rise to hold p99 15.6 ms and max 19.3 ms, with no late cell and no wrong claim.
- At 30 floods/s the maximum was 38.7 ms, still with no wrong claim (work/audit/cls/NOTES.md 4).
- A wrong number from a late pickup also needs the same fast-caller band and a deep victim, so it is orders of magnitude rarer than finding 1.
- The complaint about the specification is against monitor.md's rule 1, which today's network.md 3.3 and 3.4 have superseded (one seizure each 18 ms, and a cell up to 20 ms behind a busy classifier).
- The scan-order starvation the mechanism skeptic raised (cls sc7) needs a burst of seven in about 100 ms, which is far above any real load.

Low is right. I disagree with the verifier on one point, its 'cheaper partial fix: the rule-1 lateness bit alone ... the wrong number becomes a lost call'. It is wrong, and now measured: skeptic-mechanism/run_late_sc6_l1_d112.log (snapshot plus the lateness bit alone) shows '109.514 ms SKEPTIC hold 30 late 0 -> cell', then CLAIM at 1437 and B21 rung, FAIL 2. The make after a missed first break had M low at the last visit, so it reads as a fresh rise.

The measured hops (12.1-13.9 ms typical, about 30 ms behind a watch, 18-25 ms behind an origin sweep) and the formula K = 1 + floor((120 - first)/hop) are right.

The mismatches it reports are against superseded documents. Today's network.md 6 already uses about 12 ms typical and 22-30 ms slow, and it requires the plan to cover the slow case.

The realism point goes further than the verifier's. Slow transits are independent and rare (about 0.13% each at reference load), and a convoy slows only once. So the slow-case plan is very conservative, and a network planned to it keeps about 50 ms of margin in practice.

What is left is small:
- network.md 6 does not budget the destination's own ~18 ms watch. That is finding 1 restated, and C_LOW removes it.
- The comment at net_unit.v:55 ('it covers about ten, the documents' figure') contradicts the slow-case rule and should be corrected.

Low, bordering on info.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
C_LOW is the right minimal fix for finding 1. In C_HOLD, M low goes to C_LOW, and nothing is written. M back goes to C_HOLD with cls_ms reset. M low for longer than the threshold goes to C_UNHOLD. The copy is work/verify/C05-late-flood-guard-reach/rtl_fix/net_unit.v.

On 74HC it is essentially free:
- one more state code in the existing 3-bit cst (6 is unused)
- the same cls_ms counter
- the timeout compare is one counter bit: cls_ms[7] for ID, or cls_ms[8] for CLR

It keeps the hold standing through a dial break. BUSY stays 1, so there is no R_GONE, no fresh re-seize and no mid-digit re-forward. It is tested: sc6 l0 d112, l0 d124 and l1 d104 PASS, and tb_net is 88/0. It is better than the auditors' fix 1: that costs about 3 packages, and every owner beyond B still loses the call.

Two refinements:
(a) Prefer CLR, the C04 verifier's choice, to ID. On a port that has already armed (a low starting after T_ARM), the port itself treats a low of 128-256 ms as no release (T_REL 256). ID would unhold it and re-seize it when M comes back, which is the same misread. The cost of CLR is 128 ms more classifier block after a real death inside the watch. Such deaths come mostly from a far origin's guard abandoning a fast caller, and they delay only other floods at that exchange (about a 1% chance at reference load).
(b) A fault-only caveat. A held trunk whose M chatters with makes under about 18 ms keeps cst cycling between C_HOLD and C_LOW for as long as it chatters. The snapshot is worse in that case: it re-seizes on every cycle, taking a new cell and a new forward each time. So this is acceptable; if wanted, cap the watch's total time.

C_LOW is not complete:
- It leaves finding 2's late pickup (l1 d112 still FAILS on the fix).
- The cheap stopgap the verifier proposed (the lateness bit alone) does NOT close it. It was measured FAIL: skeptic-mechanism/run_late_sc6_l1_d112.log gives the late cell, CLAIM and B21 rung.
- The zero-gate complement is the cls slice's F4': set st on any BUSY sample, and clear it only on M low with BUSY low. It turns the armed-port case of l1 d112 into a lost copy (fix2 on cls sc7: the wrong number becomes a lost copy; fix2 regressions are net 87/88, where the one miss is the intended blip change, lfull 40/40 and chain 32/32). It has only been tested bundled with fix2's other changes, not alone.
- The residual after C_LOW plus F4' is a break less than T_ARM after the rise at an exchange whose classifier is busy. That needs D of about 104 ms or more plus a coincident seizure, which is negligible at real loads.
- The cls slice's full fix (4 watchers, a rise queue, a second delay line) closes everything, but the realism figures do not justify its parts count.

A note on 'clean'. On the fix, l1 d104 and l0 d124 are clean at B only. B's legs are written 6 ms into the first break (61.0 ms in l1 d104), so exchanges downstream are past the guard's reach and would count e-1. That is inherent to the plan, not caused by the fix. Only the network.md 6 planning rule protects them.

Documents:
- Correct the comment at net_unit.v:55 ('covers about ten').
- With C_LOW, network.md 6's budget stands.
- Without it, add the destination's ~18 ms watch.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier on all three findings: each is real but overstated. Finding 1 is medium, findings 2 and 3 are low.

Realism adds four points the verifier left out:
- **Planning.** Today's network.md 6 requires the 128 ms tap to cover the slow case, which means about 4-5 hops. On that plan the watch misread needs two or three independent slow transits on one path. That is about 0.13% each at the reference load, so its rate is effectively zero. It is live only in a network planned on the typical hop (about 10 hops on 128), which the stale comment at net_unit.v:55 still invites.
- **Callers.** No conforming caller can reach it. Joel's own diallers pause 700 ms and are safe at every tap. The 259-280 ms band on the 128 tap is roughly beyond a human with a rotary dial. The 256-tap band is within human reach but needs about 18 typical hops.
- **The claim race.** The bench has no rightful owner. In a real network a nearer (e,b) claims first, and the misreading exchange's register sees only CLR, so nobody is rung. A wrong ring needs (e,b) vacant, no nearer, or cut off behind a transit that misread.
- **Fixed cadence.** A dialler whose cadence sits inside the band misroutes the same way on every call, not at random.

Medium stays for finding 1 because it is a silent wrong number that breaks the design's stated 'never a wrong number' promise to fast callers (monitor-rules.md 5), and the fix is free.

C_LOW is the right zero-package fix for finding 1. I would prefer CLR to ID for its timeout. It is not complete: the busy-classifier late pickup remains.

The verifier's proposed stopgap for that residue, the lateness bit alone, is refuted by measurement: skeptic-mechanism/run_late_sc6_l1_d112.log shows a late cell and CLAIM, with B21 rung. The zero-gate complement is F4'.

Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C05-late-flood-guard-reach/skeptic-realism/NOTES.md. I ran no simulation of my own.

findings.real_timing: The hole is reachable at real timers, but only in a band about 2 ms wide: a key-to-e make of 129-130 ms, just above ID = 128 ms. e must also be a single pulse (codes 1x); a second pulse of e breaks inside the guard and the origin abandons. The band's width is the gap between the push and the first break signal: flood_go to the seizure push takes 10.0 ms (measured), and r_brk comes about HIT + 1 ms (9 ms) after a break starts. If the origin's sweep has to wait behind a forward sweep that is already running (up to about 10 ms more), the band widens to roughly 129-140 ms; that part is arithmetic, not run. A telephone to ES 201 187 pauses at least 720 ms, and rotary dials and dialler chips pause far longer than 140 ms, so conforming equipment never reaches it. It needs a non-conforming fast pulse source whose pause between digits lands within about 2 ms of the register's ID. A line hit inside the window does not cause this wrong number: the origin register counts the hit but the far end misses it, so the far end sees the true e b. The auditor's window of [128, 140-160] ms leaves out the HIT delay of r_brk and is overstated by about 10-20 ms. At scale 8 (HIT 1) the band is about 9 ms wide against ID 16, which is why the bench hits it easily. The auditor's 'medium' should be 'low': the protocol's promise is broken, but only for non-conforming dialling.

(2) My real-timer bench tb_c06rt.v uses site_net defaults (HIT 8, ID 128, CLR 256, T_ARM 16, T_GUARD0 128, T_CLAIM 2000). A 22 has links to B 32. A20 keys 1 with a make of 128/129/130/131/132/134/138/720 ms before e=1, then dials 3 and 2 with 720 ms pauses, meaning exchange 13, which does not exist. Snapshot run: run_rt.log (37 s sim). (3) The same bench on rtl_fixb/net_unit.v, which carries the auditor's o_brk fix only: run_rt_fixb.log. (4) tb_orig S3 and tb_net on fix b were queued as job_fixb.sh but never got a slot in 4.5 h, and I cancelled them unrun. No obj dirs are left.
findings.evidence: Mechanism checked line by line in the snapshot. pulse_rx.v:81-88: brk_stb (r_brk) is one tick, fired HIT ms into a break. mini_marker.v:415-433: flood_go comes 1-2 ticks after the key's digit strobe. net_unit.v:815: tmr is zeroed at the seizure push. net_unit.v:862 is the only place r_brk is read, and only in N_NET/N_WAITCL. N_WANT, N_HUNT and N_SEIZE (:846-857) ignore it. Nothing else guards: the far classifier sees a clean rise at the make, which satisfies monitor rule 1, and the origin's claim watch accepts a claim at any digit. Snapshot at scale 8 (run_orig_s3.log) reproduces the auditor's log: S3a control passes. In S3b, flood_go is at 1359.002 and the seizure write at 1369.286. B sees the rise at 1375.158, at the end of e's pulse. B claims at 1692.285, after A's third digit, and A is CLAIMED with guarding 0. N_DONE follows at ndig 4, B21 rings and A20 follows B21 4/4: 2 FAILs. Snapshot at real timers (run_rt.log): with a 129 ms make, e's r_brk comes at flood_go + 9.0 ms, in N_HUNT, and the push at + 10.0 ms. B sees the rise 51.2 ms after the push, at the end of e's 60 ms break. B CLAIMS at 7087 and A is CLAIMED with guarding 0: a call dialled to 13 is claimed by 32. The 130 ms make gives the same result (r_brk + 10.0). Makes of 131/132/134/138 ms put r_brk after the push, and the guard gives NOGO. The 720 ms control is claimed by nobody and gets NOGO 2 s after b. The 128 ms make is not recognised as a key at this sampling phase, so no flood starts (a bench quantisation effect). All phones and trunks return to idle after every trial. The auditor's check is sound, and the stimulus (a fast pulse source) is physically possible though non-conforming. The auditor's stated consequence, a wrong number to (b, h), is right.
findings.notes: There is one finding and one root cause. The old documents (monitor.md 3.2) budgeted the seizure 2 ms after the digit is recognised. That is shorter than HIT, so the band did not exist. The 10 ms sweep opened it. The new exchange/network.md §6 promises that a caller who pauses less than about 267 ms is abandoned ('a flood and a cannot-complete, never a wrong number'); the RTL breaks that promise in this band. tb_net scenario 7 tests only a break after the seizure (busy_a[T11]), so no committed bench covers the band before the push.

verifier.root_cause: The origin's guard reads the register's one-tick r_brk only in N_NET/N_WAITCL (rtl/net_unit.v:862), and the guard timer is zeroed at the seizure push (net_unit.v:815). N_WANT, N_HUNT and N_SEIZE (net_unit.v:846-857) drop r_brk. r_brk fires HIT ms into a break (rtl/pulse_rx.v:81-88), and the sweep puts the push about 10 ms after flood_go. So a break that starts within (sweep latency - HIT) of the key's recognition is signalled before the seizure exists. The seizure is then written inside that break, and the far monitors see its rise at the make that ends the pulse. They lose the pulse and read b as e and h as b.
verifier.best_fix:
Adopt the auditor's fix b, which is correct, complete and minimal: one flip-flop and about two gates, all on the unit. A sticky o_brk is set by r_brk in N_WANT, N_HUNT or N_SEIZE and cleared at flood_go. At h_done, N_HUNT abandons with NOGO and seizes nothing if o_brk or r_brk is set. The guard in N_NET becomes `guarding && (r_brk || o_brk)`, which covers an r_brk that comes in N_SEIZE after h_done.

It closes every reachable case. The only uncovered interval is between the key's digit strobe and flood_go. That is 1-2 ticks, much shorter than HIT, so no r_brk can fall there.

With the fix, the RTL keeps network.md §6's promise that a fast caller is abandoned. An equivalent alternative is to abandon if the register's `counting` is high at the push, but that needs a new wire on the register ribbon, so it is no cheaper.

When merging, take the o_brk lines only. The auditor's work/audit/origin/rtl_fix/net_unit.v also carries an unrelated fix c (the `lost` counter, from another cluster). The fix-b-only copy is work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/rtl_fixb/net_unit.v.

Testing so far: real timers on the fix-b-only copy (below). tb_net on fix b has not been run.
verifier.fix_tested:
Tested at real timers on work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/rtl_fixb/net_unit.v, which has fix b only (run_rt_fixb.log): 0 wrong numbers. The 129 and 130 ms makes are abandoned at h_done with NOGO and no seizure is written. The 131-138 ms makes still get the guard's NOGO, and the 720 ms control is unchanged (no claim, NOGO 2 s after b). Nothing is left busy after any trial.

At scale 8, the auditor's run_fix2.log (fix b plus the unrelated fix c) passes S3b: A claimed 0 and B21 does not ring.

tb_net on fix b was NOT run. The combined job (job_fixb.sh) never got a sim.sh slot in 4.5 h and I cancelled it. On reading the bench, tb_net never reaches the changed logic: dial_a adds 108 ms of make after every digit, so every break after the key starts at least 92 ms after the key's digit strobe (ID 16), and scenario 7 breaks only after the seizure. So 88/88 is expected but not measured.
verifier.summary:
Confirmed, but overstated; one root cause. A break that begins in the ~10 ms between the key's recognition (flood_go) and the origin's seizure write fires its one-tick r_brk while the origin is in N_WANT, N_HUNT or N_SEIZE, where it is ignored (net_unit.v:846-862). The seizure then lands inside that break, so the far monitors lose e's pulse and count b as e. I reproduced the auditor's S3b on the snapshot at scale 8 (run_orig_s3.log). My own bench also shows it at real timers (run_rt.log): with a key-to-e make of 129 or 130 ms and e = 1, exchange 32 claims a call dialled to 13 and the origin accepts the claim. From 131 ms up, the existing guard abandons the call.

The auditor overstates the window. Because r_brk lags the start of a break by HIT (8 ms), the band at real timers is about 2 ms wide (129-130 ms), and roughly 129-140 ms if the origin waits behind a forward sweep (arithmetic, not run), not [128, 140-160]. A telephone to ES 201 187 pauses at least 720 ms, so conforming equipment never reaches it; it needs a non-conforming fast pulse source, and e must be a single pulse. Severity should be low, not medium. It still breaks network.md §6's promise that such a fast caller is abandoned and never gets a wrong number.

The auditor's sticky o_brk fix (one flip-flop) closes the hole completely and is minimal. On a fix-b-only copy at real timers it turns both wrong numbers into cannot-complete (NOGO), with the other trials unchanged (run_rt_fixb.log). tb_net on the fix is unrun: the job waited 4.5 h for a sim.sh slot and I cancelled it. Reading the bench, its dialling never reaches the changed logic.

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/: NOTES.md, tb_c06rt.v, run_rt.log, run_rt_fixb.log, run_orig_s3.log, rtl_fixb/net_unit.v.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: re-derive from the RTL whether each mechanism happens exactly as claimed; look for a condition that blocks it, or a second path that makes it worse.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived the mechanism from the snapshot and it happens exactly as claimed. Nothing blocks it.

How it happens:
- pulse_rx.v:81-88 fires brk_stb once per break, HIT samples into the break.
- mini_marker.v:415-433 (and marker.v:420-427) raise flood_go on the tick after r_ndig>=1. The only condition is room>=1 in an 8-deep queue, so flood_go is effectively immediate.
- net_unit.v:842-857: N_WANT, N_HUNT and N_SEIZE never read r_brk. The guard reads it only in N_NET and N_WAITCL (:862), and tmr is zeroed at the push (:815).
- On the far side, baseband a_out is the trunk port's E, which is the caller's M through the latch. The far classifier (cls_seen) and the monitor's pulse_rx see a clean rise at the make. Nothing requires M to have stood before the first counted break. The monitor attaches about 1-3 ms after the rise.

I agree with the verifier on the band and the severity. Uncontended, the band is push - flood_go (10.0 ms) minus HIT (8 ms), about 2 ms: a key-to-e make of 129-130 ms. With contention the push slips by a running forward sweep (up to 10 ms), by about 1 ms for each classifier read that pre-empts the sweep, and by any wait for queue room. That gives roughly 129-145 ms (arithmetic, not run). The auditor's 140-160 is overstated, but neither figure changes the severity. The old monitor.md 3.2 budgeted 2 ms from recognition to seizure, which is less than HIT, so the band did not exist then. The 10 ms sweep opened it.

The verifier gets two mechanism statements wrong. Both understate the trigger set. I measured both at real timers on the snapshot in one run: work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/skeptic-mechanism/run_sk.log, tb_c06sk.v, with A=13 and B=32.

(1) 'e must be a single pulse' is false for a slow pulse train. The second break's r_brk lands at r_brk1 + T, where T is the pulse period. Its guard ends at push + 128. So any e escapes when T >= 128 + (push - r_brk1), about 129-130 ms, which is about 7.7 pps or slower. The far then counts e-1. Trial a: key make 129 ms, then e=4 at 7 pps (90/53). The first r_brk came at flood_go+9.0 in N_HUNT. The second came at tmr 142, past the guard. B (32) counted 3 2 and claimed a call dialled to 42, and A accepted the claim (CLAIMED). Trial b is the same call at 10 pps: the second r_brk came at tmr 99 and A gave NOGO. So at conforming 10+-1 pps the verifier's statement holds. 7 pps is inside the register's own design envelope (register.md 2; pulse_reg.v cites 'a 0 at 7 pps') but outside ES 201 187.

(2) 'A line hit inside the window does not cause a wrong number' is true only of the far end. The origin register counts the hit as a digit 1. Its code check (net_unit.v:866-870) then reads (1, e). At an exchange coded 1x, when the dialled e equals OWN_B, the call goes O_LOCAL: restart, local_go, and the next digits b h are taken as a local line. Trial c: key make 129 ms, a 25 ms hit, then e=3 b=2 h=1 with conforming 720 ms pauses at exchange 13. The hit's r_brk came in N_HUNT, local_go fired with the code read as 1 3, and A21 went BUSY and rang (E high 2104 of 6200 ms). That is a wrong number from one plausible fault with conforming dialling.

Neither addition changes the severity:
- Variant (1) still needs the non-conforming 129-145 ms pause, and is the rarer combination.
- Variant (2) needs a hit of at least about 15 ms that starts within about 2 ms of the key's recognition. It needs a 1x exchange and e equal to OWN_B.
- Pulse dialling already turns any hit in any inter-digit pause (a window of seconds per call) into an inserted digit. That window is about 1000 times larger.
- The project's own tester (pulse-gen.md) pauses a fixed 700 ms, so it never reaches the band.

So severity is low, not the auditor's medium. The finding is still a real break of the new network.md §6 promise of 'a cannot-complete, never a wrong number'. No committed bench covers the band before the push.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
Fix b is correct, complete and minimal: one flip-flop and about two gates, all on the unit. It is a sticky o_brk, set by r_brk in N_WANT, N_HUNT or N_SEIZE and cleared at flood_go. N_HUNT abandons at h_done on o_brk or r_brk. The N_NET guard becomes `guarding && (r_brk || o_brk)`.

It fixes the root cause shared by all three variants: a first r_brk that falls before the push. In run_sk.log the first r_brk of the slow-pulse trial and of the line-hit trial both land in N_HUNT (nst 2), so fix b turns both into NOGO. That is read from the code: my one run was on the snapshot, and fix b was not re-run on these two variants.

The interval fix b leaves uncovered is between dig_stb and flood_go. It is a few master clocks long. A break must start after dig_stb, because an earlier one would have reset ID, and its r_brk comes HIT ms later. So no r_brk can fall in that interval, and the same holds in the class marker, whose flood_go is just as immediate.

Two small points:
(a) If r_brk lands in N_SEIZE, the seizure is still pushed and then dropped on the next tick. That is correct but wasteful. The optional refinement is to test `o_brk || r_brk` in N_SEIZE and gate w_orig's N_SEIZE term with !r_brk, so nothing is written.
(b) The verifier's rtl_fixb puts the abandon after the h_ok==0 test, where the auditor puts it before. Both are fine. Merge only the o_brk lines, not the auditor's fix c.

There is a zero-flop alternative: act on r_brk directly in N_WANT, N_HUNT and N_SEIZE, going to N_END with NOGO, and gate the push on !r_brk. It works because the owner-less sweep's h_done is ignored when h_owner=0. It is no cheaper in logic and is harder to reason about, so I prefer fix b.

An optional extra defence, not a substitute and not run: in N_WAITCL, `!claimed && r_brk` gives NOGO, so a claim must arrive before the caller's next break after b. A genuine claim comes within tens of ms of b's recognition, and a conforming caller's next break comes at least about 590 ms later. This catches any claim that comes one whole digit late, whatever caused it, for example C05's e=1 late-flood variant. It does not catch the slow-pulse e-1 variant, which claims on time, or the line-hit O_LOCAL variant, which is on the origin side. So fix b is still required.

No committed bench runs the band before the push; a regression bench should. Fix b needs one real-timer trial for each of these three:
- e=1 at a 129 ms make
- 7 pps e>=2 at a 129 ms make
- a 25 ms hit at a 129 ms make at a 1x exchange
tb_net does not reach any of them, because its dialling pauses at least 92 ms after the key's ID.
skeptics.summary:
Confirmed. The mechanism happens exactly as the auditor and verifier describe, and I found no condition that blocks it. The origin's guard reads the register's one-tick r_brk only in N_NET/N_WAITCL (net_unit.v:862). A break that starts within about (sweep latency - HIT) of the key's recognition fires its r_brk in N_WANT, N_HUNT or N_SEIZE, where it is dropped. The seizure is then written inside the break, and the far monitors see their first rise at the make that ends the break.

I agree with the verifier on the band (a key-to-e make of 129-130 ms uncontended, up to roughly 145 ms under contention) and on the severity: low, not medium.

Hunting for second paths, I found two the verifier ruled out. I confirmed both at real timers on the snapshot with one run (skeptic-mechanism/run_sk.log).
(1) The pulse does not have to be a single-pulse e. With a pulse period of at least about 130 ms (7 pps or slower, inside the register's own envelope), the second break's r_brk lands past the 128 ms guard. The far counts e-1: 32 claimed a call dialled to 42, and the same call at 10 pps got NOGO.
(2) A single 25 ms line hit in the band, with conforming 720 ms dialling, is counted by the origin as a digit 1. At exchange 13 the origin read the code as its own (1 3), went local, and rang local line A21 for a call dialled to 32.
Both need rare coincidences: a non-conforming pause, or a hit inside a window about 2 ms wide at a 1x exchange. So the severity stays low.

Fix b (a sticky o_brk, one flip-flop) is correct, complete and minimal, and it covers both new variants, because both start with an r_brk in N_HUNT. It has not been re-run on them. An optional zero-flop extra defence is to give NOGO in N_WAITCL on `!claimed && r_brk`, which catches any claim that comes one whole digit late. No committed bench covers the band before the push.

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/skeptic-mechanism/: NOTES.md, tb_c06sk.v, run_sk.log, vl_sk.log and job.sh. The obj dir has been removed.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity

per_finding.reason:
The finding is real, and I agree it is low rather than the auditor's medium. I checked the mechanism in the snapshot. N_WANT, N_HUNT and N_SEIZE never read r_brk (rtl/net_unit.v:846-857); only :862 does, in N_NET and N_WAITCL. tmr is zeroed at the push (:815). r_brk fires HIT into a break (rtl/pulse_rx.v:81-88). flood_go follows dig_stb within ticks (rtl/mini_marker.v:411-433). The verifier's run_rt.log shows flood_go to push is 10.0 ms and flood_go to r_brk is about 9 ms, so the band is a key-to-e make of 129-130 ms as the register times it. At a busy exchange it can reach about 143 ms: the origin may wait up to 10 ms behind a running forward sweep (N_WANT waits for hst == H_IDLE), and classifier reads cost about 1 ms each. Queue time after the push does not widen the hole, because the guard already runs from the push.

REALISM. No conforming equipment reaches this band. ES 201 187 requires at least 720 ms between digits. A rotary dial pauses for the human rewind plus lost motion, several hundred ms. Dialler chips pause 500-800 ms. Every pulse source in this project pauses a fixed 700 ms (exchange/proposed/pulse-gen.md §2.1 and §3; exchange/card-word.md:355). exchange/analysis/dialling.md §3.2 puts timed make at about sent + 5 ms, so the band is about 124-125 ms sent. That is only about 5 ms above the point where the register merges two digits on a local call (holds at 125 ms sent, merges at 120). The only trigger is a non-conforming pulse source, such as a home-built dialler or a hook-tapper, whose pause lands 1-15 ms above ID. Such a device already fails nearly every other network call cleanly (e of 2 or more at 9-11 pps gets NOGO from the guard, and pauses of 131-267 ms get NOGO), so its owner would notice and lengthen the pause.

A plausible fault (a line hit) does not produce this wrong number. The origin counts the hit and the far end does not, so the far end reads the true e b. The sibling mechanism skeptic's run c shows a hit here can lead to O_LOCAL, and A21 rings, when the origin's own code is 1 e. But a hit anywhere in the roughly 450+ ms between the end of the guard and e gives the origin the same (1, e) reading. That is the general risk of a line hit on pulse dialling, and this band adds under 1% of the exposure.

Rate per exchange per busy hour: effectively zero with conforming equipment. Only a single mis-tuned device could reproduce it, and it would do so every time.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE VERIFIER.
(1) 'e must be a single pulse' holds only at about 7.8 pps and above. e's second r_brk comes about T after the first. The guard ends 128 ms after the push, roughly 9-10 ms after the first r_brk. So from a pulse period of about 129-137 ms (about 7.3-7.75 pps) the second pulse escapes the guard. The register is designed to accept 7-12 pps (dialling.md §2). The sibling skeptic's real-timer run on the snapshot (skeptic-mechanism/run_sk.log) settles it. At 7 pps 90/53 with e = 4 and a 129 ms key make, the second r_brk comes at tmr 142 and exchange B (32) claims a call dialled to 42, and A accepts. At 10 pps the same case gets NOGO at tmr 99. In this slow-pulse variant the far end counts e-1 and b, so exchange (e-1, b) takes h s intact and rings line h s. That is a true silent wrong number from an ordinary 5-digit number.
(2) For the e = 1 case at conforming rates, 'a wrong number to (b, h)' is mostly a misrouted claim, not a ringing line. With a 5-digit number, owner (b, h) gets only s as its h. A claimed trunk gets no dial tone (mini_marker.v:305-317), so the caller hears about 10 s of silence (NODIG), then 03 from the wrong exchange, and that exchange's single register is held for 10 s. If no exchange has code (b, h), the call gets NOGO 2 s after b, as with the fix. A line rings only if the caller dials a sixth digit (the auditor's S3b), or reaches the operator if s = 0 and the owner has a class marker. The auditor did say this; the verifier glossed it.

Neither correction changes the severity. The pause is what limits the trigger, and it lies outside what any conforming telephone does. It stays low rather than info because the fault breaks the documented guarantee, a silent wrong number is possible, and the fix is cheap.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
Fix b, the sticky o_brk, is correct, complete and small; I agree with the verifier. Once flood_go has come, no r_brk before the push can be lost any more. At h_done the call is abandoned (NOGO, nothing seized) if o_brk or r_brk is set. An r_brk in N_SEIZE sets o_brk, and the guard trips on the first N_NET tick, when tmr is 0. The one uncovered gap is from dig_stb to flood_go. That gap is ticks long and needs only marker room of 1 or more, which is far shorter than HIT, so no r_brk can fall in it. The fix covers both variants: the single-pulse e at 9-11 pps and the slow-pulse e-1 case at 7.7 pps and below, because both first show up as an r_brk in N_HUNT. It also turns a line hit inside the band into a clean cannot-complete. It does not touch the general hit to O_LOCAL risk, which lies outside this cluster. Conforming dials never reach the changed logic, so the fix costs them nothing.

For 74HC: one half of a 74HC74 and two gates. It can be simpler than the RTL copy by dropping the WANT/HUNT/SEIZE decode. Set the flop on any r_brk and clear it synchronously at flood_go (D = (Q | r_brk) & ~flood_go). The flag is read only at h_done and under `guarding`, so a set in any other state does no harm. The term (Q | r_brk) then feeds both reads. The equivalent version with no flop, abandoning at the push if the register's `counting` is set, needs a new ribbon wire and is no cheaper.

When merging, take only the o_brk lines. The fix-b-only copy is work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/rtl_fixb/net_unit.v; the auditor's rtl_fix also carries the unrelated fix c.

What is still missing is a regression test. tb_net cannot reach the band: its dial_a leaves at least 92 ms of make after each dig_stb, so 88/88 is expected and proves nothing here. A real-timer trial should be added, with key makes of 129/130 ms followed by e = 1, and 7 pps with e of 2 or more. The scratch benches tb_c06rt.v and skeptic-mechanism/tb_c06sk.v already do both.

exchange/network.md §3.4 rule 2 and §6 should also say that the guard covers from the key's recognition (flood_go), not only from the seizure write.
skeptics.summary:
Real, overstated by the auditor; low severity is right. A break that starts 1-2 ms (uncontended) or up to about 15 ms (behind a running forward sweep) after the key is recognised has its r_brk dropped in N_WANT, N_HUNT or N_SEIZE. The far monitors then lose e's first pulse. Timed at the register, the key-to-e pause must be 129-130 ms, or up to about 143 ms at a busy exchange, which is about 124-125 ms sent. That is five or more times shorter than ES 201 187's 720 ms. No rotary dial, dialler chip or pulse source in this project comes near it; all of the project's sources pause 700 ms. Line hits do not cause this wrong number. Only a non-conforming or hand-tuned dialler, or a hook-tapper sitting just above ID, can trigger it. Such a device is about 5 ms from merging digits on local calls and already fails most of its other network calls cleanly. For a conforming population the rate is effectively zero per exchange per busy hour; a single mis-tuned device would hit it every time.

I disagree with the verifier on two points about the consequence. (1) e need not be a single pulse. At about 7.7 pps and below (7 pps is inside the register's design range), e's second pulse falls after the guard ends. The sibling skeptic's real-timer run on the snapshot shows 32 claiming a call dialled to 42 at 7 pps, and NOGO at 10 pps. In that variant, exchange (e-1, b) rings line h s: a true silent wrong number from an ordinary 5-digit number. (2) In the e = 1 case at 9-11 pps, a 5-digit number usually ends in about 10 s of silence and then 03 from the wrong exchange, whose single register is held for 10 s. A line rings only if the caller dials a sixth digit, or reaches the operator when s = 0 at a class-marker owner.

Fix b is correct and complete for 74HC: one flop and two gates, and it can drop the three-state decode (set on any r_brk, clear at flood_go). A real-timer regression trial is still needed, because tb_net cannot reach the band. I ran no simulations and relied on the verifier's logs and the sibling's skeptic-mechanism/run_sk.log. My notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C06-pre-seizure-break/skeptic-realism/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers with a conforming dial (10 pps 60/40, 720 ms interdigit make), but only with a fault: the whole link has to be out for about 8 to 256 ms while the caller dials e b (before the claim) or h s (after it). Causes would be a disturbed connector or cable, or a glitch in the far card's power or clock. On MF8 it would take a loss of carrier of 8 ms or more. The auditor's two cheaper routes are overstated. First, DEAD = 47 us does not matter: pulse_rx counts a break only after 8 consecutive 1 kHz samples (pulse_rx.v:84), so an outage under about 7 ms can never count. Second, an MF8 re-frame lasts about 1 ms (mf8-spec.md 4.2: 8-15 frames, then a 32-frame lock), which is under HIT. It is rare per call, but silent, and every link on the path is exposed; a local trunk exposes all 8 channels at once. A single-conductor fault on A alone (link_up still true) is out of reach of any card, just as a loop fault is.

verifier.root_cause: One root cause. baseband_card.v:154 (a_tx = a_s2 && link_up && settled) and local_trunk.v:188 (a_tx = live ? x_a : 0) show a detected link outage to the port as A = 0 for exactly as long as it lasts, which is what exchange/network.md section 2 asks for ('Link down ... drops A'). A physical cut reads A = 0 anyway. Nothing further down can tell that break from the caller's own: pulse_rx.v:84 counts any break of HIT or more. Nor can anything tell the link's return from a new seizure (net_unit.v:283 cls_seen). The origin reads its own caller and never learns. An outage under T_REL becomes an extra pulse; an outage over T_REL that ends mid-dial becomes a fresh seizure counted from mid-number. The three findings are this one mechanism in its two windows, and the third finding is a duplicate of the first.
verifier.best_fix: 'An outage is a release, never a pulse', done on the card, as the audit proposes. But the audit's copy (work/audit/proto/rtl_fix/baseband_card.v) is INCOMPLETE. It clears the poison once its link is up and its OWN port's A_RX has been idle for 300 ms. In a one-way outage only B's receivers lose the link, so only B poisons. A, the origin with the caller's M on the wire, never poisons. 300 ms after B's link returns, B clears, and the caller's M reaches B as a fresh seizure: my sc5 shows B claiming at 4109.9 ms, reading h s = 2 3 as its e b. Minimal completion, in work/verify/C07-link-outage-pulse/rtl_mut/baseband_card.v: (1) clear only when the circuit is idle BOTH ways, `if (poison && link_up && !a_rx && !a_s2)`. That is one gate input. A poisoned far card sends A = 0, so two poisoned cards never wait on each other. (2) Gate the word with !poison (one gate), so no hunt takes a trunk during its 300 ms of poison. Cost: the audit's half '4040, a '74 and two gates, plus two gate inputs. An alternative, a poisoned card stopping its TX_CLK for 8 ms (half a '123) so the far card poisons too, is in rtl_echo/ and untested; the both-ways clear is cheaper. The price is unchanged: an established call dies on any outage of 4 ms or more. Still to do, untested: local_trunk.v needs the same, with entry for the whole group at once and a clear per channel (the audit estimates about 2 packages). exchange/network.md section 2 ('Link down' row) and trunks.md section 1 (the gating row) should say: 'A must never show a break the caller did not make; an outage of 4 ms or more is a release, held until the circuit has been idle both ways for 300 ms.'
