per_finding.reason: Re-derived from the code, and nothing blocks it. baseband_card.v:154 (and local_trunk.v:188) gate A with link_up. port.v:176-181 rides out any outage under T_REL. pulse_rx.v:78-90 counts any run of 9 consecutive zero samples at 1 kHz (a little over 8 ms, so the verifier's 'under about 7 ms never counts' is on the safe side). The cell decides on that count (net_unit.v:633-645). Two things that could have stopped it do not: the C_HOLD watch only acts in the 18 ms after a hold, and a resolver's R_GONE needs BUSY to fall, which the hold's bsy keeps up. The auditor's two cheap routes are wrong, as the verifier says: DEAD = 47 us is swallowed by HIT, and an MF8 re-frame takes 0.58-1.3 ms to acquire and at most 13 frames to recover from a slip, with 0 LOF up to 3e-2 BER (mf8-spec.md 4.1-4.2). The verifier missed one thing. The likely form of this fault, a disturbed connector, is a burst rather than a clean gap, and one burst can add MORE than one pulse. My sc6 put 13 cycles of 3.0 ms open and 60 us closed 30 ms into b's last make. B's monitor counted b = 4 for a dialled 2 (d_stb cnt 04 at 2319.0 ms). The card never poisoned, so in that regime it behaves exactly like the snapshot card. There is a second trigger: a trunk card whose 100 ms power-up RC re-runs shows a 100 ms break, which is always inside the pulse window. Medium is right: a silent wrong number, but it needs a fault while digits are in flight.

The mechanism is as traced. The outage's M-down samples clear st (net_unit.v:566-567). A released port shows BUSY clear, so cls_seen (283) takes the returning M as a seizure. The origin sees nothing, because its trunk's backward A was 0 before the claim. The verifier's mid-digit wrong-line case (sc4) is right. There is a second trigger the audit and the verifier missed: a restart of the RECEIVING exchange. A /RESET of B (the marker, a pushbutton, or a glitch on the line; mainboard.md 153/736) clears B's hold, st and monitor cell. /RESET never reaches a trunk card: the channel socket has no such pin, baseband_card's rst_n is power-on only, and clock_card.v:9-10 has no reset but power-on. So A20's M stays on B11, the link never drops, and B takes the next rise as a fresh seizure counted from mid-number. I reproduced the net effect WITH THE VERIFIER'S FIX in place. In sc7, B alone was reset for 1 ms at 1100 ms (in e's 1st break), with the card reset too and a 100 ms HOLDOFF. The fresh rise came at 1240 and the cells at 1241-1243, with cnt 2 at 1570 and cnt 3 at 2550. 'B raises att' at 2550.3 and A's origin took the claim at 2551.2. B21 rang: A20 dialled 43-21 and got 23-21. One limit: a full power cycle of B that stops its TX_CLK for 4 ms or more IS covered by the fixed variant, because A's card then poisons and stays poisoned while its origin holds A11. The restarts left uncovered are /RESET and any restart with a clock gap under RIDE. Medium, understated: the consequence is a wrong line, and there is one more way in than stated.

This duplicates link-outage-dial-pulse. Its 47 us trigger is at most one or two 1 kHz samples, against the 9 that pulse_rx needs. Its fix (a) cannot work. A held trunk is already BUSY from its hold's bsy, so the cell cannot tell MUTE_BLK's BUSY from it, and the baseband card ignores MUTE anyway (baseband_card.v:161). One nuance on fix (b). The verifier dismisses it, and on its own it is pointless below 8 ms. With the poison fix, though, dropping link_up from the a_tx gate stops the card turning a glitch burst on the clock conductor alone (A solid) into breaks. That is a small companion to the poison, not a fix.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The direction is right: the card should make an outage a release, never a pulse. The verifier's completion is needed on top of the audit copy: clear only when idle both ways (`!a_rx && !a_s2`) and gate the word with !poison. I re-derived the audit fix's sc5 failure from the code. But the completed fix only closes CLEAN outages. My one run on RTL_mut.list shows two gaps (run_mut_sc192_p680.log).

(1) RIDE is a CONTINUOUS 4 ms. dn is reset by any frame with link_up, which one far clock edge gives. A disturbed-connector burst of sub-4 ms opens therefore never poisons, while a_tx = a_s2 && link_up is 0 at nearly every 1 kHz sample. sc6: no poison, and B counted b = 4. Minimal fix: make the entry cumulative. Reset dn only after link_up has stood continuously for about 2 ms, more than one sample period, so no closure the samplers can miss resets it. That is a '4040 stage and a gate.

(2) Restarts. poison is cleared at power-on, and /RESET never reaches a trunk card. A /RESET of the receiving exchange, or a restart whose clock gap is under RIDE, wipes the hold, st and monitor cell while the far card keeps the caller's M on the port. sc7 gave a wrong line with the fix in place. Fix: preset the poison '74 from the power-up RC and from /RESET, bringing /RESET to the card on the socket's spare a14. That costs no package, but it changes the socket contract, and every bench must then allow about 300 ms of idle after reset.

(3) The designed price lands in C11. A claimed call cut before its last digit still reaches N_DONE (net_unit.v:881, 818-822). N_DONE then writes caller<-trunk onto a trunk whose M is already 0. The caller is latched to a dead channel and can later overhear it. The fix LOWERS C11's trigger from 256 ms to 4 ms, so C11's fix is a prerequisite, or the price is silence rather than cannot-complete.

(4) Low: the both-ways clear is asymmetric in a one-way outage. The unpoisoned end's word stays valid, so its hunt can seize the channel into a deaf, still-poisoned far card, which re-arms that card's poison. The window is about 44 ms after a drop (CLEAR 300 against the fE hold of T_REL 256), or 300 ms on an idle channel. The result is a lost direction and a failed call, never a wrong number. The untested rtl_echo variant would close it.

(5) Still untested: local_trunk.v, and tb_chain, tb_lnet, tb_lfull and tb_lchain on the fixed card.

The price is real, and a cumulative entry raises it: a call in conversation dies on any 4 ms or longer outage, including a bumped cable. A narrower option, untested: poison only if A has changed within the last NODIG (10 s), so a call in conversation rides outages as it does today.

The spec text should say: 'A must never show a break the caller did not make. An outage of 4 ms or more, counted cumulatively, and a restart of either end are releases, held until the circuit has been idle both ways for 300 ms.'
skeptics.summary: I agree with the verifier on all three verdicts and severities. link-outage-dial-pulse is confirmed-overstated, medium. link-return-fresh-seizure is confirmed-understated, medium. link-hit-extra-pulse is a duplicate, low. I re-derived the mechanism from the RTL (baseband_card.v:154, port.v:176-181, pulse_rx.v:78-90, net_unit.v:283/566/633-645) and found nothing that blocks it; the auditor's DEAD and MF8 re-frame routes are wrong. My one run on the verifier's fixed card adds two things. First, a disturbed-connector burst (sc6) never poisons the card, and B's monitor counted two extra pulses (b = 4 for a dialled 2). Second, a restart of the RECEIVING exchange (sc7) gives a fresh seizure counted from mid-number: a wrong line (A20 dialled 43-21, B21 rang) with the fix in place. A /RESET never reaches a trunk card and never drops the link, so no card-level fix can see it. So the proposed fix closes clean outages only. It also needs a cumulative entry, and a poison preset on power-up and on /RESET. Its designed price widens C11 (caller latched to a dead claimed trunk) from 256 ms to 4 ms, so C11 must be fixed with it.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity

per_finding.reason: The mechanism is exact. baseband_card.v:154 and local_trunk.v:188 force A to 0 for as long as the link is down, and pulse_rx.v:84 counts any break of 8 consecutive 1 kHz samples. port.v rides anything shorter than T_REL. The verifier reproduced it at real timers with a conforming 720 ms interdigit make. Its trigger is always a fault. The 47 us DEAD and an MF8 re-frame (0.2-0.7 ms; false-lock releases 0.5-2.7 ms) never count, so 'high' is overstated. The fault must be on any flood-tree link during e b (every link carries every flood for about 3 s before the claim) or on a path link during h s. It can be a bumped or intermittent connector (chatter bursts are the commonest form), a cut and restore, a glitch in the far card's power or clock, or an MF8 carrier loss of 7 ms or more (an outdoor pair with a bad splice, or impulse bursts). Order of magnitude on the C03 reference net (10 exchanges, 500 floods/BH): a busy link has someone in a vulnerable phase about 40% of the time. P(wrong connection | inserted pulse) is about 0.2-0.4, highest in the key's pause, where (1, e) lands on hub codes. That gives about 0.1 wrong numbers per 8-256 ms event. At in-room fault rates (a few per link-year) that is about 1e-5 per link-BH, about 2e-5 per exchange-BH and about 4e-7 per call, roughly 10x rarer than C03. On a flapping outdoor MF8 pair it is several an hour while the fault lasts. For the subscriber: a stranger's phone rings with no sign from the network, and a redial works. This is the same symptom a hit on the caller's own loop gives. Silent, but gated by a fault and rare: medium, not high.

The verifier's traced sc4 (run_tr_sc16_p680.log) shows that a return mid-digit connects a wrong LINE (43-21 dialled, 23-21 rang), not only a false claim. So the consequence is understated. The level stays medium. The trigger is realistic: a connector re-seated, a card swapped or a card power-cycled within the caller's remaining 2-4 s of dialling, which is ordinary maintenance. It only goes wrong when the remaining digits happen to form a code beyond the link, about 0.05 per event, so it is rarer per event than finding 1. When it lands in a pause the result is a false claim, then a NOGO or B's only register held for NODIG (10 s). That also blocks B's local callers for 10 s. With the verifier's both-ways clear, a re-seated card that powers up unpoisoned is still covered: its clock vanished at the far card, which poisons and keeps the caller's M off the trunk.

This duplicates link-outage-dial-pulse. Its stated trigger, a 47 us drop, is one or two probe samples at most, against the 8 that HIT needs, so it can never count. Everything real in it is finding 1. Its fixes fail: dropping the cell on MUTE does not reach the owner's register after the claim or the fresh seizure, and a baseband card ignores MUTE. Holding A through a longer hit deletes or merges breaks, which is a wrong digit too. Fold it into finding 1.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
'An outage is a release, never a pulse', done on the card, is the right direction for 74HC. The verifier's two additions are needed and correct: clear only when the circuit is idle both ways (!a_rx && !a_s2), and gate the word with !poison. The audit copy's one-way hole is real (sc5). But the fix is not complete against REAL faults.

(1) Contact chatter defeats the entry. MEASURED, one short run: work/verify/C07-skeptic-realism/tb_chat.v, the verifier's rtl_mut card plus a pulse_rx fed one sample of A_TX a millisecond, as the probe does; log run_chat_mut.log. The CLK pin chatters for 30 ms (opens of 2.8 ms, closures of 0.2 ms): the break is counted at 159 ms, a digit 1 at 309 ms, and the card never poisons. With CLK and A chattering together the result is the same. The control, a clean 30 ms cut, poisons at 4.02 ms. The cause is that dn resets on any frame with link_up, while the 1 kHz probe misses sub-ms closures. With a random closure phase, a mostly-open burst still counts almost surely. A bumped connector usually chatters, so the fix misses a large share of its main trigger. Cure: hysteresis. Reset dn only after link_up has stood for about 2 ms, so down-time adds up across a burst. That is a counter stage or a '74, about half a package. local_trunk needs the same.

(2) A single-conductor open on A (or an open RS-422 A pair, whose failsafe level reads 0) leaves link_up true and is not caught. It is not 'out of reach of any card': a complementary A (A and /A, with 00 treated as a fault that poisons) catches every open that would show a false break. The cost is one conductor each way and a gate. It is a cost call, but the spec should say which way it went.

(3) Other carriers. local_trunk is untested, and one outage there hits 8 calls. The MF8 unit, the usual carrier, needs the same rule on MUTE: RIDE must sit above its ordinary re-frame mutes (up to about 3 ms) and below about 7 ms, so 4-6 ms. pots-trunk cannot meet the rule at all. Its link-down takes 100-200 ms, and 'no tone' means make, so a cut deletes breaks and then inserts one when link-down fires. It needs its pilot before it carries dialled calls.

(4) The spec text must also forbid HIDING a break (an outage over a make merges two breaks), and should state the 4 ms as cumulative within a burst.

(5) The price, which the auditor and verifier both state, is large per event. Every 4-256 ms hit now drops the 1-3 talking calls on a busy link, where today it is a click. That is about 10-30 dropped calls per wrong number avoided. Visible failures are acceptable (CEPT-style release on fault), but the drops can be avoided for about one package: poison only if A has moved either way within the last NODIG (10 s). A quiet circuit, talking or ringing, keeps today's ride-through, and no counter listens to it. This is optional.

(6) Low residual: B clears while A, the origin side with the caller up, is still poisoned. B's hunt can then take this trunk and lose one flood leg (a clean cannot-complete) until A's origin drops the leg.
skeptics.summary: I agree with the verifier on all three findings and on the severities. link-outage-dial-pulse is real but gated by a fault: medium, not high. An outage has to last about 7 ms or more to count, so the 47 us DEAD and the MF8 re-frame routes do not. At in-room fault rates it gives about 2e-5 wrong numbers per exchange-BH (about 0.1 per 8-256 ms event on a busy link), roughly 10x rarer than C03. On a flapping outdoor MF8 pair it is several an hour. link-return-fresh-seizure's consequence is understated: a return mid-digit connects a wrong line (verifier's traced run). Its trigger is realistic, a re-seated connector or a card swap during dialling, but rarer per event, so it stays medium. link-hit-extra-pulse duplicates the first finding and its 47 us trigger is not a pulse. The fix, with the verifier's both-ways clear and word gate, is the right direction but incomplete for real faults. I measured that a chattering clock contact never poisons the card while the probe still counts a pulse (tb_chat.v, run_chat_mut.log); an entry with hysteresis, about half a package, cures it. The fix also misses an open on the A conductor alone, which a complementary A would catch. MF8, local_trunk and pots-trunk still need their own versions, and the spec must forbid hidden breaks as well as inserted ones. Its price, dropping talking calls on 4-256 ms hits, is about 10-30 drops per wrong number avoided. Poisoning only when A has moved within the last 10 s would avoid that for about one package. Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C07-skeptic-realism/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: No timer is involved in the stuck state, so it is reachable at real timers. It needs a hardware fault. The likeliest is an open A conductor or pair into a receiver whose failsafe reads 1 while the clock conductor still runs, so the link reads up; the project's own benches model a cut exactly that way (tb_lnet.v:57, tb_ltu.v:53, tb_tie.v:36), and so do AM26LS32-class receivers. A driver stuck on, or a short to +5 V, also does it. Conforming equipment never produces it: a real origin always drops within T_KEY + T_CLAIM, and a power loss or reset at the far end stops the clock or clears the fabric, both of which give A = 0. The fault is plausible (one bad crimp or bent pin), and the effect is permanent and silent until the conductor is mended. On a local trunk one open A conductor is eight phantom seizures (local_trunk.v:127/168/188 watch only HCLK). By code reading, at real timers the 17-18 ms T_ARM watch per hold outlasts the 10 ms sweep, so the second phantom is also forwarded, and B's 2 cells and 2 resolvers are both gone, with two phantom floods downstream. I wrote tb_c08lt.v to run this and it did not run.
findings.ran: Code read at every cited line of the snapshot. Auditor's log work/audit/proto/run_pchain.log sc1 read: it shows the claimed state, identical at 100 ms and 1.1 s. My re-run of the reproducer (run_pchain.sh work/RTL.list base_sc2 +sc=2) was queued on sim.sh but got no slot in about 4 h: all 5 slots were held by work/load runners and other verify jobs. Log path would be work/verify/C08-phantom-seizure/run_base_sc2.log. I also wrote tb_c08.v (sc1 waited out to 3.0 s scaled = 24 s real, with pool timestamps and checks for a parked B11 and a leak on A11) and tb_c08lt.v (the local-trunk case at real timers). Their queued runs were waiting out wrapper timeouts, so I killed them to requeue as one job, and the permission classifier denied the requeue. They did not run and I did not requeue them. Runs that did complete: tb_net and tb_chain on the fixed copy (below).
findings.evidence: Mechanism checked step by step. (1) The monitor cell is freed only by a decided digit that does not match (net_unit.v:636-646), a CLR break (647-649) or the claim (659-665). pulse_rx.v has no timeout for a steady make: t saturates, and dig_stb and clear never fire. (2) The resolver is freed only by R_LEG, R_GONE (681-708) or rs_mine at a local claim. (3) The held B11 is bsy=1 with M stuck at 1, so fM stays 1; E is 00's M, 0, so fE never rises. port.v:176-194 then has no falling edge and B11 never releases. The one-leg forward re-patches B11 to listen to B14 (rs_two, 727-733). B14's E is B11's M (1), which goes out as A into C11: C holds it with a cell, and B14 stays up for good. (4) The classifier's T_ARM watch (584-588) ends in C_IDLE because M never falls. (5) Nothing in mini_marker or top_net touches a port that reads BUSY. The auditor's log matches all of this (B mon 01 res 01, B11->14, B14->11 bsy 1, C mon 01, unchanged at 1.1 s) and releases correctly when mended, so it is not a bench artefact: the stimulus is the bench's own cut model applied to one conductor. OVERSTATED part: 'every network call from A fails / A can't reach B' is real in the bench, but the missing unit timeout does not cause it. B never sees a rise on 11 while the conductor is stuck, held or not. A's sweep takes the lowest free E trunk (759-766), and A11 looks free because the far hold sends no backward A. This is a killer-trunk effect: it happens only when the dead channel is the hunt's first choice, and it also happens with a conductor stuck at 0. Fixes (a)-(c) leave it; only the optional (d) touches it. It is listed below as a separate root cause.
findings.notes: One real finding, bundled with a second, independent root cause (next entry). The auditor's fix (b), 'drops the legs and frees itself', is incomplete as worded. For a one-leg forward the incoming (B11) was re-patched to listen to the leg (B14). Dropping only the leg leaves the parked B11 listening to B14. When C later seizes C11->B14, B11's E (port.v:153, a_rx = E) goes to 1 and comes out on A11 toward A: a phantom seizure and a C-path crosstalk at A. The aged resolver must also write the incoming back to 00 with the hold (bsy=1). My rtl_fix does that. The 'naive' variant (rtl_naive/) was prepared to show the leak in simulation but did not run. Related C10 (MUTE_BLK keeps BUSY, so R_GONE never fires) has a different mechanism: a resolver timeout would only bound it to 10-15 s, and C10's own rs_lf fix is still needed.

findings.real_timing: Same fault as above (stuck at 1 or at 0), no timer involved. It harms calls only while the dead channel is the near sweep's first choice: the lowest free, or the highest with g. Then every flood from that exchange in that direction takes it and gets cannot-complete after T_CLAIM (2 s after b).
findings.ran: Auditor's run_pchain.log sc1 ('OBS A20 keys 1: A dirs 0100, A11 busy 1 A12 busy 0' / 'FAIL A20 can still reach its neighbour B'); code reading. Not re-run (see above).
findings.evidence: net_unit.v:759-766 keeps the lowest (or, with g, the highest) free candidate, and there is no memory of a trunk that failed to claim. The link carries no backward busy: B's hold on B11 sends A = 0 (baseband_card.v:98 a_out = a_rx = E of a port listening to 00), so A11 reads free at A. A's origin seizes A11 each time, B never sees the edge (M already 1, B11 BUSY), and the call times out. baseband.md 3.3 already accepts this cost for a four-wire link ('one call per attempt while it is broken'). Here it becomes every call, because the hunt is deterministic.
findings.notes: Separate root cause from the unit's missing timeout: the timeout fix does not change it. A remedy is the auditor's (d): an EV_NOCLAIM event naming the trunk at T_CLAIM expiry, plus a small 'failed last time' register the sweep skips, or rotating the start of the hunt.

verifier.root_cause: Root cause 1: the network unit has no timeout on a monitor cell or a resolver (permanent-signal treatment). A cell is freed only by a decided digit, a CLR break or a claim (net_unit.v:633-649, 659-665). A resolver is freed only by R_LEG, R_GONE or a local claim (681-708). pulse_rx.v has no timeout for a steady make, and a port releases only on a falling detector (port.v:176-194). The trunk cards gate A only on the clock conductor's link-up (baseband_card.v:109/154; local_trunk.v:127/188), so an A conductor that a failsafe-high receiver reads as 1 is a live seizure with no origin behind it, held for good at every exchange the flood reaches. Root cause 2 (separate): the near origin's deterministic hunt (net_unit.v:759-766) keeps taking the dead channel, because the far hold sends no backward signal and the hunt remembers no failure.
verifier.best_fix: Use the auditor's (a)+(b), with one correction. Fixed copy: work/verify/C08-phantom-seizure/rtl_fix/net_unit.v (RTL_fix.list). Each cell and each resolver gets a 2-bit age. One shared strobe steps it every T_KEY (on the board, a '4040 tap on TICK), and the age resets at attach or allocation. At age 3, i.e. 2-3 x T_KEY (10-15 s real, 1.25-1.9 s at scale 8), it expires. The legitimate maximum is T_KEY + T_CLAIM + T_REL, about 7.3 s for a resolver, and T_KEY + CLR, about 5.3 s for a cell, so a real call is never cut. An expired cell simply frees; the HOLD stays, so the faulty port is parked BUSY and releases by itself when the conductor is mended. An expired resolver takes a new action, R_AGE: it drops every leg, and for a one-leg forward (rs_two) it also rewrites the incoming to 00 with the hold. Without that rewrite the parked incoming stays patched to the leg, and the leg's next seizure leaks back out toward the faulty link. The auditor's (b) as worded misses this. Dropping the leg makes each downstream hold release (M falls, then T_REL), and each downstream cell frees at CLR, so one expiry cleans the whole flood tree. Cost is about 8 FFs (NMON = NRES = 2), a 13-bit prescaler and gates: roughly 3 packages. A cheaper equivalent uses 1 FF per cell or resolver and a Q13 tap (8.192 s), expiring at the second strobe (8.2-16.4 s): about 4 FFs plus one '4040. An event word naming the port (auditor's c) is worth adding for the alarm but is not needed for correctness. The auditor's (d) (EV_NOCLAIM at T_CLAIM, plus a skip or 'failed last time' register in the sweep) is the only item that addresses root cause 2. Tested: regression only (tb_net and tb_chain on the fixed copy, identical to the baseline). The fix's effect on the phantom itself was not simulated.
verifier.fix_tested: I ran two regressions on rtl_fix. tb_net: 88/88 PASS, output identical line for line to work/base-net.log (work/verify/C08-phantom-seizure/run_net_fix.log). tb_chain: 32/32 PASS, identical to work/base-chain.log (run_chain_fix.log). No cell or resolver expired falsely at scale 8, where the unscaled sweeps make the margin tightest. NOT run: the reproducer on the fix (tb_c08.v, which checks that the pools clear by 3 s scaled, B11 stays parked on 00, and nothing leaks out of A11), the naive variant without the incoming re-hold (rtl_naive/), and the real-timer local-trunk bench (tb_c08lt.v). The base re-run of tb_pchain +sc=2 was queued but got no sim.sh slot in about 4 h, and the requeue of the other runs was refused by the permission classifier. All benches and scripts are in work/verify/C08-phantom-seizure/ (job_fix.sh, job_naive.sh, job_lt.sh, job_all.sh) and can be run as they are.
verifier.summary:
CONFIRMED by reading every cited line of the snapshot and by the auditor's log; not re-run, because no sim slot came free in about 4 h. A seizure with no origin behind it is held for good: a monitor cell at every exchange the flood reaches, a resolver at each forwarding exchange, and one channel on each link of the tree. The cause is a stuck-at-1 A conductor, for example an open A conductor on a failsafe-high receiver while the clock conductor keeps the link up. Nothing on the net unit times out a cell or a resolver, and the held port has no edge to release on. It is silent, permanent and plausible. On a local trunk, one open A conductor is eight phantom seizures. By code reading, B loses both cells and both resolvers, and two phantom floods go on downstream. Severity high, but the trigger is a hardware fault; no conforming-equipment path reaches it.

Two root causes, not one. The bench's 'A cannot even reach B' is a killer-trunk effect: the near origin's deterministic hunt keeps taking the dead channel. The unit timeout does not fix that; only the auditor's optional (d) does.

The proposed resolver timeout (b) is incomplete as worded. For a one-leg forward, the incoming must also be written back to 00, still held. Otherwise the parked trunk stays patched to the freed leg and later leaks that leg's next seizure back toward the faulty link.

A fixed copy with 2-bit ages on one T_KEY strobe (expiry 10-15 s real, against a legitimate maximum of about 7.3 s) passes tb_net 88/88 and tb_chain 32/32 with output identical to the baseline. Its effect on the phantom itself is untested: those benches were written but not run.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: I re-derived each step from the snapshot RTL, looked for a blocking condition, and looked for a second path that makes it worse. Read-only; I ran no simulation.

per_finding.reason:
MECHANISM CONFIRMED at every cited line; all the citations are accurate.

(1) A cell frees only on a mismatching decided digit (net_unit.v:635-645), on d_clr (647-649) or on the claim (656-665). On a steady make, pulse_rx's t saturates; dig_stb needs cnt!=0 and clear needs !m, so neither ever fires.

(2) A resolver frees only on R_LEG, R_GONE (689: the incoming's BUSY clear) or rs_mine. On a phantom, the leg's M is the far hold's backward A (0), and the incoming stays bsy=1.

(3) B11 has m=1 and fm=1. Its E is 00, or B14's M after the one-leg patch (732-735); both are 0. So rel (port.v:180/186) never fires.

(4) Link-up watches only the clock conductor (baseband_card.v:109/154; local_trunk.v:127/170/188).

The auditor's sc1 log matches all of this. It started clean: idle_all passed after sc0, and the 'cla 1' flags are stale registers, not state. I found no blocking condition. The st bit and the T_ARM watch both behave as the verifier says.

WHAT BOTH MISSED: the reach. A flood has no TTL, and transits have no timers, so a phantom flood goes wherever a real flood goes. On a local trunk the verifier's arithmetic shows B forwards two phantoms: C_HOLD ends at cls_ms=18, and a read adds about 1.1 ms, so the classifier takes a hold about every 19 ms. The forwarder is free again after about 11 ms (64x9 frames plus a 1 ms confirm).

The same arithmetic holds at every downstream exchange. The second flood arrives about 18-19 ms after the first. If it lands inside C_HOLD it waits, because its st bit is still clear, and is classified just after. By then the forwarder is free and one resolver is left, so it is forwarded too.

So every exchange that both floods reach, over links with at least 2 free channels, loses both cells (NMON=2), and every such transit also loses both resolvers (NRES=2), for good. After that it can never claim and never forward. One open A conductor on one local trunk, with HCLK still running, therefore stops network calls across the whole reachable network, silently, and no event names the port. A is also cut off, because all eight of its channels in that direction are black holes.

Even the single baseband phantom leaves every exchange it reaches with 1 cell and 1 resolver. At network.md §10's load of about 0.19 E, one resolver loses about 16% of floods at each transit (Erlang B with one server, 0.19/1.19), against 1.4% with two.

NUANCES:
- Only channels idle at the moment of the fault become phantoms. A channel carrying a call has st=1 (M seen under BUSY) and is never re-classified. When its call ends it is left with M up and BUSY clear: a dead channel that the marker re-reads once a pass, with no flood.
- The trigger is a plausible single fault, not conforming equipment: an open A conductor or pair into a failsafe-high receiver while the clock conductor runs, the benches' own cut model applied to one conductor.

Why critical and not high: one conductor can remove claim and transit network-wide, permanently and silently. This is code reading; the multi-exchange two-flood case is not simulated.

Agreed; it is a separate root cause. B cannot see a rise on a stuck-at-1 M, held or not, and a stuck-at-0 conductor gives the same black hole. The far hold's a_rx is E of 00 (baseband_card.v:98), which is 0, so A11 reads free. The sweep (759-766) deterministically keeps the lowest free trunk (or, with g, the highest), so every flood from A in that direction takes the dead channel and times out at T_CLAIM. A cell or resolver timeout does not change this.

Two additions:
- On a local trunk with an open A conductor, all eight channels are dead at once. Every flood from the far end in that direction fails, and auditor fix (d)'s single-entry skip register cannot help there.
- For a leaf exchange whose only direction is the faulty one, this is total outward isolation.

I keep medium because the flood seizes every direction, so only routes that run solely through the broken direction fail. baseband.md 3.3 also already accepts a per-attempt cost for a four-wire link.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's fix is the right shape: auditor (a)+(b), plus its correction that an aged one-leg forward must re-hold the incoming on 00. I checked that correction: without it, the parked B11 stays patched to B14, and C's next seizure on B14 leaks out of A11 toward A. The ageing arithmetic is sound. Expiry falls between 2 and 3 T_KEY (10-15 s real). The legitimate maximum is about T_KEY + T_CLAIM + T_REL, roughly 7.26 s, for a resolver, and about T_KEY + CLR for a cell. Cells, the st bit and the parked hold all behave correctly afterwards, and one expiry cleans the downstream tree through M falling, then T_REL, R_GONE and CLR at each hop.

It is not complete. R_AGE writes blindly: it drops every leg, and for rs_two it writes ent(in,00,bsy=1) whatever the incoming's state is.
- If the incoming has already released (M down, fM down), this strands it BUSY with no edge to release on. That is exactly the hazard the classifier's T_ARM watch exists to prevent. The port stays stuck until a far seizure of at least T_ARM followed by a drop clears it, and that far call is lost.
- On the C10 path (a local-trunk cut: MUTE_BLK holds BUSY, so R_GONE never fires), the incoming and every leg have already released themselves through fM and fE. The aged resolver's drops can then land on legs that now carry other calls, and it re-holds a dead incoming.
- With C10's rs_lf fix in place that path dissolves first. What is left is a mend race: the write lands just after rel, a window of about 1-2 ms per 5 s strobe.

Better: let the resolver's existing once-a-pass watch latch the incoming's M, and gate R_AGE on it.
- M up: drop the legs and re-hold the incoming. The legs cannot have self-released, because their E is that M.
- M down: dissolve and write nothing.
T_REL (256 ms) is far longer than the gap between the latch and the write (2 ms or less), so no race is left.

Also:
- (c), the event word naming the port, should be required, not optional. After the fix the stuck port is parked silently, and the far end's killer-trunk effect continues, so only an alarm leads anyone to the conductor.
- (d) is the only remedy for root cause 2, but a single-entry 'failed last' register does not help a local trunk, where all 8 channels die together. A per-direction no-claim count (EV_NOCLAIM) feeding an alarm, plus a maintenance make-busy, is the practical remedy.
- The cheaper Q13 variant keeps only about 0.9 s of margin (8.19 s against 7.26 s) and breaks if the T_KEY or T_CLAIM straps change. Prefer the strobe derived from T_KEY.
- The fix's effect on the phantom itself is still unsimulated; only the tb_net and tb_chain regressions ran.
skeptics.summary:
The core finding is confirmed by an independent re-derivation at every cited line. The citations are accurate, I found no blocking condition, and the auditor's sc1 log is clean and consistent. A seizure with no origin behind it can come from an open A conductor into a failsafe-high receiver while the clock conductor runs. It holds its port, a monitor cell, a resolver and a channel at every hop, for good. Nothing on the unit times a cell or a resolver out, and the held port has no edge to release on. The verifier is right that the near-end killer trunk is a separate root cause that (a)-(c) do not fix, and right that auditor fix (b) needs the one-leg re-hold.

The verifier and auditor understate the reach. A flood has no TTL, and the verifier's own real-timer arithmetic repeats at every downstream exchange: a classifier hold every ~19 ms against a forwarder that is free again after ~11 ms. So one open A conductor on a local trunk sends two phantom floods that take both cells and both resolvers at every exchange they both reach over links with at least 2 free channels. That silently ends network calls, both claims and transit, across the reachable network. I rate it critical rather than high. That rests on code reading; the multi-exchange case is not simulated.

The verifier's fix has an unconditional-write hazard. R_AGE re-holds the incoming BUSY, and drops legs, even when the incoming has already released. That strands a port BUSY with no edge to release on and can write to reused legs (the C10 path, or a mend race). Gating R_AGE on the incoming's M, latched by the resolver's existing watch, closes both.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity: whether it happens at real timers with real telephones, cards and plausible faults; how often; what the subscriber hears; whether the severity is right; whether the fix suits 74HC hardware and is complete

per_finding.reason: I read the code and it confirms the mechanism. A monitor cell is freed only by a mismatching digit (net_unit.v:633-646), a CLR break (647-649) or a claim (666-668). A resolver is freed only by R_LEG, R_GONE (681-708) or rs_mine. The held incoming port has no falling edge to release on (port.v:176-194). The bench stimulus (tb_pchain.v:125, ba_i[T11] = stuck11 || aa[T11]) is a fair model of the fault, and run_pchain.log sc1 shows the state unchanged 8.8 s (real) later and released after the mend. REALISM: no conforming-equipment path reaches it. Every origin drops within T_KEY+T_CLAIM. A far power loss or card pull stops the clock, and link_up then masks A. A permanent-loop subscriber never floods without key 1. The trigger is a hardware fault on A alone while the clock conductor stays up (baseband_card.v:109/154, local_trunk.v:127/188). With the documented parts it is plausible: baseband.md 3.4 and local-trunk.md put 26LS32 receivers between racks, and those read HIGH with their inputs open. One nuance on 'one bad crimp or bent pin': on RS-422 one open wire of a pair usually still receives, so the whole pair must open (a half-seated connector, a damaged pair). On the single-ended 74HC baseline one conductor is enough, but the docs never say how the A input is pulled. baseband.md 3.3's 'A = 0 either way' holds only for a whole-cable cut. The documented 4-wire population (no clock conductor) with fail-high receivers makes a pulled cable N phantoms, which is the most common link fault. RATE: the trigger is measured in faults per link-year, not per busy hour. Once present it acts in every busy hour until repaired, and nothing alarms. One phantom on one baseband channel takes a monitor at every exchange downstream and a resolver at every downstream transit. On the documents' own loads (monitor.md 4: 0.09-0.26 E a leaf; network.md 10: 0.19 E a transit), going from 2 to 1 raises the loss from about 0-2.6% to about 8-21% of calls to each downstream exchange, and from about 1.5% to about 16% of floods at each downstream transit. That is roughly 5-9 extra lost calls per exchange per busy hour on monitor.md's 48-line model. An open A pair on a local trunk gives 8 phantoms, of which min(8, NRES) are forwarded at real timers because the 18 ms T_ARM watch outlasts the 10 ms sweep. B and every exchange behind it then lose all their cells and resolvers: 100% of network calls into or through that subtree fail. More stuffing does not help, because 8 exceeds any plausible pool. A C-side exchange whose only channel is held gets no trunk at all. WHAT THE SUBSCRIBER HEARS: after dialling 1 e b, silence, then cannot-complete 2 s after b, or at once where no trunk is left. It is never a wrong number and never crosstalk in the unfixed RTL: B11 and B14 are patched only to each other and C11 listens to 00. So it is not critical. Silent, permanent loss of network service far from the fault, from one plausible fault, is high. I agree with the verifier on the verdict, the severity and the split of A's failure into a second root cause.

This is a separate root cause, as the verifier says. B11 reads a stuck M either way, so B never sees A's rise whether the port is held or not. A11 looks free at A because B11's a_rx is E from 00, which is 0. The hunt (net_unit.v:759-766) keeps taking the lowest free candidate and remembers nothing, so the timeout fix leaves this untouched. The log shows it: 'A20 keys 1: A dirs 0100, A11 busy 1', then no claim. REALISM: a conductor stuck at 0 reaches it too, and stuck at 0 is the fail-to-idle polarity I recommend below. The same deterministic hunt also turns an open C conductor into the classic killer trunk (the call completes with no speech). So once the phantom is fixed, this becomes the usual symptom of an open A. On a single baseband channel it multiplies a 1-of-N channel loss into about 100% failure of A's floods in that direction whenever the dead channel is A's first choice, which it always is if it is the lowest. That is roughly all of A's ~43 network calls per busy hour when A sits at the end of a chain. On a local trunk the whole link is dead one way anyway, so it only makes the failure 2 s slower and silent. Every failure is a clean cannot-complete 2 s after b, from a rare hardware fault. That matches baseband.md 3.3's knowingly accepted 'one call per attempt' cost for a 4-wire cut, so medium is right. On the remedy: the auditor's (d) misfires as sketched. A vacant code, which is an ordinary misdial, also ends in no claim at T_CLAIM on the trunk of every direction. A one-shot 'failed last time' skip only halves the failure rate against a true killer (fail, skip, retry, fail), and a sticky skip removes good trunks after misdials. The protocol has no seizure acknowledgement, so the origin cannot tell a dead channel from a vacant code on one attempt. The realistic remedy is an EV_NOCLAIM event naming the trunk, feeding per-trunk ineffective-attempt counts for maintenance (counters.md). Rotating the hunt would break the opposite-order glare rule (network.md 5).

skeptics.fix_assessment: The verifier's rtl_fix is correct and minimal for the RTL, and cheap in 74HC (work/verify/C08-phantom-seizure/rtl_fix/net_unit.v). It adds a 2-bit age per cell and per resolver on a shared T_KEY strobe, expiring in (2,3] x T_KEY, which is 10-15 s. R_AGE is set only from R_NONE, and a same-tick R_GONE or R_LEG from the watch overrides it because it is assigned later in the source. R_AGE drops every leg (695: != R_LEG) and puts a one-leg incoming back on 00 still held. That re-hold is necessary. The auditor's (b) as worded leaves B11 patched to B14, and C's next seizure on that channel would leak out of A11 into A as a seizure carrying C's caller's pulses. Timing margin: the legitimate maximum lifetime is about 7.3-7.4 s at real timers. The worst case is a cell in M_DONE waiting on the marker's att_ack, freed by CLR after the origin's T_CLAIM drop: T_KEY+ID+T_CLAIM+CLR. The floor of 2 x 5 s leaves about 2.6 s. Built from '4040 taps, use Q13 with a 1-bit age (8.2-16.4 s) or Q12 with a 2-bit age at count 3 (8.2-12.3 s). Both keep at least 0.8 s of margin. Board cost is about 2-3 packages (two '393s or '74s, a '4040 tap, gates), plus one more write type for the stepping sequencer that network.md 10 already needs. Any order of expiry across exchanges converges, because a downstream re-hold still releases when its M falls. Regression is clean: tb_net 88/88 and tb_chain 32/32 are identical to the baseline. The fix's effect on the phantom itself is still not simulated. It is incomplete in three ways. (1) It emits no event. Without one, the parked port at B and the killer channel at A stay silent, and the symptoms show up exchanges away from the fault. An event word naming the port at expiry costs almost nothing, since the ev_glare and ev_notrunk path already exists, and it should be part of the fix, not optional. (2) A zero-cost hardware complement is missing from both the auditor's and the verifier's fix: specify that the A receiver fails to IDLE (A = 0) on an open line. On the 26LS32 that means choosing the pair's polarity; the A path's '14 already inverts. On the single-ended baseline it is one pull resistor. Also correct baseband.md 3.3's 'A = 0 either way' and say the same in local-trunk.md. This keeps the likeliest trigger (an open pair or conductor, or a pulled 4-wire cable) from ever reaching the unit, and it avoids a floating RC-and-'14 input, which would flicker into pflap-type pulses. The timeout is still needed for stuck drivers and shorts. (3) A negligible race, a nit: if the fault is mended, or an upstream expiry drops M, and a strobe with age 2 falls within about 1.5 ms of the incoming port's release, R_AGE can re-hold a port whose M and fM are already 0. That port stays BUSY with no edge to release on. The odds are about 3e-4 per event. Gating the re-hold on the incoming still showing M at its last turn (1 FF per resolver) closes it. The intermittent form of the same conductor fault (the proto slice's tb_pflap: an outage counted as a dial pulse, a wrong number) is a separate and worse cluster, and this fix does not touch it.
skeptics.summary: I agree with the verifier on both findings. The phantom seizure is real and needs a hardware fault. I found no conforming-equipment path: origins always drop, and power loss or a card pull stops the clock, which masks A. The trigger is an A-only stuck-at-1 while the clock conductor stays up. With the documented 26LS32 receivers (open pair reads HIGH) and the single-ended baseline's unspecified input pull, it is plausible, though on RS-422 the whole pair has to open, not one pin. Its rate is in faults per link-year. Once present it is permanent and silent. One baseband channel's phantom cuts a monitor and a resolver at every exchange downstream: calls lost there rise from about 0-3% to 8-21%, and floods lost at each transit from about 1.5% to about 16%, on the documents' own loads. An open A pair on a local trunk exhausts every cell and resolver in B's subtree, so 100% of network calls into or through it fail, whatever the stuffing. Callers hear silence, then cannot-complete; never a wrong number or crosstalk. Severity high is right. The near-end killer trunk is a separate root cause, rated medium. It is also reached by a conductor stuck at 0 and by an open C conductor, and the auditor's 'failed last time' remedy misfires on vacant codes. The verifier's fix (2-bit ages, R_AGE dropping legs and putting a one-leg incoming back on 00, still held) is correct, costs about 2-3 packages and passes regression, but its effect on the phantom is unsimulated. It should add an event word at expiry, and the docs should require A receivers that fail to idle, which costs nothing (pair polarity or a pull resistor) and stops the likeliest trigger. A one-in-thousands race at repair time can leave one port BUSY for good; it is a nit. I ran no simulation, because none would settle a disagreement.
