findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers. The mechanism has no timer race. The claim's backward A has to be gone for at least T_REL (256 ms), so that the trunk port clears itself, at some point between the claim and N_DONE. That window runs from b counted to s counted, about 0.8 to 3.5 s. A loss within about T_ARM after the N_DONE write also strands the caller. Known triggers, all rare: (1) a link outage of 256 ms or more. This is a fault, and a cheap one to hit: baseband_card's '123 drops A within about 50 us of losing TX_CLK, and local_trunk does the same. Examples are a pulled or loose tie cable, a carrier resync, or a far or transit exchange reset or brown-out. (2) Glare on the last free channel, followed by the far origin abandoning. This needs no fault: the far caller hangs up, dials its own code (O_LOCAL drop), dials 8 or 9, or hits the 5 s rule. A cut on either side of a transit does the same, because T_in's A drops. The far end's own outcomes are NOT triggers: refusal, busy, NODIG and cannot-complete all keep CLM=1 (mini_marker.v:326,370,407,488). The only far writes with CLM=0 follow the far register's r_gone, which comes after this side has gone. Consequences: the stranded caller always gets silence with no NOGO and is BUSY until on-hook. The listen-in additionally needs another call to take the freed channel while the stranded caller still waits. That is likely at busy times, because the dead trunk (A11) is the lowest-numbered east trunk, the first an outgoing sweep takes. The listen-in is one-way: the stranded caller hears the far party.
findings.ran: (1) Rebuilt and re-ran the auditor's S4 in my own bench, work/verify/C11-claimed-trunk-loss/tb_c11.v. It is tb_orig's two-exchange site plus plusargs for B's crystal (+bppm, +boff), a scenario S7 (the caller hangs up 20 ms plus 0-1 ms after the claim, 12 trials with B at +100 ppm so B's tick phase walks across the whole ms), and an optional port T_REL define. Runs were at scale 8 through sim.sh. Logs are under /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C11-claimed-trunk-loss/: c11_snap.log is the snapshot (S4 and S7). c11_fix.log is rtl_c11/net_unit.v, the auditor's `lost` fix alone with no o_brk and no mini_marker changes. c11_fix_trel26.log is the auditor's fix with ports' T_REL 26 against CLR 32 (S7). c11_alt.log and c11_alt_trel26.log are my alternative, rtl_alt/net_unit.v. net_c11.log and net_alt.log are tb_net on both fixes, and lfull_c11.log and lfull_alt.log are tb_lfull on both. All obj dirs are deleted. Running this at real timers would decide nothing, because nothing in the mechanism depends on the ratio of timers.
findings.evidence: RTL: net_unit.v:794-804 sets `claimed` and `trunk` on the first M sample and never looks at them again. N_WAITCL (:881) goes to N_DONE on claimed && o_last && dmo==0, and N_DONE (:818-822) writes caller<-trunk with BSY. During the flood the caller listened to 00. Once N_DONE is written its E is the trunk's M, which is already 0, so fE never rises, and port.v:176-193 releases a port only on a fall of fM or fE. The trunk port clears itself T_REL after its M falls and is huntable again. This contradicts the old network.md: 'The claim is a level, not a wink'. The new network.md 4.1 has no claim-loss row, and its section 10 lists 'a cut during a dialled call' as not run. My re-run on the snapshot (c11_snap.log) matches the auditor's run_s2_5.log: A nst stays 5 through the cut, then N_DONE writes A20<-A11 and A20 is BUSY. A22's call takes A11, and the log shows 'A22 follows B20 4/4; A20 follows B20 4/4' and FAIL 'A20 does NOT hear A22's call'. This is not a bench artefact: the cut is all three conductors, which the baseband card sees as link-down, and the phones dial conforming scaled pulses.
findings.notes: This is one root cause: a claim treated as an edge rather than a level. The auditor's fix (c11_fix.log) closes S4: nst 5->7 about 4 ms after the cut, NOGO goes to A20 ('A20 follows B20 2/4'), and it passes tb_net 88/88 (net_c11.log). It is not safe as specified. (a) Its safety against callers who hang up rests on an absolute margin of about 2 ms. On the snapshot, the claim's drop reaches A 0.844 ms before r_gone in 10 of 12 phases (c11_snap.log S7), and the fourth low sample comes about 2.2 ms after gone. That holds only while every port's T_REL (an RC-and-'14 on the board, port.v:134,175) is no faster than the register's counted CLR by more than about 2 ms, which is under 1% of 256 ms. With ports' T_REL 26 against CLR 32, all 12 callers who hung up after the claim were left BUSY on-hook: the NOGO landed at +29.3 to +31.2 ms, after A20's own release at 26 ms (c11_fix_trel26.log). Every caller who abandons a network call between the claim and the last digit would hit this, the C17 hazard made common. (b) It turns documented glare (network.md section 5) into two cannot-completes, and tb_lfull goes red: 'B21 hears A31' and 'A31 hears B21: residual glare joins the two callers' FAIL (lfull_c11.log). The auditor's 'realistic' note, 'the persistence is required', is right, but 4 samples is too short a persistence.

verifier.root_cause: net_unit.v:794-804 latches `claimed` on the first M sample of a held trunk and never re-reads it. N_WAITCL (:881) then writes caller<-trunk at N_DONE (:818-822) whatever the trunk's M is now. A claim lost for T_REL before N_DONE leaves the trunk port cleared and huntable, and the caller latched to it with no fM or fE edge left to release it (port.v:176-193). The RTL treats the claim as an edge, although the spec calls it a level.
verifier.fix_tested: Auditor's fix alone (rtl_c11, fix c only): tb_c11 S4 plus S7 at T_REL=CLR passes 19/19 (c11_fix.log) and tb_net passes 88/88 (net_c11.log). tb_c11 S7 with ports' T_REL 26 against CLR 32 fails: 12/12 callers were left BUSY on-hook (c11_fix_trel26.log). tb_lfull gives 40 checks, 2 errors: the two glare 'joins the two callers' checks (lfull_c11.log). Alternative (rtl_alt: 16-pass persistence plus N_DONE gated on lost==0): tb_c11 S4 plus S7 passes 19/19 (c11_alt.log), S7 at T_REL 26 passes 16/16 checks with 12/12 trials clean (c11_alt_trel26.log), tb_net passes 88/88 (net_alt.log) and tb_lfull passes 40/40 with glare still joined (lfull_alt.log). The snapshot baseline fails S4 with the listen-in, 'A20 follows B20 4/4' (c11_snap.log). All logs are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C11-claimed-trunk-loss/.
verifier.summary: Confirmed, medium: one root cause, and the RTL departs from the spec's own rule that 'the claim is a level'. The origin latches the claim once and never re-checks it. When the claimed trunk's backward A is lost for T_REL or longer before the last digit, the trunk clears itself, but N_DONE still latches the caller to it. The caller then gets silence with no NOGO, and later hears the far party of the next call that takes that channel. I reproduced it on the snapshot ('A20 follows B20 4/4'). It is reachable at real timers, but only with a link outage or far reset of 256 ms or more, or glare followed by the far origin abandoning. Far refusals and busy do not trigger it, because they keep CLAIM. The auditor's 4-sample fix closes the hole and passes tb_net 88/88, but it is not safe as it stands. Its protection for callers who hang up rests on a margin of about 2 ms between the ports' RC T_REL and the register's counted CLR: with ports 19% fast, 12/12 such callers were left BUSY. It also breaks tb_lfull's documented glare result (2 FAILs). A 128 ms persistence (16 passes at scale) with N_DONE gated on the claim level fixes both, for the same cost: S4 closed, S7 clean at both T_REL settings, tb_net 88/88, tb_lfull 40/40. Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C11-claimed-trunk-loss/ (NOTES.md, tb_c11.v, rtl_c11/, rtl_alt/, the logs).

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: I re-derived each step from the RTL on my own, looked for a condition that blocks it, and looked for a second path that makes it worse.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived the mechanism on my own and it holds step by step. net_unit.v:794-804 latches `claimed`/`trunk` on the first M sample, and the watch is gated on !claimed, so nothing reads the trunk again. N_WAITCL :881 needs only claimed && o_last && dmo==0. N_DONE :818-822 writes caller<-trunk with BSY. Through the flood the caller listened to 00 (log: 'A wr dst 20 src 00 bsy 1'), so its fe=0. After N_DONE its E is the trunk's M, which is already 0, so fE never arms, and port.v:176-193 releases a port only on a FALL of fM or fE. The caller is held BUSY with no edge until it goes on-hook.

I found nothing that blocks it:
- o_gone looks only at the register.
- The classifier is masked off the trunk by `mine`, because d_held still names it.
- T_CLAIM runs only while !claimed.
- The guard applies only before f2.

I checked every far-side write in mini_marker.v. All of them keep CLM=1: lines 326, 370, 407, 424, 437, 443, 450, 477, 488-489 and 545. CLM goes to 0 only on the r_gone paths (400, 470) and in S_YIELD (520), which a claimed trunk can never reach. So the claim is a constant level (a_rx = e||clm) from CLAIM to release. That means a level watch is valid, and far refusals, busy and NODIG are not triggers. The verifier is right on this.

I checked the logs, and they match the verdict:
- c11_snap: 'A20 follows B20 4/4', FAIL.
- c11_fix: S4 closed.
- c11_fix_trel26: 12/12 callers left BUSY on-hook.
- lfull_c11: the 2 glare FAILs.
- c11_alt and c11_alt_trel26: PASS.
- tb_net: 88/88 on both fixes, which is the baseline count (base-net.log 88).

The one-way direction is right. A20 captures A11's C, which is B's side. Nobody listens to A20.

My additions and corrections:

(1) Timing. The freed trunk clears at T_REL (fM falls) but stays BUSY for another T_REL through fe. Its E was the off-hook caller, and after rel it listens to 00. So it becomes huntable about 2*T_REL after the loss, not T_REL. This changes nothing material.

(2) A mitigation neither report mentions. Once the overheard call's A has stood T_ARM at the stranded caller, its fE arms. When that call ends, A falls and the stranded caller releases itself (dial tone if still off-hook). So the listen-in is bounded to one call.

(3) An aggravation neither report mentions. Suppose the far end reseizes the freed channel while the origin waits.
- If the rise comes while A11 is still fe-BUSY, st is set. The far flood is then never held here, and at N_DONE the caller is connected to the far caller's flood.
- If the rise comes after that, `mine` hides it from the classifier until N_DONE clears d_held. It is then classified late, so this exchange's monitor misses the rise, and so do downstream monitors, which see only the late forward's rise. That breaks monitor.md rule 1 and risks a wrong number.
Both cases are rare and share the same root cause. The fix closes them, because N_DROP runs at P, before the far port can release and be reseized.

(4) The transit resolver takes a claim on one sample in the same way (R_LEG, :683-687). Its unguarded window is only about T_ARM plus the write latency, and a loss there reaches the origin through T_in's E, so the origin-side fix covers it.

(5) I tested a candidate fault-free trigger and it is not reachable. The candidate was a late one-leg F_WRITE way-back (f_in<-leg, CLM 0) landing after this exchange's own claim. F_WRITE follows classification by 10-30 ms, and a claim needs e and b (more than about 1 s).

(6) Framing. 'The RTL departs from the spec' is overstated. The new network.md §4 table says 'claim: the FIRST M seen on a held trunk. Keep it' and 'connect: at the last digit write the caller listening to the kept trunk', and the RTL implements exactly that. 'The claim is a level' concerns the far end holding CLAIM, which it does. The defect is a spec gap: release-by-level assumes the caller is patched to the trunk, and it is not until connect. The spec and the RTL both need the rule.

Severity: medium is right. In kind it is a privacy failure (one-way listen-in by a caller who dialled someone else) plus a silent dead call. The trigger is rare: a link outage or far reset of 256 ms or more inside a window of about 0.8-3.5 s, or glare on the last free channel followed by the far origin abandoning. The caller must also still be waiting in silence when the channel is reused.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The auditor's 4-sample `lost` watch closes S4 but should not be adopted. Its safety for a caller who hangs up after the claim rests on an absolute margin of about 2 ms between the far port's RC T_REL and the register's counted CLR. With ports at T_REL 26 against CLR 32, 12/12 such callers were left BUSY on-hook (c11_fix_trel26.log). That failure needs the caller's own port to be fast as well, which is likely with correlated RC parts. The watch also turns documented glare into two cannot-completes (tb_lfull, 2 FAILs).

The verifier's alternative is correct and close to minimal. It has two parts:
1. Keep counting M-low samples of `trunk` while claimed in N_NET/N_WAITCL, and abandon with O_NOGO through N_DROP at a persistence P of about 128 ms real (16 passes at scale), checked after o_gone and the guard.
2. Gate N_DONE on lost==0.

It costs one counter and an AND term, and its evidence holds: S4 closed, S7 clean at T_REL 32 and 26, tb_net 88/88, tb_lfull 40/40.

I would state the bounds on P explicitly for Joel:
- P must exceed the longest dial break (about 75 ms), so glare stays joined.
- P must exceed the skew between the ports' RC T_REL and the counted CLR, so r_gone wins for a caller who hangs up.
- P must stay below the earliest moment the far port can release and be reseized (the far RC T_REL, about 180 ms at -30%). The watch cannot tell a claim from a new far seizure, and a reseize would reset `lost` and pass the gate.

128 ms sits inside that window of roughly 80 to 180 ms. The same N_DROP at P also closes the late-classification variant (a far reseize hidden by `mine`).

What remains open is a loss that starts within about T_ARM of the N_DONE write, about 1% of the window. It can be closed optionally by keeping the same comparator watching until the trunk's M has stood T_ARM after the write, and writing the caller to NOGO if `lost` reaches P first. The caller's own hang-up cannot fire this, because its claim drop comes T_REL later. It is low priority.

network.md §4 needs the matching rule, for example 'claim lost for 128 ms before connect: drop the trunks, nogo'. §10's 'a cut during a dialled call' should become a run bench; tb_c11 S4 is ready for it.
skeptics.summary:
Confirmed, medium, and I agree with the verifier on substance. I re-derived the mechanism on my own. The origin latches the claim on one M sample (net_unit.v:794-804), and N_DONE (:881, :818-822) connects the caller whatever the trunk's M is at that moment. The caller listened to 00 through the flood, so its fE never arms, and port.v releases a port only on a detector fall. The caller is stranded BUSY in silence, and the trunk clears itself and can be hunted again. I found no blocker. Every far write to a claimed trunk keeps CLM=1 except after r_gone, so the claim really is a constant level, which makes a level watch valid.

Refinements the verifier and auditors missed:
- The freed trunk becomes huntable about 2*T_REL after the loss, because fe keeps it BUSY for a second T_REL.
- The listen-in is bounded. When the overheard call ends, the stranded caller's fE, armed by that call's A, falls and releases it.
- A far reseizure of the freed channel during the wait is hidden from the classifier by `mine`. If it arrives after the trunk's BUSY has cleared, it is classified only after N_DONE, so the monitors miss the rise and a wrong number becomes possible. If it arrives while the trunk is still BUSY, the flood is never held here, and at N_DONE the caller hears the far caller's flood instead. The same fix closes both.
- The transit resolver takes a claim on one sample in the same way. Its window is only about T_ARM, and the origin fix covers it.
- 'Departs from the spec' is overstated. The new network.md §4 table literally specifies 'the FIRST M seen ... keep it', so this is a spec gap rather than an RTL deviation.

On the fix: the auditor's 4-sample watch is unsafe. It relies on a 2 ms margin between RC and counted timers, and it breaks documented glare. The verifier's version (about 128 ms of persistence, with N_DONE gated on lost==0) is correct. P must sit between the longest dial break and the far port's earliest re-release, about 80 to 180 ms, and 128 ms does. A small window after the N_DONE write is left, and a post-connect T_ARM watch can optionally close it.

I ran no simulation; every disagreement follows from the RTL. My notes are at /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C11-skeptic-mechanism/NOTES.md.

skeptics.lens: REALISM AND SEVERITY: real timers, real telephones, real 74HC cards, plausible faults; rate per exchange per busy hour; what the subscriber experiences; is the fix right for 74HC

per_finding.reason:
The mechanism is real and correctly explained. I re-read the snapshot. net_unit.v:795-804 latches `claimed` once. N_WAITCL (:881) goes to N_DONE on o_last whatever the trunk's M is now, and N_DONE (:818-822) writes caller<-trunk with BSY. port.v:176-193 releases only on a fall of fM or fE, so a caller whose E never stood T_ARM has no edge to clear it. c11_snap.log S4 shows exactly this: N_DONE writes A20<-A11 at 789, A22 takes A11 at 859, and 'A20 follows B20 4/4'.

One detail is loose. The dead trunk is not huntable T_REL after the loss. Its E was the caller's hook, so fe keeps it BUSY for a second T_REL: about 512 ms in all.

REAL TIMERS. The mechanism involves no timer race. It needs only the claim gone for at least about 256 ms (min of the far port's RC T_REL and the owner's CLR). That loss has to start inside the claim-to-last-digit window, which is about 2.5 s: 3311 to 5828 ms in network.md 4.3, and 1.8-3.6 s at 0.8 s pauses.

TRIGGERS. I agree with the verifier's list. The far exchange's refusal, busy, NODIG and cannot-complete keep CLM: mini_marker.v:326, 370, 407, 437, 477 and 488-489 all use ctx_clm, and only the writes after r_gone clear it. The baseband tie and the local trunk drop A within a few frames of losing the far clock. So the plausible faults are:
- a pulled or loose tie cable, or a reseated card;
- far or transit power loss;
- a far or transit reset of any length, which clears CLM for good.
MF8 relock takes milliseconds, so it belongs to C07, not here. Glare is the fault-free trigger, when the other glared caller then hangs up, dials its own code (O_LOCAL), dials 8 or 9, or hits the 5 s rule.

RATE. I used the documents' traffic: 3 calls per line per hour, 20-50% leaving, so about 15-65 network originations per exchange per busy hour.
- Each interruption of 256 ms or more (or reset) of a path element during the busy hour has about a 3-10% chance of stranding one caller. At one such fault per element per month, that is roughly 1e-4 strands per exchange per busy hour.
- Glare: the chance that exactly one channel is free is about 1.0-1.6% (Erlang, at the reference loads). About 0.12 flood seizures a second each way, and a 3-10 ms blind window, give roughly 0.005-0.02 glares per link per busy hour. 10-30% of those strand a caller, about 5e-4 to 6e-3 per link per busy hour. A small network sees about 100 times fewer, because the rate goes with the square of the flood rate.
- Glare already joins two strangers by design (network.md 5), so glare-plus-abandon adds only modest harm.

LISTEN-IN. The dead trunk was this origin's first choice, so its next flood takes it again, and so does a transit forward. I put the listen-in at about 5-20% of strands at the busy hour. The verifier says 'likely'; I think that overstates it. It needs a call claimed through that direction whose ringback arrives before the stranded caller gives up. Once ringback arrives, the stranded caller stays on the line.

WHAT THE SUBSCRIBER HEARS. After the last digit there is silence with no tone, and the line is BUSY to incoming calls. Hanging up clears it cleanly. Sometimes, seconds later, the caller hears ringback, then a stranger's 'hello', one way only. The overheard pair never know.

SEVERITY. This is not a silent wrong number for the caller, who knows the call failed. It is a silent privacy leak for a third party, and it comes from an event the specification names ('a cut during a dialled call'; the 'Link down' row promises that a call in progress releases). It is rare and needs a fault or glare. Medium is right: above a clean cannot-complete, below critical.

The verifier's evidence and reasoning are otherwise right. Two wording errors do not change the verdict:
- The longest conforming dial break is 102.9 ms (register.md 1: 7-12 pps, 56-72% break), not 'about 70 ms'.
- The 'shorter persistence of roughly 40 ms, still above the RC skew' is below the verifier's own tested skew: 19% is about 49 ms real, and 40 ms is 5 passes at scale against a 6 ms skew.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
REJECT THE AUDITOR'S 4-SAMPLE FIX. The verifier is right. At real timers its margin over the register's gone stays about 2 ms in absolute terms, because the 1 ms sample quantisation does not scale, and that is under 1% of CLR. The '14 RC detectors vary far more than that. Their spread is unmeasured (fabric.md 8), but the '14's VT- spread alone gives roughly 0.7x to 1.4x the nominal time.

With that fix, a caller who hangs up between the claim and the last digit is left BUSY on-hook in two conditions together: the far or transit port's RC releases more than about 2 ms before CLR, and the caller's own RC releases before the NOGO lands. The verifier's 'every caller' holds only because its bench gave every port the same T_REL (12/12 at T_REL 26 against CLR 32). On real boards it is still a large fraction of abandons after the claim, which happen on a few percent of network calls. That is on the order of 0.1-0.5 stuck lines per exchange per busy hour, far worse than C11 itself. It also turns documented glare into two cannot-completes (tb_lfull, 2 FAILs).

ACCEPT THE VERIFIER'S ALTERNATIVE. Its shape is right: persistence of about T_REL/2 (128 passes, 16 at scale), fired after o_gone and the guard check, with N_DONE gated on the last sample being high (rtl_alt: S4 closed, S7 clean at T_REL 32 and 26, tb_net 88/88, tb_lfull 40/40 with glare still joined).

It is cheap and idiomatic in 74HC:
- one 74HC4040 on TICK, asynchronously reset by each high sample of the claimed trunk (or by !claimed or !o_net), with Q8 = 128 ms, the same parts and taps as the register's own 8/128/256 timer;
- half a '74 for 'the last sample was high';
- the origin's existing d_trunk comparators, which after the claim match only the kept trunk.
The origin's tmr cannot be reused, because the guard counts on it in N_NET.

Refinements:
1. State the persistence's three bounds at real timers.
   - Above 103 ms, the longest conforming break, so glare stays joined. The bench's 12 ms breaks are 96 ms real, so tb_lfull 5 already tests close to the worst case.
   - Above CLR minus the fastest T_REL on the path plus a pass, so that gone wins when the caller hangs up. The claim falls at the first incoming-side port on the path to release, so a multi-hop path samples the fast tail.
   - Below about 2 x the minimum T_REL. The dead trunk stays BUSY through fe until then, so N_DROP never writes over a re-hunted channel. The verifier's 'shorter than T_REL' is conservative.
   128 ms meets all three while no RC runs more than about 45% fast. Either write that tolerance into fabric.md, or also take C17's fix (CLR clearly shorter than the worst RC T_REL), which makes the margin independent of the RCs.
2. Drop the verifier's '~40 ms' option. It is unsafe without C17's fix, and it breaks glare joins.
3. A residual remains: a loss that starts within about T_ARM plus write latency after the connect, about 1% of the original exposure. It can be closed by keeping the watch running for T_ARM plus the persistence after N_DONE and writing NOGO to the caller if it fills. That is the same pattern as the marker's S_WATCH and the unit's C_HOLD. It is optional.
4. Add a 'claim lost for 128 ms before the connect: drop the trunks, nogo' row to exchange/network.md 4.1, and put the cut in the not-run list of section 10 as the S4 bench.
5. The fix does not touch C07: outages of 8-128 ms are still counted as pulses by the owner's register.

No simulation was needed. The disagreements are arithmetic on the logs and documents already cited.
skeptics.summary:
Confirmed at medium severity; I agree with the verifier on the finding and its severity. The origin treats the claim as an edge (net_unit.v:795-804, :881). A claim lost for about 256 ms or more between b and the last digit leaves the caller latched to a dead trunk, with silence and no tone, and BUSY until they hang up. In an estimated 5-20% of those cases at the busy hour, the next call to use that freed channel is overheard one way.

It is reachable at real timers and needs no timer race. The triggers are:
- a cut, loose or reseated tie;
- far or transit power loss, or any far or transit reset;
- glare, followed by the other glared caller abandoning.
Far refusal, busy and NODIG are not triggers, because they keep CLM.

On rough rates, this is about 1e-4 strands per exchange per busy hour at one qualifying fault a month. Glare adds roughly 5e-4 to 6e-3 per link per busy hour in the reference network, and far less in small networks.

Corrections to the verifier:
- 'Likely' overstates the listen-in odds.
- The dead trunk becomes huntable about 2 x T_REL after the loss, not T_REL.
- The longest conforming dial break is 103 ms, not about 70.
- Its '~40 ms' shorter-persistence option is unsafe at its own tested 19% RC skew (about 49 ms real).

The auditor's 4-sample fix should be rejected. It would leave many callers who abandon after the claim stuck BUSY on-hook, with a ~2 ms margin against unmeasured RC spread, which is worse than the bug, and it breaks the documented glare join. The verifier's 128 ms persistence with a gated N_DONE is the right 74HC fix: a '4040 on TICK with Q8, half a '74, and the existing comparators. Its margin against fast RC detectors should be stated, or C17's fix (CLR shorter than the worst T_REL) taken with it. A post-connect watch would optionally close the remaining ~T_ARM window.

Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C11-skeptic-realism/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: Yes. tb_fx runs at real timers and the window comes from the sweep and bus, which are never scaled. It needs the link's last free channel, with both ends seizing within about ±1.3 ms (the D window). That is the ordinary residual-glare rate, multiplied by the number of links a flood crosses. The bench's S neighbour takes S40 while 41-43 are free, which a conforming g-ordered far end would not do. From B's side it is the same as S40 being the last free channel, so it is not an artefact in effect.
findings.ran: Built work/audit/fwd tb_fx (copied to work/verify/C13-leg-glare/, with an arming monitor on B's own probe and a new sc7 that raises the far M a set delay after B's leg write) on the snapshot RTL, through sim.sh. Ran +sc=3, +sc=7 +dly=300 and +sc=7 +dly=1200, all at real timers. Logs: work/verify/C13-leg-glare/run_fx_sc3.log, run_fx_sc7_d300.log, run_fx_sc7_d1200.log. Also a Monte Carlo of the arming condition (in NOTES.md).
findings.evidence:
run_fx_sc3.log is line for line the auditor's run_fx_sc3.log. Leg S40 is written at 42.424 and R_LEG fires at 42.521. Legs 74 and 10 are dropped, port 30 goes to src 40 at 42.959, and n_glare/EV_GLARE go 0->0. The mechanism holds: the resolver watch at net_unit.v:682-690 takes any M on a held leg, and w_res at 691-706 re-points and drops. The only glare counter is in the origin (795-804).

Overstated in two ways. (1) The join is documented design: exchange/network.md §5 says 'At a transit a glared leg is its resolver's claim; not run', and decisions.md records that glare is taken as the claim and the callers are joined. (2) The glare is not counted at the transit, but it is counted elsewhere. At real timers the join's backward A reaches the upstream origin about one hop (12-30 ms) after that origin's seizure. That is inside its 128 ms guard, so the origin counts EV_GLARE, naming its own first trunk (the wrong link). A far end that is an origin counts it on the right channel. Only the transit, and a transit-to-transit link, go uncounted.
findings.notes:
The proposed armed-leg fix is incomplete, as sc7 shows. With the far M only 300 us after B's leg write, B's probe had already sampled S40 with BUSY 1 and M 0 at 42.521, 97 us after the write, so the leg was armed. R_LEG then fired, the other legs were dropped and 30 was patched to 40: joined and uncounted, the same at 1200 us.

A Monte Carlo of baseband glare puts about 51% of transit glare events in this armed case. With any carrier delay over about 1 ms it is nearly all of them. The fix also does nothing for a one-leg forward, whose way back is patched at forward time (net_unit.v:732-736), so the upstream origin sees the glare M before the resolver acts. A leg age compared against the guard (the protocol auditor's (b)) is the discriminator that works.

findings.real_timing:
Structural. The glare comes from unscaled sweep timing, and the collapse in pass 1 (B's own monitor claims at b and the CLAIM write re-points B11 while its E is up) happens the same way at real timers, with T_REL 256 in place of 32. Pass 0's trigger, a break inside the far origin's 16 ms scaled guard, cannot happen with conforming dials at real timers. The same steady-fall branch does happen when the stranger hangs up, dials its own code (local) or dials a reserved digit.

One-leg forwards are the normal case for a two-direction transit, so this is the common transit form of residual glare. It is still rare (last free channel, about ±1.3 ms). At real timers the upstream origin also counts EV_GLARE against its own first trunk, which is arithmetic from the trace's 16 ms against the 128 ms guard (not run).
findings.ran: Rebuilt tb_pchain (work/audit/proto, copied) on the snapshot and ran +sc=1 +trace at scale 8 through sim.sh: work/verify/C13-leg-glare/run_pchain_snap.log. Ran the same bench on the F3' fixed copy: run_pchain_f3.log.
findings.evidence:
Every T/OBS/ok/FAIL line of run_pchain_snap.log matches the auditor's run_pchain_trace.log exactly (diff empty). In pass 1, B14 and C11 are both written at 2128.284, B11 goes to 14 at 2128.418, and B's resolver acts and frees at 2130.203. B's monitor claims at 2389.999, and 'B11 -> 0 clm 1' follows at 2390.284. B11 releases (clm 0) at 2422.999, then A11 at 2454.999 and B14/C11 at 2486.999. A20 goes to 11 and C20 to 11: both callers end on released trunks, and A20 never reaches B21.

The RTL matches each step. F_WRITE patches the one-leg way back at once. w_res with rs_two frees without writing. w_claim writes the in-port to 00+CLAIM (net_unit.v:654-668). port.v releases on the fE fall T_REL later and clears CLM. The origin never re-checks after its claim.
findings.notes:
Of the auditor's fixes, (a) 'the origin re-checks its claim' is the essential one, but as a one-sample check it races the caller's own hang-up (T_REL equals CLR). The C11 verifier reproduced that race: NOGO lands on a releasing caller and leaves it BUSY.

I tested F3', the glare-specific half: while claimed and before N_DONE, if the kept trunk's M stays low for 4 samples and then rises again, abandon with NOGO. In pass 1 both callers get cannot-complete within 2 ms (A at 2193.156, C at 2194.156), B's monitor never claims, and B releases cleanly at 2226. F3' does not cover pass 0, where the stranger leaves and M stays low; that branch is C11's claimed-trunk loss and needs its steady-low abandon.

Fix (c), writing the one-leg way back away at w_claim, does not stop the release, because the release comes from re-pointing B11, not B14. Fix (b), the resolver age check, also needs the one-leg way back deferred until the claim, or the upstream origin has already seen the glare.

findings.real_timing: Real timing: the window is wiring and bus timing, the same at both scales. It grows with any carrier delay.
findings.ran: Arithmetic: recomputed the rate table (Erlang-B state probabilities, holding time 8 s, lambda per end = A/2h, D = 1.35 ms), plus a Monte Carlo of the two ends' confirm, write, E-capture and card timing (NOTES.md). No simulation was needed. tb_pchain glared on try 0 in both passes of both of my runs.
findings.evidence: The Monte Carlo gives a glare window 2D = 2.64 ms, matching the auditor's 2 x 1.35 ms (0.5 rest of the confirm pass + 0.156 WAIT + 0.133 word + 0.5 E capture + 0.031 card). Their table reproduces exactly only with an extra factor of 2. The rate of pairs with |tX - tY| < D is P1 x lamX x lamY x 2D, with no further 2, so every rate is 2x too high. Corrected: 2-channel link 0.2 E 1 per 4000 h, 0.5 E 1 per 342 h, 1.0 E 1 per 66 h; 8-channel link 2 E 1 per 1900 h, 4 E 1 per 27 h, 6 E 1 per 5 h, 8 E 1 per 2 h. The conclusion does not change: negligible at design load, and hours to days on an overloaded central link.
findings.notes: The glare-reserve mitigation (the non-g end never takes the last free channel it sees) is sound in principle, but it needs a 'second free seen' bit per direction, not one gate. It narrows glare rather than removing it, because the two ends' views can differ. Not tested.

verifier.root_cause: One root with two consequences. The unit takes the first M on a held trunk or leg as the claim and never re-checks it: net_unit.v:682-690 (resolver R_LEG, with no guard and no counter) and :795-804 (origin claim, counted only inside the guard). At the instant of seizure a stranger's glare seizure looks exactly like a claim. The collapse adds two more defects: the one-leg forward patches the way back at forward time (:732-736), so the upstream origin sees the glare at once, and w_claim (:654-668) re-points an in-port whose E is up, which port.v:183-193 turns into a self-release T_REL later. All of it rests on residual glare on the last free channel, whose window is about ±1.3 ms.
verifier.best_fix:
Watch the origin's claim until the connect (F3', about one package: a 3-bit low counter, one flip-flop and the existing trunk comparator). Before N_DONE, if the kept trunk's M stays low for 4 or more samples and then rises again, abandon with NOGO. A real claim is a steady CLAIM, a release never comes back, and a stranger's hook breaks when the stranger dials.

Combine it with C11's steady-low abandon, which needs persistence and has to be ordered after the register's gone, for the branch where the stranger leaves. Together they turn every glare join and collapse, at an origin or at any transit, into two clean cannot-completes. That departs from the documented 'residual glare joins two callers', so it is Joel's decision.

Optional extras for completion rate and correct counting:
- At the transit, treat M on a leg younger than the guard as glare: count it and write that leg away while keeping the others.
- Defer the one-leg way back until R_LEG.

The forwarder auditor's armed-leg fix is not sufficient. The one-sample form of (a) races the caller's own hang-up.
verifier.fix_tested:
F3' copy at work/verify/C13-leg-glare/rtl_f3/net_unit.v (RTL_f3.list):
- tb_pchain +sc=1 +trace (run_pchain_f3.log): pass 1 goes from both callers stranded to both cannot-complete. Pass 0 is unchanged (the steady-fall branch, C11's).
- tb_chain: 32/32 PASS (run_f3_chain.log; baseline 32/32).
- tb_net: 88/88 PASS (run_f3_net.log; baseline 88/88).

Not run on F3': tb_lfull (its scenario 5 expects the documented join and would now see two cannot-completes), tb_lnet, tb_lchain.

The armed-leg fix was not built. tb_fx sc7 on the snapshot (run_fx_sc7_d300.log, run_fx_sc7_d1200.log) shows the leg already armed before the glare M arrives, so that fix would still take the glare as the claim.
verifier.summary:
All three findings are real and share one cause: the flood takes the first M on a held trunk or leg as the claim and never checks it again.

- **leg-glare-joins-uncounted (confirmed-overstated, low):** my re-run at real timers matches the auditor's log line for line. The transit resolver joins the flood's caller to the far exchange's own caller and drops the other legs. But the join is the documented design (network.md §5, decisions.md). The transit counts nothing, yet the upstream origin does count it, inside its guard, against its own first trunk. The proposed armed-leg fix misses glare whose far M lands after the leg's first BUSY sample: sc7 at 300 us and 1200 us, about half of baseband cases by Monte Carlo, nearly all with a carrier delay. It also does nothing for one-leg forwards.
- **forward-glare-collapse (confirmed, medium but rare):** my snapshot trace is identical to the auditor's. B's own claim re-points an in-port whose E is up, it releases itself T_REL later, and both callers end latched to released trunks. The fix that works is the origin re-checking its claim. As a one-sample check it races the caller's own hang-up (as C11's verifier found), so I tested the glare-specific form F3' (low for 4 ms, then rising). It turned the collapse into two clean cannot-completes and kept tb_net 88/88 and tb_chain 32/32. The steady-fall branch (the stranger leaves) is C11's.
- **residual-glare-rate (confirmed-overstated, low):** the window is right (2D is about 2.6 ms) but the rate table carries a spurious factor of 2. Negligible at design load.

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C13-leg-glare/ (NOTES.md, tb_fx.v with sc7, rtl_f3/net_unit.v, the run_*.log files). All obj dirs are deleted.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM: re-derive each mechanism from the RTL, hunt for blocking conditions or a missed second path

per_finding.reason:
Re-derived from the RTL, and nothing blocks it.
- The resolver watch (net_unit.v:682-690) sets R_LEG on any sp_m on a held leg. It has no BUSY, arming or age term.
- w_res (691-706) drops the other legs and, for a multi-leg forward, points the in-port at the glared leg (701-705).
- A transit has no n_glare or EV_GLARE path; the only counter is the origin's (795-804).

I looked for a blocking condition and found none:
- `mine` (430-441) covers the candidate from F_WRITE onward. During H_CONFIRM the next visit to the port is a full pass away, which is after fst goes to F_WRITE, so the classifier cannot take the glared channel.
- The mini marker reads the word and leaves trunks to the unit (mini_marker.v:360-367).
- Strapped links are never forwarded into (network.md §7), so one flood cannot glare with itself.

I checked the verifier's sc7 logs: an arming sample at 42.521 (BUSY 1, M 0), the far M at 42.723, R_LEG at 43.521, then the join. So the auditor's armed-leg fix really does miss glare that rises after the leg's first BUSY sample. It also does nothing for a one-leg forward.

The overstatement stands. The join is documented (exchange/network.md §5: 'At a transit a glared leg is its resolver's claim'). At real timers the upstream origin sees the join's M about 12-30 ms after its seizure, inside its 128 ms guard, so it counts EV_GLARE, but against its own first trunk.

One correction to both the auditor and the verifier: the 'join' outcome holds only when the call's destination is NOT upstream of the glared link. Otherwise this finding becomes forward-glare-collapse, for multi-leg forwards as well (see below).

The mechanism is confirmed exactly as stated:
- F_WRITE patches the one-leg way back at forward time (732-736).
- w_claim writes the in-port to 00+CLAIM (656-658).
- In port.v, E is e_cap of the source's M (106, 173). Port 00 is unfitted, so a re-point to 00 drops E to 0. fE falls T_REL later (183-187), and rel clears addr, bsy and CLM (193).
- At real timers B's in-port releases at claim+256 ms, well before h (the pause is at least 720 ms). So pass 1's outcome does not depend on the timer scaling.

The scope is understated, by the verifier as well. The collapse is not tied to one-leg forwards, nor to the destination being the glaring transit.
- For a multi-leg forward, w_res writes the in-port to listen to the glared leg (701-705), so its E carries the stranger's hook exactly as in the one-leg case.
- The glare M also climbs the tree: every transit between the glared link and the origin takes it as R_LEG on its own leg and points its in-port at that leg.
- So a destination D anywhere upstream of the glared link (chain O-D-T-X, glare on T-X) has its in-port listening to the stranger. D's monitor, still held on that in-port, claims at b. w_claim re-points the in-port, it releases itself T_REL later, and the path unwinds under both callers.

Every transit glare in the destination's downstream subtree is therefore this collapse, not the documented join. In a chain with a uniform destination that is roughly half of them. The verifier's framing, 'one-leg forwards are the normal case, so this is the common transit form', points at the wrong condition.

The severity stays medium. The rate is still bounded by residual glare, but the outcome is worse than the documented join: a call that would have completed is lost, both callers end latched to released trunks, and there is a listen-in hazard when those trunks are reused. I disagree with the verifier on scope and on the fix evidence (below), not on the mechanism.

I re-derived the rate. Glare needs -D_Y < c_X - c_Y < D_X, where c is each end's confirm visit. That gives rate = P1 x lamX x lamY x (D_X + D_Y), with no further factor of 2. For N=2 at 0.2 E: P1 = 0.1639 and lam = 0.0125/s, which with 2D = 2.7 ms gives 1 per 4017 h. That matches the verifier; the auditor's table is 2x high. The window D (about 1.35 ms mean) is right: the rest of the confirm pass, WAIT 156 us, a 133 us word, the source's E capture (up to 1 ms) and 31 us for the card.

Three second-order additions, none of which moves the conclusion:
- A queue backlog (w_claim, w_cls and w_res outrank w_orig and w_fwd) lengthens D.
- The 2nd to 4th words of a multi-leg burst land 133 us apart each, which lengthens D further.
- The 9 ms sweep's view can be stale: a channel freed after its read lets the two ends collide with two channels free. That depends on the release rate times 9 ms, which is negligible.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's evidence for F3' comes from lock-step dialling. tb_pchain starts dial_a and dial_c on the same tick: 'M at B11 0' and 'M at B14 0' are both at 2180.258 in run_pchain_f3.log. C's F3' fired on A20's make only because that make reached C11 1 ms before A's abandon did (2193.149 against 2194.149).

The mechanism behind this is general. F3' at one origin fires when the other caller's first break ends. Its write-away then leaves the other origin's kept trunk steady low within a few ms, so the other origin's F3' never fires unless the two first makes are within about 2 ms of each other.

My one run settles it: work/verify/C13-skeptic-mechanism/run_pchain_f3_cdly150.log, the F3' copy, pass 1, with C20 dialling 150 ms after A20.
- C gives cannot-complete at 853.159.
- A's trunk goes steady low and A never fires.
- A11, B11 and B14 release at 886.
- A20 is connected to the released A11 at 1308 and fails 'A20 reached B21'.

So F3' alone gives one clean cannot-complete and one stranded caller in almost every real glare. C11's steady-low abandon is essential in every glare, not only 'when the stranger leaves'. Even F3' plus C11 only turns glare into two cannot-completes. It cannot save the destination's call in the widened collapse case.

A more complete and still cheap fix never lets a glare M act as a claim. It has three parts:
1. At the transit, M on a leg younger than the guard is glare: count it, write that leg away and keep the others (a per-resolver 'young' bit or age counter).
2. Defer the one-leg way back to w_res, by deleting the popc==1 patch at 732-736 and the !rs_two term at 701. One-leg forwards then work like multi-leg ones, the glare never climbs, and the collapse cannot happen.
3. At the origin, the RTL already computes `guarding`, and network.md §5 and §6 say no real claim can arrive inside the guard. So M on a held trunk inside the guard should be counted and dropped through dmo (NOGO if no trunk is left), not claimed. This is immediate and needs no dial break.

Keep F3' plus C11's steady-low (the latter needs its persistence and its ordering after the register's gone) as the backstop for glare past the guard's reach and for a claimed trunk that is lost.

One caveat on F3': a backward-path outage of 4-256 ms between the claim and the connect now abandons the call, where the snapshot rode it through.

All of this departs from the documented 'residual glare joins two callers', so it is Joel's decision, and tb_lfull scenario 5 would need its expectation changed.
skeptics.summary:
All three findings are real. I agree with the verifier on leg-glare-joins-uncounted (low) and residual-glare-rate (low, the auditor's table carries a spurious factor of 2). I disagree on forward-glare-collapse's scope and on the evidence behind the recommended fix.

**Mechanism.** Re-derived from net_unit.v:682-706 / 725-743 / 795-804 / 656-668 and port.v:106-193, with no blocking condition found. `mine` closes the classifier hole, the marker leaves trunks to the unit, and strapped links rule out self-glare.

**The missed second path.** The collapse is not a one-leg quirk:
- A multi-leg forward's w_res (701-705) also points the in-port at the glared leg.
- The glare M climbs every transit between the glared link and the origin.
- So any destination upstream of the glared link has its own claim re-point an in-port whose E is up, and that in-port releases itself T_REL later.

Every transit glare in the destination's downstream subtree therefore strands both callers, roughly half of transit glares in a chain. The documented join holds only for the rest.

**The fix evidence.** The verifier's F3' result (two clean cannot-completes) came from the bench dialling both callers in lock-step. I made one run of the F3' copy with C20 dialling 150 ms after A20 (work/verify/C13-skeptic-mechanism/run_pchain_f3_cdly150.log). C gets cannot-complete, A's trunk goes steady low, and A20 is left latched to the released A11. C11's steady-low abandon is therefore mandatory, not optional, and even together they cannot save the destination's call.

**Better fix.** Treat young M as glare: a leg-age rule at the transit resolvers, the one-leg way back deferred to w_res, and the existing `guarding` term at the origin turned into drop-that-trunk instead of claim. Keep F3' plus C11's steady-low as the backstop. Dropping the documented join is Joel's decision.

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C13-skeptic-mechanism/ (NOTES.md, tb_pchain.v with +cdly/+p0, job.sh, the run log); the obj dir is deleted.

skeptics.lens: realism and severity

per_finding.reason:
The mechanism is real at real timers. net_unit.v:682-690 sets R_LEG on any M on a held leg, and :691-706 re-points the in-port and drops the other legs. The only glare counter is the origin's, at :803. The verifier's run_fx_sc3 matches the auditor's run.

The realism point the cluster understates: this is not a corner case of glare, it is nearly all of the glare a flood network has. Every flood crosses every link, so a link's seizure rate is the whole network's call rate. On traffic.md s8.5/8.6's 63-exchange design tree, the tandem link's X-side seizure comes from an origin only 1/21 of the time and its Y side 1/42, so about 99.9% of backbone glare involves a transit. On a leaf link about 98% is an origin against a transit. The documented case, an origin against an origin counted on the right trunk, is the exception.

Rate at design load (rate.py): about 1 event per 200 network busy hours. That is about 8e-5 per exchange per busy hour and 6e-6 per network call, against the 6.7 calls per 1000 the network already loses.

What the subscriber gets (about 85-90% of events): at their own last digit, an open line to another caller who has also just dialled. Nobody is rung, both notice at once and redial. It is not a silent wrong number.

The counting defect is systematic but only affects maintenance. EV_GLARE lands on the upstream origins' own first trunks, usually leaf links that never glared, or nowhere when the join's backward A arrives after the 128 ms guard (possible for glare 7-8 hops out). That points link sizing at the wrong links. So the severity is low.

I agree the armed-leg fix is insufficient. In a glare at baseband, the far M reaches B's probe at most about 4.4 ms after B's leg write (1.03 + 1.3 + 1.03 ms plus one probe turn). No real claim can come sooner than about 850 ms after any leg write, because it needs e, a pause of at least 720 ms, b and ID. So an age gate of 16-128 ms separates the two with margin, carriers included. I also checked for a classifier gap (the far M landing between B's confirm visit and its leg write): there is none. The port's next probe turn after its confirm visit always falls inside `mine` (f_cand in F_WRITE, rs_held after w_fwd).

The mechanism holds at real timers, as the verifier says. w_claim (:656-658) re-points an in-port whose E is up, and port.v then releases it T_REL later. I disagree on severity and on the fix evidence.

(1) Frequency. The collapse needs the call's owner to lie on the flood's path between its origin and the glare transit. On the backbone that is about 3/62 per side, plus the branch where the stranger leaves (hangs up, dials its own code after 1, reserved digit, T_KEY). That is about 10-15% of glare events: about 1e-6 per network call, or 1 per 1500-2000 network busy hours at design load.

(2) It is not 'the common transit form because one-leg forwards are normal'. Every transit in the design tree has at least 3 directions, so one-leg forwards happen only in chains or when every other onward direction is full. The hub path (R_LEG re-points the in-port, then the owner's claim re-points it again) collapses the same way.

(3) No wrong party is ever rung. At real timers the claim is at about b_last+128 ms and the in-port releases 256 ms later. The next upstream port releases 256 ms after that, so the owner's in-port M falls steady at about b_last+640 ms, before a conforming h (b_last+720 ms or later). A faster dialler produces a steady low, which the register ends as gone, never a completed digit.

(4) What the subscriber gets is dead air after dialling. The one-way listen-in is C11's mechanism, needs the channel reused and a conversation started before the caller gives up (under about 1% of events at a leaf), and is rated in C11.

A rare, unclean cannot-complete with a negligible privacy tail is low, not medium.

The verifier's F3' evidence is a bench artefact. tb_pchain.v:325-326 forks A20 and C20 to dial in lock-step; run_pchain_f3.log shows 'M at B11 0' and 'M at B14 0' both at 2180.258, so each origin saw the other's break. With real, independent callers only the origin that sees the other's break first fires. Its drop leaves the other origin a steady low, with no rise, so F3' never fires there. The first dialler is stranded, which is C11's outcome. This is reasoned from the F3' diff and the trace, not run.

The verifier's factor-2 correction is right. The rate is P(N-1 busy) x lamX x lamY x 2D; I recomputed 0.5 E on 2 channels and got 1 per 342 h.

The A/(2h) model with an 8 s hold is not the flood network's structure, though. Each link's seizure rate is the network's call rate split by subtree size, whatever the link's own erlangs. On the design tree (rate.py, rate.out):
- Design load: each tandem-tandem link (12 ch, 5.81 E, 0.93% blocked) has 1 glare per about 434 busy h; about 1 per 195 busy h across the network. Outer 12-channel links are negligible; 6-channel mid links are 1 per about 1900 h.
- Twice the busy hour: about 1 per 3 busy h across the network, 1.7e-4 per call. That is noise beside the roughly 12% the network already loses.

The glare-reserve mitigation is not free here. The non-g end sees 11 of 12 channels, so B(11, 5.81) = 1.94% against 0.93%: the backbone's loss doubles for half the floods to remove one event per 200 busy hours. 'None needed at design load' is right, and the reserve should not be fitted.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
I disagree with the verifier's best fix in two ways.

(1) F3' is neither needed for the collapse nor sufficient on its own.
- Not needed: C11's verifier's 'alt' fix (128 ms steady-low persistence, with N_DONE gated on lost==0) closes the collapse by itself. In pass 1, after B11's self-release, A sees a steady low and drops; C then sees a steady low and drops. That gives two clean cannot-completes. It closes pass 0 too, and keeps documented joins: tb_lfull 40/40 and tb_net 88/88 in C11's runs. I reasoned this for tb_pchain; I did not run it.
- Not sufficient: F3' alone strands the first dialler in almost every real event. Its 'both clean' result comes from the bench's lock-step dialling.
- F3' is therefore only a policy tool, turning joins into cannot-completes, which is Joel's call. Its 4-sample threshold also makes a 4 ms line hit on a legitimately claimed trunk drop the call. About 16 samples (one '161) would still catch every dial break.

(2) The root fix belongs at the transit, and since nearly all glare is transit glare it is not optional. The verifier listed it only as an extra.
- Give each resolver an age gate: M on a leg younger than about 16-128 ms is glare. The safe bound is at least 4.4 ms at baseband, and a real claim is at least about 850 ms away.
- Count it at the transit, with EV_GLARE naming the leg, which is the right link.
- Write that one leg away and keep the others (a new resolver action that drops one leg and keeps the resolver).
- In chains, defer the one-leg way back to R_LEG (rs_two always 0). This removes logic. It conflicts with C14's option (b), which would free one-leg resolvers.
- Pair it with the origin: inside the guard, write the glared trunk away and count it instead of claiming. The guard test already exists, so that costs a few gates. Otherwise a far origin claims on the transit's M and is stranded when the leg is written away.
- Cost in 74HC: about half a package per resolver (a '393 half, or two '74 bits on a shared slow tick), plus about one package for the leg/event register. That is about 2-3 packages at NRES 2 and 4 at a five-resolver hub.
- Result: no joins and no collapses, a hub's flood carries on in its other directions, and a call whose owner is upstream completes. Keep C11-alt as the general backstop.
- None of this has been tested, and all of it departs from the documented 'glare joins two callers', so it is Joel's decision.

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C13-skeptic-realism/: NOTES.md, rate.py, rate.out.
skeptics.summary:
All three findings are real; for the realism lens they are all low severity. I disagree with the verifier's medium on forward-glare-collapse, and with its fix evidence.

On traffic.md's 63-exchange design network, glare happens about once per 200 network busy hours. That is about 1e-4 per exchange per busy hour and about 6e-6 per call. Almost all of it is on the tandem backbone, and about 99.9% of it involves a transit. So leg glare is effectively the only glare a flood network has, not a corner case.

What subscribers get:
- About 85-90% of events: the documented join, an open line to another caller who just dialled, with nobody rung. Both notice and redial.
- About 10-15%: dead air after dialling (the collapse, or the stranger leaving). A one-way listen-in is possible but under 1% of those events, and is C11's harm.
- No path rings a wrong party. The owner's in-port goes steady low about 80 ms before a conforming next digit, and a steady low ends as gone.

The counters point glare at the origins' own first trunks, or nowhere, which misleads link sizing; that is a maintenance issue. The verifier's factor-2 rate correction is right.

On the fix, the verifier's F3' result is a lock-step-dialling artefact (tb_pchain.v:325-326; both breaks at 2180.258 in run_pchain_f3.log). With independent callers, F3' strands the first dialler. C11's 128 ms steady-low abandon alone cures the collapse; F3' only matters if Joel wants joins refused. The proper 74HC fix is at the transit: a per-resolver age gate (at least about 4.4 ms at baseband; a real claim is at least about 850 ms away), counting at the transit, writing the glared leg away, and deferring the one-leg way back. Pair it with the origin writing a glared trunk away inside its guard, for about 2-4 packages.

I ran no simulations; the notes and rate arithmetic are in work/verify/C13-skeptic-realism/.

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers with conforming equipment, and shown to be. A subscriber who dials key 1 and hangs up drops the flooded M live at every hop. If the hang-up falls in the one 1-ms pass that ends at port 77's CONFIRM sample (about 11 ms after B's hold, about 140+12k ms after key 1's last make), B locks up. A second conforming trigger, from code reading only: an origin that takes glare as the claim drops its other directions inside T_GUARD. The auditor's 'far origin's guard abandoning' cannot happen with a conforming dial: key 1 is followed by a pause of at least 720 ms, and the guard is 128 ms from the seize. All three conditions must hold: (1) the death lands in that 1-ms pass; (2) the incoming trunk is in socket 77, and this can be the preferred channel of a group, because the far end hunts in its own glare order; (3) the forward has exactly one leg (a chain, or the other directions busy, strapped or unfitted). Other ports are exposed only if F_WRITE waits 2 or more bit-times, which needs the unit's queue at least 13/16 full. Rare. At scale 8 it cannot happen: the watch ends about 4 ms after the hold, before any h_done.
findings.ran: (1) The auditor's tb_fcan on its knob RTL (work/audit/cableb/RTL_k.list), rebuilt and run through sim.sh: +mode=0, +mode=1, +mode=0 +fixfc. Logs: work/verify/C09-fwrite-ignores-fcancel/run_fcan_mode0.log, run_fcan_mode1.log, run_fcan_mode0fixfc.log. (2) My own bench, work/verify/C09-fwrite-ignores-fcancel/tb_c09.v, built from site_net. Two exchanges: A11 cabled to B77, and B13 to a far end that is up but never seizes. No loopback and no bench blip. ALL timers real (site_net defaults). A20 dials 1 at 60/40 ms and hangs up when B's scan reaches 4 in B's forward CONFIRM. Stage 2: A20 calls B21 (1 2 3 2 1). Stage 3: idle check. Run on the snapshot (run_c09_base.log) and on rtl_fix (run_c09_fix.log).
findings.evidence: The mechanism holds step by step. C_UNHOLD is set on the sample that shows cls_port low (net_unit.v:581-583). w_cls pushes the unhold and sets f_cancel on the next tick (590-594). That is the same tick on which F_HUNT sees the registered h_done and reads the old f_cancel=0 (720-724). F_WRITE (725) and w_fwd (492-493) never test f_cancel, so the next tick pushes the leg and the one-leg way back (732-736). The sweep is locked to the scan: its last read is h_idx = 1+9*63 mod 64 = port 70, and CONFIRM counts 64 sp_fresh from 00 (769-785). So h_done always lands on port 77's sample, and taking the reader for C_WAIT shifts the sweep by whole passes but never changes its phase. The rerun matches the auditor's log line for line: 'UNHOLD pushed for 77 ... FORWARD pushed: f_in 77 f_ok 0100 f_cancel 1', then cable B 77<-00 b0, 13<-77 b1, 77<-13 b1, and at 485 ms both ports BUSY with res 01 (FAIL 3/6). mode1 and +fixfc PASS. My real-timer bench shows the same thing with a real caller: B77's M falls at B scan 18, h_done and the UNHOLD fall on one tick at 733 ms, the FORWARD goes out with f_cancel 1, and 3 s later B77 (addr 13 bsy 1) and B13 (addr 77 bsy 1) are BUSY with res_b 01 (FAIL x3). Overstated parts: 'for good' and 'the trunk group loses two channels'. A still sees A11 as free and uses it for the next call. That seizure passes through B's stuck 77<->13 patch unseen, because cls_seen needs !sp_busy, so B does not hold it, monitor it or flood it on. A's call to B was lost at T_CLAIM (FAIL 'B claimed A20's call'). The seizure armed B77's fM, and at the end of the call B77 cleared and R_GONE dropped 13 (8439 ms). Stage 3 was idle. So the state lasts until that channel's next use from either end, and it costs one call if that call needed B or B's other directions. 'NRES exhausted by a second occurrence' is right, but only while both pairs stay unused. The 2-3 leg case is clean, as the auditor says: 77 is left not BUSY and R_GONE drops the legs.
findings.notes: The loopback and the ORed blip in tb_fcan are bench artefacts, but they do not produce this result: every A in the loop is 0 after the death, so nothing latches. The same failure happens with a real far exchange and a real subscriber at full real timers. The auditor's mixed timers (T_ARM real, the rest at scale 8) were representative. Severity lowered to low: the trigger is a 1-ms coincidence; the pair heals at its next use; the loss is at most one call plus a held resolver meanwhile. The code does break network.md §3.3 ('if M falls writes the hold away and calls off the forward').

findings.real_timing: The same as the first finding: real timers only, with a conforming trigger (the caller abandons after key 1; shown in tb_c09 at full real timers). It needs a one-leg forward and the incoming trunk in socket 77. 'One port in 64' can understate the risk where 77 is the far end's first-choice channel. 'One pass in ~18' is about right: the 1-ms pass at the forward's end, within the roughly 18-ms watch.
findings.ran: The same runs as the first finding. This audit's own evidence is the cableb log. It also points to work/audit/fwd/rtl_fix/net_unit.v, which bundles this gate with the unrelated rs_lb/rs_lf changes (tb_chain and tb_lchain green there, per runfix_chain.log and runfix_lchain.log). I tested the gate on its own instead: work/verify/C09-fwrite-ignores-fcancel/rtl_fix/net_unit.v.
findings.evidence: Every cited line checks out: 593 sets f_cancel; only 714 and 722 read it; 488 lets w_cls outrank w_fwd; 732-736 write the way back. The watch outlasts the forward at real timers (T_ARM+2 = 18 ms against about 11 ms to h_done) but not at scale 8 (4 ms). The misroute consequence is confirmed, and run_c09_base.log adds a case this audit did not cover. The audit says the pair heals only when the leg's far end seizes the channel. It also heals from the other side: A re-seized A11 (B77's far end), the call went through B unseen and was lost (A never claimed, B's register never taken), and then B77's armed fM cleared the pair and R_GONE freed the resolver.
findings.notes: The same root cause and the same fix as the first finding: two audits found the same defect. The only corrections are the healing path above, and that the triggers are conforming (an early hang-up, or glare taken as the claim), not only faults.

verifier.root_cause: One defect. C_UNHOLD sets f_cancel (net_unit.v:593) on the same tick that F_HUNT reads the old f_cancel at h_done (720-724), and F_WRITE (725) and w_fwd (492-493) never test it. The sweep is locked to the scan (769-785), so h_done always falls on port 77's CONFIRM sample. When 77's seizure first reads low on that sample, the unhold goes out first and the one-leg way back (732-736) then re-holds the dead 77 BUSY, listening to its leg. The seizure never stood T_ARM, so neither port gets a detector edge (port.v:176-194), and the resolver waits for an R_LEG or R_GONE that only the channel's next use can supply.
verifier.best_fix: In F_WRITE: `F_WRITE: if (f_cancel) fst <= F_IDLE; else if (w_fwd) begin ...`, and add `&& !f_cancel` to w_fwd. The w_fwd term is optional: it only saves one tick in which w_res and w_ev are locked out. This is the auditors' fix and it is one gate. It is complete. When an UNHOLD of f_in and F_WRITE are both pending, w_cls outranks w_fwd, and anything that blocks w_cls (room<1 or w_claim) blocks w_fwd too, so the unhold always goes first and F_WRITE always sees f_cancel. In the opposite order (legs first), the later unhold overrides the way back and R_GONE drops the legs, which is already clean. The auditor's alternative, a combinational cancel in F_HUNT, covers only the h_done tick and misses an F_WRITE waiting on queue room, so it is weaker, not cheaper. f_cancel is cleared at every new forward's start (619), so a stale value never kills a live forward. Tested on a copy with only this change: work/verify/C09-fwrite-ignores-fcancel/rtl_fix/net_unit.v (RTL_fix.list).
verifier.fix_tested: tb_c09 at full real timers with a real caller hang-up: snapshot FAIL 4/7 (run_c09_base.log), minimal fix PASS 7/7 (run_c09_fix.log). With the fix, the next call is held, forwarded, claimed by B and connected to B21. tb_fcan mode0 +fixfc (the same gate as a knob): PASS 6/6 (run_fcan_mode0fixfc.log), against mode0 FAIL 3/6. On the minimal fix copy: tb_net 88/88 PASS (run_net_fix.log) and tb_chain 32/32 PASS (run_chain_fix.log), with output identical to base-net.log and base-chain.log apart from timing lines. That is expected: at scale 8 the gate is provably inert. All logs are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C09-fwrite-ignores-fcancel/, and every obj dir has been removed.
verifier.summary: Both findings are the same defect, and it is real. F_WRITE ignores f_cancel. So a seizure on port 77 whose first low sample is the forward's last CONFIRM sample gets its unhold and then its forward's leg and way back, in that order. The dead port and its one leg stay BUSY and a resolver stays held. I reproduced the auditor's bench exactly. I then built a cleaner reproducer (tb_c09.v): two exchanges, a real far end, all timers real, and a conforming trigger (the caller hangs up right after key 1, timed into B's CONFIRM). It fails the same way. The cableb finding overstates the consequence. The state is not 'for good' and the channels are not lost: the stuck pair is a live patch that heals at the channel's next seizure from either end. That next call passes through B unseen and is lost if it needed B, as tb_c09 stage 2 shows, and the resolver stays held until then. Its severity should drop from medium to low. The forwarder finding is accurate except that it gives only one of the two healing paths. It is rare: a 1-ms coincidence, the incoming trunk in socket 77, and a one-leg forward. It still breaks network.md §3.3. The one-gate fix is complete and minimal, and I tested it green: tb_c09 7/7, tb_fcan +fixfc, tb_net 88/88, tb_chain 32/32. skeptics.lens: MECHANISM + REALISM AND SEVERITY (independent skeptic, read-only; no simulation run)

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived the mechanism from the snapshot and it holds. Only socket 77 can hit it, and that is built into the design. The last sweep read is port 70. word_rx raises done at the a_stb of the eighth frame after the select, which is the middle of port 00's bit-time (word_rx.v:105-121). The probe publishes 00 at the end of that bit-time (probe.v:79-85). So CONFIRM counts 00..77, and h_done is registered on 77's sp_fresh, the same edge on which the watch sets C_UNHOLD (net_unit.v:581-583, 779-785). On the next edge w_cls pushes the unhold and sets f_cancel (590-594) while F_HUNT reads the old 0 (720-724). On the edge after that, w_fwd, which has no f_cancel term (492-493), pushes the leg and the way back (725-736). The stuck state checks out against port.v:176-194: 77 has m=0 and cm never reached T_ARM; e is 13's M, which is 0; 13 is the mirror image. There is no rel, R_LEG needs 13's M, and R_GONE needs 77 not BUSY.

I agree the finding is overstated, and I would go further than the verifier on one point. The auditor says 'a second occurrence exhausts NRES'; the verifier says that is right 'only while both pairs stay unused'. In practice it cannot happen. The next fitted sample after h_done is port 01, 64 ticks later, so no other port can win the race unless F_WRITE is blocked for at least 2 bit-times. For the one-leg forward, the only harmful case, that needs room < 2: at least 15 of 16 queue entries. The verifier's 13/16 figure is wrong; 14/16 is the 3-leg figure, and 3 legs are harmless. An UNHOLD held back by room 0 across h_done would need a full 16/16 queue. Meanwhile a stuck 77 is BUSY, so cls_seen never takes it again until it heals. An exchange can therefore hold at most one C09 pair, and the resolver pool is halved, not exhausted.

The auditor's 'other ports in 1-3 ticks behind a claim, hold or origin write' is also wrong, because the next sample is 32-64 ticks away. 'Loses two channels' is half right: B's own hunts do lose 77 and 13 until the pair heals, but A and C still see their ends as free, and their traffic simply bypasses B.

I agree the 'far origin's guard' trigger is not conforming. Rate at real timers: the conforming trigger is a caller who abandons about 150-250 ms after key 1, inside a 1-ms pass. If about 1e-5 of calls abandon in any given ms (my assumption, generous), that is about 1e-5 per exposed forward. Worst case is a chain (one leg is certain) with 77 as the far end's first-choice channel: about 1e-3 to 5e-3 per exchange per busy hour at 100-500 floods/BH on 77. A typical site is 10-100x lower.

The long-run fraction of time degraded is about the per-use trigger probability, whatever the channel's traffic: the trigger needs one use of the channel and the heal needs the next. What the subscriber sees: the abandoning caller sees nothing. Later, B has two fewer channels for its own calls, and transit blocking at B rises while it runs on one resolver (my estimate: roughly 1% to 14% at 0.17 E of resolver load). At most one later call, one that needed B or B's other directions, gets a clean cannot-complete about 2 s after b, and a redial works. There is no wrong number from C09 itself. Low is right.
per_finding.verifier_note: Verifier right on mechanism, reproduction, healing and severity; wrong on 13/16 and too generous on NRES exhaustion.

per_finding.reason:
This is the same defect, and every line it cites checks out: 593 sets f_cancel; only 714 and 722 read it; 488 lets w_cls outrank w_fwd; 732-736 write the way back. 'Only at real timers' is right: the watch runs T_ARM+2, about 18 ms from the hold at real timers but only about 4 ms at scale 8, while h_done comes about 10-11 ms after the hold.

'One port in 64' is really 'exactly socket 77, by construction'. That port can be the far end's first choice, as the verifier says. 'One pass in ~18' is about right as a share of the watch; the real window is the single 1-ms pass that ends the forward's CONFIRM, and M must not yet have stood T_ARM.

The healing account is incomplete. The verifier correctly adds that a reseize from A's side heals it too: 77's fM arms, then falls T_REL later, R_GONE fires and 13 is dropped. The verifier's tb_c09 shows this at 8182/8439 ms.

One interaction neither audit raises: while the pair is stuck, B's monitor cell on 77 stays held for CLR (256 ms). A reseize of that channel inside 256 ms would be counted one digit out of step by that stale cell. That is C03's wrong-number mechanism, rare here, and fixed by C03's fix (free the cell at C_UNHOLD), not by C09's.

The glare-as-claim trigger that the verifier found by reading the code is real, but by my timing estimate it almost never lands. An origin sees glare 1-5 ms after its seize, so the drop reaches the neighbour 2-5 ms after that neighbour's rise, and F_WANT or F_HUNT cancels it cleanly. Only residual glare coming back through a one-leg patch downstream lands near h_done. That is negligible beside the abandon trigger.

Plausible faults raise the per-event odds. A noisy channel on 77 that makes short (<16 ms) phantom seizures reaches the window about 1 time in 13 per blip. Such blips never arm fM, so they don't heal the pair either. That fault is C08's bigger problem anyway.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's minimal fix is correct, minimal and complete for this race. It is in work/verify/C09-fwrite-ignores-fcancel/rtl_fix/net_unit.v: `&& !f_cancel` on w_fwd, and `F_WRITE: if (f_cancel) fst <= F_IDLE; else if (w_fwd) ...`. It is complete because w_cls outranks w_fwd, and anything that blocks w_cls also blocks w_fwd: w_claim directly, room<1 because cnt_fwd>=2. So a pending UNHOLD of f_in always lands before the legs, and F_WRITE then sees f_cancel. In the opposite order (legs first), the later unhold overwrites the way back and R_GONE drops the legs, which is clean. f_cancel is cleared at every new forward's start (619), so a stale value cannot kill a live forward.

I agree the auditor's alternative (a combinational cancel in F_HUNT) is weaker. It misses an F_WRITE that waits behind w_claim, and an UNHOLD held back by a full queue.

A correction for 74HC hardware: the verifier calls the w_fwd term 'optional', but that is only true of the RTL's coding, where the pushes sit inside the F_WRITE branch. On the board the push strobes are w_fwd itself, so the !f_cancel gate on w_fwd is what actually stops the writes. The F_WRITE->F_IDLE exit on f_cancel is also required: f_cancel clears only when a new forward starts, and a new forward needs F_IDLE, so without the exit the forwarder would hang in F_WRITE. Both parts are needed. A cheap equivalent is f_cancel as a synchronous clear on the forwarder state register plus the w_fwd gate. Either way it is about one gate input.

Two things this fix does not cover:
1. C03's stale monitor cell on the same C_UNHOLD path. Fix it there by freeing the cell at the unhold.
2. A hardware-only exposure outside this cluster. The watch is a counter that ends about 18-20.5 ms after M rises; the arming is an RC and a '14, nominally 16 ms. An RC slower than the watch leaves a seizure that dies in the gap held BUSY, with no watch and no detector edge to clear it. The RTL shares one T_ARM parameter between the two, so it cannot show this. A resolver/hold timeout (M low while held for more than T_REL) would cover that, C08's phantom seizures and C09 as a backstop, but C09 does not need it.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier on both findings: the defect is real, and its severity is low. I re-derived the race from the snapshot, and it happens exactly as claimed. The h_done-on-77 phase is built into the design: word_rx finishes reading port 70 in the middle of 00's bit-time, so CONFIRM counts 00..77. The C_UNHOLD and h_done register on the same edge, F_HUNT reads the old f_cancel, and F_WRITE and w_fwd never test it. So the unhold is followed by the leg and, for a one-leg forward, the way back, which re-holds the dead 77. Neither port gets a detector edge, and the resolver waits for an R_LEG or R_GONE that cannot come.

Corrections to the auditors and the verifier:
- Only socket 77 is exposed unless the queue is at least 15/16 full (not 13/16).
- A stuck 77 is BUSY and cannot be classified again, so an exchange holds at most one C09 pair. 'NRES exhausted by a second occurrence' is practically unreachable, not merely 'only while both pairs stay unused'.
- The state heals at the channel's next use from either end. So the long-run fraction of time degraded is about the per-use trigger probability (around 1e-5).
- The glare-as-claim trigger almost never lands in the window by my timing estimate; the realistic conforming trigger is a caller abandoning about 150-250 ms after key 1.
- Worst-case rate: a chain with 77 as the far end's first-choice channel gives about 1e-3 to 5e-3 per exchange per busy hour.

What subscribers see: B loses two channels for its own calls, transit blocking at B rises while one of its two resolvers is held, and at most one later call gets a clean cannot-complete. There is no wrong number from C09 itself. Separately, the stale monitor cell left on 77 is C03's wrong-number path, and C03's fix covers it.

The verifier's one-gate fix is complete. In 74HC both halves are needed: the !f_cancel gate on w_fwd stops the pushes, and the F_WRITE exit keeps the forwarder from hanging. Out of this cluster, the counter watch against the RC arming time is a hardware-only margin the RTL cannot show.

I ran no simulation. My notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C09-skeptic-mechanism/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers: the bench runs at real timers and both variants reproduce. It needs a fault: a local-trunk (LTU) link outage longer than T_REL (256 ms) that starts while a forward from that link is held at this exchange. The outage can come from a cable pulled or cut, or from the far exchange losing power or its clock (its HCLK stops); all are plausible on a breadboard network. network.md's own traffic figures put a hub's resolver load at 0.26 E (8 exchanges of 48 lines) and 0.64 E (20 exchanges), so each incoming link holds a forward about 5-15% of the time. The auditor's 5-25% is a little wide. Once triggered, harm is likely rather than rare. The old legs are freed and the sweep takes the lowest free trunk a direction, so the next origin call or forward in those directions picks exactly those legs. Any M on an old leg (an incoming flood, or a claim) fires the stale R_LEG, and the mend fires the stale R_GONE. A baseband cut is not affected: baseband_card has no mute, so the incoming's BUSY falls at T_REL and R_GONE fires normally. MF8 is not in the RTL; only the LTU reaches this today, though a spec MF8 trunk group would too.
