findings.evidence:
The mechanism holds step by step in the snapshot:
- local_trunk.v:187-189: a dead link gives a_tx=0 on all 8 channels and mute_blk=1.
- port.v:147: BUSY includes mute_blk.
- net_unit.v:688-689: R_GONE needs the incoming to read !BUSY, so it cannot fire while muted.
- No other exit applies. w_claim (:659) needs a monitor wanting the incoming, and that monitor was dropped on d_clr at 347 ms. The resolver has no timer.
- The legs latch src=incoming with bsy=1, and their E is the incoming's M, now 0. Their fE falls T_REL later and rel clears the latch (port.v:176-193), so the legs become free and sweepable. They are still `mine` (:436) and can still fire R_LEG (:684-687) on any M.
- The mend makes the incoming read !BUSY, and R_GONE writes 00/bsy0 to every old leg (:694-698).

My reruns show the same events as the auditor's logs:
- var0: B20's origin seized the old legs at 999 ms. At the mend, '2050.141 rs_busy 01 -> 00' is followed by 'port 40 latch -> src 00' and 'port 30 latch -> src 00': B20's flood is cut mid-dial. After the origin takes the M on E30 as its claim, B20 hears E but E hears nothing. E30, now not BUSY and not `mine`, is then classified and forwarded W and S (4730-4742 ms): a phantom.
- var1: '500.395 rs_busy 01 -> 00' then '500.813 port 10 latch -> src 30 bsy 1' is the stale R_LEG pointing the dead B10 at the E caller's E30. After the mend, '4630.009 far LTU ch 0: M seen by W neighbour -> 1' lasts until the E-B21 call ends.

The spec has the same gap. Old network.md 3.2 says "frees itself when the incoming trunk reads BUSY = 0", and the new exchange/network.md 3.5 says the same, while local-trunk.md, mf8-unit.md and fabric.md 5.2 force BUSY on a muted group. The RTL follows the spec faithfully.

Some details are overstated:
(a) "Resolver lost for the whole outage" holds only until the first M on any old leg, or the mend. At a busy hub that comes quickly, but every exit writes stale.
(b) var0's E-party "claim" at about 3240 ms is not something the called exchange would send. After the stale drop at 2051 ms, E30 carries nothing, the E monitor clears (CLR) and never sees b. The realistic var0 outcome is B20's call failing with cannot-complete (T_CLAIM). The same M on E30 can still come from an unrelated E seizure of E30, which E sees idle, because the origin's watch (net_unit.v:795-804) takes any M on a held trunk as the claim. So the half-connected call and the phantom are reachable, but need that extra event.
(c) var1's stimulus is fully realistic: E seizes the idle E30 to call B21, and the cable is mended during that call.
(d) The var1 failure 'B holds E30 as an incoming seizure' is a bench-check artefact, not part of the bug: the one-leg forward correctly re-points E30 at S40.

verifier.root_cause: A resolver stays alive only until its incoming trunk reads BUSY = 0 (net_unit.v:688-689, as network.md 3.2/3.5 specify). MUTE_BLK holds that BUSY for the whole of a dead LTU link (local_trunk.v:189, port.v:147). Meanwhile the legs release themselves on their own fE detectors (port.v:176-193) and go back into service. The resolver outlives its legs and later writes to ports that other calls now use: R_LEG at :684-705 and R_GONE at :694-698.
verifier.best_fix:
I recommend the auditor's fix, work/audit/fwd/rtl_fix/net_unit.v. Each leg gets two flip-flops: rs_lb (seen BUSY) and rs_lf (then seen free, meaning it released itself). A resolver whose held legs are all rs_lf dissolves without writing anything. rs_lf legs are left out of `mine`, R_LEG, the w_res drops and the w_claim drops.
- Cost: about 8 flip-flops and a few gates per resolver, roughly 2 packages; it lives in net_unit only and needs no spec change to MUTE_BLK.
- The legs' own RC detectors serve as the timer, so the fix covers any cause of a stuck-BUSY incoming, not only MUTE.
- It keeps R_GONE for legs that never released (an incoming that died inside T_ARM of the leg writes leaves no fE edge).
- It also removes the normally redundant R_GONE writes to legs that have already released.
- The copy also carries the separate C09 F_WRITE f_cancel gate, which can be split off.

One leftover window, untested: on a leg's first free sample rs_lf is still 0, so an M in that same pass still fires R_LEG. One gate closes it: make R_LEG require `sp_m && !rs_lf && (sp_busy || !rs_lb)`.

I rejected a cheaper variant with 1 flip-flop per leg that dissolves on the first leg seen free. It can leave a leg latched for good when the incoming dies while the legs straddle T_ARM.

A zero-part alternative, tested: leave MUTE_BLK out of BUSY on trunk-group adapters (fabric.md 5.2 already makes the OR a jumper). A dead trunk group's words already float to NONE, and the BUSY force exists for terminals (mf8-unit.md). With it, tb_fx sc2 behaves like a baseband cut: R_GONE fires at 346 ms, var0 has no stale drops and var1 no phantom. But it is a spec change: local-trunk.md, mf8-unit.md, fabric.md, and the checks at tb_ltu.v:454-464 and tb_lnet.v:243 all say MUTE_BLK busies the group. It also leaves the resolver's lifetime tied only to the incoming's BUSY, so it is the second choice.
verifier.fix_tested:

- The auditor's earlier runs: tb_fx sc2 var0 18/18, var1 all but the known one-leg re-point artefact, sc4 PASS, tb_chain 32/32, tb_lchain 48/48.

No-mute alternative on the snapshot net_unit:
- tb_fx sc2 var0 17/18 and var1 14/16. The only failures are the MUTE_BLK-busies-group check (by construction) and the var1 bench artefact (run_nm_sc2var{0,1}.log).

The one-gate R_LEG refinement is not tested.
verifier.summary:
Confirmed, medium; one root cause. I re-ran the auditor's real-timer reproducer (tb_fx +sc=2, var0 and var1) on the snapshot, and both logs match the auditor's line for line.

On a local-trunk link outage longer than T_REL, the incoming port keeps reading BUSY because of MUTE_BLK, so the resolver never gets its R_GONE. Its legs, meanwhile, release themselves and are reused. The stale resolver then:
- cuts B20's live flood trunks at the mend (var0);
- points the dead incoming at an unrelated E caller's trunk, so after the mend the W neighbour sees a phantom seizure carrying that caller's hook and voice for the whole call (var1).

It takes a fault (a link down for more than 256 ms while a forward from it is held, about 5-15% of the time per link at a hub). Once that happens, the harm is likely, because the sweep reuses exactly the freed legs.

Some details are overstated:
- The resolver is lost only until the first M on an old leg or the mend, not necessarily for the whole outage.
- var0's post-cut "claim" is not something the called exchange would send; the realistic var0 outcome is B20's call failing. An unrelated E seizure can produce the same half-connected call and phantom.
- MF8 is not in the RTL yet.
- The var1 failure 'B holds E30 as an incoming seizure' is a bench-check artefact.

The auditor's per-leg seen-BUSY/seen-free fix closes the hole, and I added the missing check: tb_net passes 88/88, identical to baseline. An optional one-gate refinement would close a remaining one-pass window. A zero-part alternative (leave MUTE_BLK out of BUSY on trunk groups) also clears both variants but changes the spec and two bench checks.

Files are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C10-resolver-muted-incoming/: NOTES.md, the run_*.log files and site_fx_nomute.v.

skeptics.lens: Skeptic review of mechanism, realism and severity, and of the fix. Read-only: snapshot RTL, the auditor's tb_fx bench and logs, the verifier's runs, and old and new specs. No simulation run.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived the mechanism from the snapshot and every step holds.
- A dead link sets a_tx=0 and mute_blk=1 (local_trunk.v:187-189), and port.v:147 ORs mute_blk into BUSY. R_GONE needs the incoming to read !BUSY (net_unit.v:688-689), so it cannot fire until the mend.
- The legs listen to B10. Their fE falls T_REL later and rel clears the latch (port.v:183-193), so they become free. The sweep checks only M and BUSY (:756-759, :781), so it will take them again. They are still `mine` (:436) and can still fire R_LEG (:684-687). The logs match: run_fx_sc2var0.log :106-108 and run_fx_sc2var1.log :64-65 and :115.

The verifier's corrections are right:
- The resolver is lost only until the first M on an old leg, or the mend.
- var0's E claim after the cut is not realistic; the real var0 outcome is a clean T_CLAIM cannot-complete.
- The var1 'B holds E30' failure is a bench artefact.

I refine two points.
(1) A ONE-LEG forward is nearly harmless. R_LEG with rs_two=1 drops nothing and writes no way back (:694-705). Only the stale R_GONE at the mend can cut its one old leg. So the phantom needs a hub forward (two or more legs).
(2) var1's stimulus is not the typical way in. The far end hunts from the opposite end of the group (local-trunk.md: "from the glare end the key hunts from the top"), so it takes B's first channel only when the group is nearly full. The common way in is B's own next forward or origin. Its sweep picks exactly the old legs, since they are again the first candidates. The far CLAIM on one of them fires the stale R_LEG, which writes B10 -> claimed leg with bsy 1. The new call still completes, because its own resolver writes the correct way back. But B10's stale latch now lasts as long as that call.

A second path that the auditor and verifier both missed makes it worse. The forward B held when the link died belongs to the ORIGINAL call, whose origin is at W (or upstream, through W's resolver). That call is still pending, with W's ch0 still d_held, until b + T_CLAIM (up to T_KEY). Suppose the stale R_LEG has fired and the link mends inside that window. W's origin claim watch (net_unit.v:795-804) accepts the stale M on ch0 as THE claim: it is past the guard, so it is not treated as glare. At o_last, N_DONE connects the W caller to ch0, which is B10 listening to the claimed old leg. The W caller hears one side of a stranger's call (ringback, then a voice) and cannot be heard. Through W's resolver the same thing happens one hop further up. This is a crossed connection, not a cannot-complete. It needs a narrow timing, though: an outage of roughly 0.3 to 5 s, an M on an old leg inside it, and the mend after that M. My estimate is about 1% of triggers, so roughly 0.1-0.5% of outages that start under a forward. It combines with C12.

If W's ch0 is already free at the mend, W classifies it as a seizure. It floods network-wide and holds a trunk per link, a monitor per arrival and a resolver per transit for the unrelated call's duration (C08-like, but bounded). At network.md §10's 0.19 E, losing one of two resolvers raises unforwarded floods at each transit from about 1.4% to about 16% for those minutes. If the leg's call is still being dialled (var1), W's monitors count a suffix of the number, and a mis-parsed claim is possible but very rare. A stale drop that hits another resolver's current legs gives that resolver stale legs too (a cascade). The fix covers that.

On realism: it needs a link fault. An outage longer than 256 ms starts under a forward from that link 5-15% of the time at a hub, which matches network.md 3.5/10. After that, at a busy hub, the stale way back is likely within seconds. Per exchange per busy hour it is far below 0.01 unless outages are frequent. The outcomes, most likely first:
- a bounded network-wide phantom and capacity loss after a mend;
- cut pending flood branches (cannot-complete);
- rarely, a one-way crossed connection.

There is no silent wrong-number on the common path, so medium is right. Only the LTU reaches this in the RTL; spec MF8 trunk groups would too.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The auditor's rs_lb/rs_lf fix is correct for this mechanism, and I recommend it together with the verifier's one-gate refinement (R_LEG needs sp_m && !rs_lf && (sp_busy || !rs_lb)). I read the diff against the snapshot:
- rs_lf legs are excluded from mine, R_LEG, the w_claim drop and the R_GONE drop.
- lb/lf are cleared at allocation.
- The dissolve and w_res cannot fire on the same tick, because each tests rs_act differently.
- The refinement is safe: a latched leg is always BUSY, so a real claim never arrives on a leg that reads !BUSY after lb is set.
- The fix also covers the cascade, and any other stuck-BUSY incoming, such as a /HB driver stuck low.

Corrections and gaps:
(1) The cost is understated. Eight flip-flops per resolver is already 2 x 74HC175 before any set/qualify gating, the dissolve term, and the extra !lf input on R_LEG, mine, the claim drop and the R_GONE drop for each leg. Realistically that is about 5-8 packages per resolver, 10-16 for NRES=2, not "about 2". That matters under the two-layer-board rule.
(2) The zero-part alternative deserves more weight than "second choice": leave the MUTE_BLK OR out on TRUNK adapters. fabric.md 5.2 already makes the OR a jumper. mf8-unit.md:689-692 says the BUSY force is "what it asked for on a terminal", while the floating words are what network.md asks for on any carrier. The verifier's run shows it clears both variants. If card space is tight, it is a sound first step, and lb/lf is the general cure. It is a spec change: tb_ltu.v:454-464 and tb_lnet.v:243 would change.
(3) Regression gap: the fix edits `mine`. tb_lfull, the bench that found the `mine` glare case, and tb_lnet were not run on it. Run both before adopting it.
(4) Residuals neither fix closes, both outside this cluster:
- If the far end's release RC is faster than B's leg's, the far end can re-seize the channel while B's leg is still latched and BUSY, and R_LEG takes that as a claim. The window is the RC spread, tens of ms, and it is not specific to MUTE (C13).
- B10 at the mend is re-classified as a fresh seizure mid-dial (C07).
- A leg whose fE never rose, written less than T_ARM before the link died, stays latched until the mend: a lost trunk if the link never comes back. This is rare and pre-existing.
skeptics.summary:
Confirmed, and medium is the right severity; I agree with the verifier. I re-derived the whole mechanism from the snapshot and it holds exactly as claimed. A dead local-trunk link forces BUSY through MUTE_BLK, so R_GONE cannot fire. The legs release themselves T_REL later and are swept again. The stale resolver then:
- fires R_LEG on the first M on an old leg, dropping the other old legs and writing the way back onto the dead incoming;
- or fires R_GONE at the mend, cutting whatever is using the old legs by then.

The verifier's corrections stand. I add four points:
- A one-leg forward is nearly harmless: its R_LEG writes nothing.
- var1's far-end seizure of B's first channel is atypical, because the far end hunts from the opposite end. The common way in is B's own reuse of the old legs followed by a far claim, with the same stale way back.
- A missed, worse path: the original call's origin at W (or upstream) is often still pending. If the mend comes inside a narrow window, it accepts the stale M as its claim and connects its caller one-way to a stranger's call. Rare, around 1% of triggers, but a crossed connection.
- The phantom seizure at W floods network-wide and ties up a resolver and a monitor at each exchange for the unrelated call's duration.

The per-leg fix plus the one-gate refinement is right and complete for this mechanism. Its cost is understated (about 5-8 packages per resolver, not 2), and tb_lfull and tb_lnet were not run on it. The zero-part change, leaving MUTE_BLK out of BUSY on trunk adapters, matches mf8-unit.md's own rationale and is a sound cheap first step.

Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C10-skeptic/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: Yes, at real timers, but it has no conforming trigger of its own. It is a second line of defence: it turns into a wrong number any upstream miscount that claims before b. The triggers are C03's stale cell, (1,e) variant, at exchanges whose e is 1 (the C03 verifier reproduced this with a conforming trigger in tb_c03g). Others: a C07 link hit between the seizure and e at an e=1 exchange, glare past the guard's reach at a transit (C13/C05), and a far A stuck at 1 (a card fault). The C03 verifier found that C03's fix and C04's C_LOW fix reopen the hole when merged, so this origin-side check keeps its value whatever the merge.
findings.ran: All at real timers through sim.sh. (1) The auditor's tb_mc2 on the snapshot, mc2_snap.log. (2) A new tb_c12.v on the snapshot, scenario S3: A=1 held on A12's receive wire from 300 ms after e, c12_snap.log. (3) Both again on the fixed copy with the C12_TRACE define, mc2_fix.log and c12_fix.log. All logs are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C12-origin-claim-acceptance/.
findings.evidence: Code: net_unit.v:794-804 sets claimed and dmo on the first sp_m sample on any d_held trunk in N_NET or N_WAITCL. Nothing checks f2 there; `guarding` only decides whether it is counted as glare. N_NET then carries the claim through b (866-873) to N_DONE at o_last (881). The spec says the same ('the FIRST M seen on a held trunk', new network.md 4.1; old network.md 3), so the RTL follows the spec and the finding is a hardening gap. mc2_snap.log matches the auditor's run_mc2.log line for line: A claimed=1 at 1895 in N_NET, b at 2893, X22 rung at 3894, 3 FAILs. c12_snap.log S3: A claimed A12 at 20108 in N_NET (b came at 20797), dropped A11 toward the owner Y, and connected A20 to A12 at 22697, although X had claimed nothing. On the fix, mc2_fix.log: X's stale cell still claims at 1894, but A sees the rise (tmr 1191, outside the guard), marks it EARLY at 1897 and gives nogo at 1898. X's register is freed at 2156, X22 is never rung, and A21 hears cannot-complete. c12_fix S3 gives nogo 4 ms after the rise. The finding's premise holds: across 19 legitimate claims in tb_net, tb_chain and tb_lfull, M rose 1.14-4.17 ms AFTER the origin's f2 (1.14 on the local trunk, 2.16 on a baseband neighbour, 4.17 over two hops), never before.
findings.notes: The one FAIL left in mc2_fix ('A21 is not talking to X22') is a known bench artefact that the C03 verifier also found. The bench lifts X22 regardless, X gives it dial tone, and the check busy_x[22] && rx_a[21]==0 trips on the cannot-complete zeros; the printed samples show A21 never follows X22. The fix does not stop the (e+1,b) variant, or any miscount that claims at or after b. The auditor's cost of 'one flip-flop and a tap on tmr' is optimistic: measuring a few ms from the rise needs either restarting tmr (which moves T_KEY) or its own small counter.

findings.real_timing: The mechanism shows at real timers, but the trigger needs a carrier fault: a false A=1 sample on a held outgoing trunk between the seizure and the true claim (2-4 s). On local_trunk, A is a clocked bit with no RC (local_trunk.v:30-33), so one bit error on the A conductor gives one frame of A=1, sampled by the port's 1 ms turn 1 time in 8. On baseband it would take an impulse longer than the RC and over the '14 threshold. Slips cannot make a 1 out of a steady 0. MF8 is not built. Rare with conforming equipment.
findings.ran: tb_c12.v scenario S2: 1 ms of A=1 OR-ed onto the X->A wire of A12, 300 ms after e (outside the guard, before b), in the topology Y(31)-A11 A(22) A12-X(13), with A20 dialling 1 3 1 2 1. Run on the snapshot (c12_snap.log) and on the fix (c12_fix.log), at real timers through sim.sh.
findings.evidence: Snapshot: A claimed trunk 12 at 11105 in N_NET. dirs went from 1100 to 1000: A11, toward the owner Y, was dropped at once by dmo. A connected A20 to A12 at o_last (13695). Y never claimed and Y21 never rang (3 FAILs). After hang-up all three exchanges were idle, so nothing is left stuck. That matches the finding's consequence exactly: the caller sits in X's hold listening to 00. Fix: the trace shows the glitch gave ONE rise sample, which was ignored. Y claimed at b, A kept A11, Y21 rang, PASS.
findings.notes: Transit resolvers have the same one-sample, any-time acceptance (net_unit.v:683-687, R_LEG). The finding does not mention it and neither fix covers it. A glitch on a transit's leg drops the owner's legs, and the origin gives nogo at T_CLAIM. With C11's `lost` fix and no persistence, a one-sample false claim becomes a NOGO about 4 ms later instead of silence, but the call is still lost. The 2-4 sample persistence avoids losing it.

verifier.root_cause: Both findings have one root cause, the origin's claim detector at net_unit.v:794-804. It is a single unqualified sample: `if (o_net && sp_fresh && sp_m && !claimed)` over the held trunks. It has no persistence (so it catches glitches, finding 2) and does not check that b has been counted (so it catches early claims, finding 1). The spec's 'the FIRST M seen on a held trunk' (network.md 4.1) says the same thing.
verifier.best_fix: Use one small circuit on the origin bank for both findings. It is written and tested in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C12-origin-claim-acceptance/rtl_fix/net_unit.v (diff in fix.patch). A claim is M standing N_CL=4 samples running on the first held trunk seen high. It uses cl_n (3 bits) and cl_j (2 bits), plus cl_g, which latches `guarding` at the rise so that glare is classified as before. When the fourth sample comes: if it rose inside the guard, or b is in (f2), it is the claim, as before (dmo, glare counted). Otherwise `early` is set, and N_NET gives nogo through N_DROP. f2 clears `early`, so a rise up to 3 ms before b is still accepted. Cost: about 7 flip-flops, roughly a '161 and a '74 plus gates, about 2 packages. It adds 3 ms to every claim and glare, which does no harm. It can share one counter with C11's `lost` counter, which counts M-low samples after the claim. Cheaper variants: (a) the auditor's pending flip-flop, for finding 1 only. (b) Since legitimate claims were measured 1.14-4.17 ms after f2, even 'M on a held trunk outside the guard before f2 means nogo', with no slack, passed every case seen, but the counter's slack costs nothing and removes the phase doubt. Untested improvements: drop only the early trunk (dmo on cl_j) instead of giving nogo, so a true owner in another direction can still claim; and put the same 4-sample stand on the resolver's R_LEG watch. Neither fixes the root of C03 (the stale cell still claims and briefly takes X's register), so C03's own fix is still needed.

verifier.summary:
Both findings hold, and they share one root cause: the origin takes the first single sample of M on any held trunk as the claim, whether or not b is in (net_unit.v:794-804). The spec says the same thing, so this is a hardening gap, not a departure from the spec.

**origin-accepts-early-claim: confirmed, medium.** I re-ran the auditor's tb_mc2 and it matches their log exactly: A accepts X's claim in N_NET, 1 s before b, and X22 rings. My new tb_c12 S3 reproduces it on its own. It has no conforming trigger of its own; it turns upstream miscounts that claim before b into wrong numbers:
- C03's stale cell, (1,e) variant;
- C07 link hits before e at an e=1 exchange;
- glare past the guard's reach.

It is worth keeping as a second line, because C03's and C04's fixes conflict when merged.

**claim-on-one-sample: confirmed, low.** An injected 1 ms A glitch between e and b (tb_c12 S2):
- makes A drop the owner's direction and connect the caller into X's hold at o_last;
- leaves Y unclaimed and Y21 unrung;
- leaves nothing stuck after hang-up.

The trigger needs a carrier fault; the local trunk's A has no RC. Transit resolvers have the same weakness, and neither the finding nor the fix covers it.

**Fix:** one combined change, about 7 flip-flops. A claim must stand 4 samples, and one that stands outside the guard before b gives nogo.
- On the fix: tb_net 88/88, tb_chain 32/32, tb_lfull 40/40, tb_c12 12/12, tb_mc2 safe (8/9; the one FAIL is the known bench artefact).
- Legitimate claims were measured 1.14-4.17 ms after b, never before.

C03 still needs its own fix: this one stops the wrong number at the origin, not the stale cell's claim.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM + REALISM/SEVERITY (independent skeptic, read-only; no simulation run)

per_finding.reason:
MECHANISM: I re-derived it from the snapshot's net_unit.v. The claim at 794-804 is `o_net && sp_fresh && sp_m && !claimed` on any d_held trunk, with o_net = N_NET|N_WAITCL. f2 is never tested there; `guarding` only decides whether n_glare counts it. The claim sets dmo at once, which drops the owner's direction before b. N_NET then carries `claimed` through f2 into N_WAITCL, and to N_DONE at o_last (lines 866-881). The spec says the same thing (exchange/network.md table l.203, 'the FIRST M seen on a held trunk'), so this is a hardening gap and not a departure from the spec. mc2_fix.log matches the verifier's account: X claims at 1894 and holds its register until 2156; A marks it EARLY at 1897 and gives nogo at 1898.

TRIGGERS, three corrections:
(1) The 'far A stuck at 1' trigger is mostly blocked. The sweep refuses a trunk whose M is up at its select (h_m) or at the confirm pass, and the classifier would take such a trunk as a seizure. Only a card that fails inside the roughly 3 s window matters.
(2) There is a second path the verifier missed, and it makes the snapshot worse. A C07 outage of 8-256 ms in the pause between e and b is counted as a digit '1' by every monitor beyond the link. Exchange (e,1) then claims before b and gets the wrong exchange. If the dialled b is itself 1, the TRUE owner claims early, and its register reads the caller's b h as h s: the wrong line at the right exchange. Either way it is a claim before b, which the snapshot connects and the fix turns into nogo. The verifier listed only the pre-e (1,e) case.
(3) 'Legit claims never before f2' is a bench artefact. tb_net and tb_chain run every exchange on one clock, and their callers (ports 20-27) sit above their trunks (10-17). From the RTL constants, a direct neighbour's claim is seen at lag = (p-q)/64 + ~0.32 ms (WAIT 156 us + 17 bits 133 us + sync frames) + u + w, with u, w in [0,1), p the caller's port and q the far trunk's port. I checked the model against the lfull_fix C12T trace: there, lag = r/64 + 0.015 + k, rising 1/64 ms per origin trunk port r, with 1 ms jumps. With a low-numbered caller and a high-numbered far trunk, a real claim can come about 0.6-0.8 ms BEFORE f2.

The finding's premise still holds: a claim a whole digit before b is never real.

REALISM: nothing conforming triggers it on its own. It is the last line that decides between a wrong number and a cannot-complete, for C03 (1,e), C07 pre-e and e-b outages, and glare beyond the guard's reach. Those are rare, roughly 1e-6 to 1e-5 per call, more on a flapping link, but each one that gets through is a wrong number. C03's and C04's fixes conflict when merged. Medium is right.

MECHANISM confirmed. One probe sample of M on any held trunk sets claimed and dmo, in N_NET or N_WAITCL. tb_c12 S2 shows the result: the owner's direction is dropped, and at o_last the caller is connected into the far hold, listening to 00. Nothing is left stuck, and there is no wrong number. Once the glitch is accepted the owner never sees b, or loses its trunk and its register clears at CLR before h is dialled. Without C11's `lost` fix the caller hears silence; with it, nogo.

CORRECTION to the verifier's rate: a frame is 15.6 us (64 kHz TX_CLK; 8 cells at 512 kbps on the local trunk). The port's M is on /HA once a 1 ms pass. So a one-frame A error is seen 1 time in 64, not 1 in 8, and the rate from bit errors is 8x lower than stated. On a local trunk that makes the chance per call about 3000 x BER per held trunk: negligible on a healthy link.

A second fault path, also rare: on the local trunk, a glitch on the far HCLK can shift the receive cell count for up to one frame, until TX_CLK re-aligns it. That puts a neighbouring channel's A on the held trunk, and A is 1 on any established call. The same 1/64 sampling applies.

On baseband it takes an impulse longer than the RC that lands on a frame edge. The transit resolver's R_LEG (lines 686-692) has the same single-sample acceptance, but it only ever produces a clean loss (T_CLAIM nogo). Low is right.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's combined fix (rtl_fix/net_unit.v, fix.patch) is correct, and I recommend it. A claim must be M standing 4 samples on the first held trunk seen high. If it rose outside the guard and b is not in by the 4th sample, the origin gives nogo; otherwise it is the claim, with cl_g keeping glare classified as before.

Correct:
- The 3 ms of slack is necessary, not just harmless. By my timing analysis, a legitimate claim from a direct neighbour can be seen up to about 0.6-0.8 ms before f2, when the caller's port number is low and the far trunk's is high. The 4th sample then lands about 2.3 ms after f2, so it is accepted.
- The verifier's cheaper variant (b), 'M before f2 outside the guard = nogo' with no slack, is unsafe. It would give cannot-complete on a small fraction of real calls: several percent for unlucky port pairs, and it drifts through every phase at ±20 ppm. The benches missed this because tb_net and tb_chain share one clock and put callers above trunks.
- The auditor's 'pending flip-flop plus a tap on tmr' fix has slack in principle, but it needs its own timer. tmr carries the guard and T_KEY.

Minimal: cl_n needs only 2 bits (0-3), not 3, so the fix is 6 flip-flops. Realistically that is a '74 or half a '163 for the count, a '175 for cl_j, cl_g and early, a half '139 to decode cl_j against the existing four trunk matches, and a few gates: about 2-3 74HC packages. It can share the counter with C11's `lost` counter, since that one counts only after the claim.

Complete for its scope:
- It turns every early claim that stands before b outside the guard into nogo. That covers C03 (1,e), C07 outages before e and in the e-b pause, and glare past the guard, including early claims relayed through transits.
- It filters glitches shorter than 4 samples.
- It does NOT cover claims at or after b: C03 (e+1,b), an outage inside b, or glare after b.
- It does NOT cover the transit resolver's single-sample R_LEG.
- It does not remove the root causes: C03 and C07 still need their own fixes. With this fix, X's stale cell still takes X's register for about 260 ms.

Suggested refinements:
- Apply the same 4-sample stand to R_LEG, which is cheap.
- Consider dropping only the early trunk (dmo = 1<<cl_j) instead of nogo, so an owner in another direction still completes. It cannot make things worse: the port's fE busy holds the dropped channel for T_REL, so no C03-style re-seizure follows, and an early claim from the true owner's own direction still ends in a clean nogo at T_CLAIM. It is untested; nogo is simpler and also safe.
skeptics.summary:
Both findings are real. The verifier's verdicts (confirmed, medium; confirmed, low) and the recommended 4-sample fix stand, with three corrections.

- **Early claims (origin-accepts-early-claim), medium:**
  - The origin takes one M sample on any held trunk as the claim, with no check that b is in (net_unit.v:794-804). This matches the spec's 'FIRST M seen', so it is a hardening gap.
  - It has no conforming trigger of its own. It is the last line that turns upstream miscounts into wrong numbers instead of cannot-completes.
  - There is a second path the verifier missed. A C07 link outage of 8-256 ms in the e-to-b pause makes exchange (e,1) claim before b. When the dialled b is 1, the true owner claims early and rings the wrong line.
  - The 'far A stuck at 1' trigger is mostly blocked, because the sweep never seizes a trunk that shows M.
- **Single-sample claims (claim-on-one-sample), low:**
  - A false sample gives silence (or nogo with C11's fix), never a wrong number.
  - The verifier's rate is 8x too high: a one-frame A error is 15.6 us, so the 1 ms probe sees it 1 time in 64, not 1 in 8.
  - A far HCLK glitch on the local trunk is a further rare fault path.
- **Legit claims can come before b:**
  - 'Legit claims always come after b' is a bench artefact: tb_net and tb_chain run on one clock and put callers above trunks.
  - Timing analysis, checked against the lfull trace (lag = r/64 + k), shows a real direct-neighbour claim can arrive about 0.6-0.8 ms before f2.
  - So the fix's 3 ms of slack is required, and the no-slack variant (b) would reject real calls.
- **Fix:** cl_n needs only 2 bits, making it about 6 flip-flops and 2-3 packages. It does not cover claims at or after b, or the resolver's R_LEG. C03 and C07 still need their own fixes.

No simulation was run. My notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C12-origin-claim-acceptance-skeptic/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: The resolver half happens at real timers with conforming equipment: it needs more than NRES (2) floods pending at one transit. A resolver is held from the forward until the claim (about 1.8-3 s of e b dialling), or until the drop plus T_REL, or about 4.5 s for a doomed flood. Arithmetic (43 floods/h an exchange, 2.9 s hold, Erlang then Engset): 8 exchanges 2.3% then 1.6% not forwarded; 20 exchanges 11.6% then 10.8%. NRES=3 gives 0.2% at 8 exchanges and NRES=4 gives 0.4% at 20. For a 3-leaf star at design load the loss is about 5e-4 (hub load study). The forwarder-busy half needs a local origin sweep to start within about 5 ms before the first flood's classification, with a second flood within about 20 ms of the first: about 1e-8 per second at design rates, so negligible. In every other case the ~19 ms T_ARM watch spaces classifications past the ~10.6 ms forward: transit study T9 at real timers had 0 losses in 9 crossings, including 6 with gaps of 8.6 ms or less.

findings.notes:
The mechanism is exactly as stated, and the loss is silent: n_nofwd is only a bench output. The finding is overstated in two places:
- The forwarder-busy half is practically unreachable at real timers. It is not a bench artefact, but its rate is about 1e-8 per second.
- The quoted 'contradicts network.md 3.2' refers to the superseded document. That document was itself inconsistent: a chain transit 'holds nothing', yet the owner's claim clears 'the patch toward 25', which needs the leg remembered.

Fix bullets:
- Bullet 1 (stuff NRES) is right and is a parameter.
- Bullet 3 (a pending slot) works; see fix_tested.
- Bullet 2 (patch-and-forget fallback) is unsafe unless the leg is stored somewhere; see chain-forward-holds-resolver.
- Bullet 4 (claim-to-refuse at a chain transit) is UNSAFE. The owner can be upstream of that transit: in chain A-B-C-D, A calls B and C cannot forward to D. C hears b 1-3 ms after B, and its refusal travels back through B's both-ways one-leg patch. It races B's own claim, and the caller could get cannot-complete for a reachable number.

findings.real_timing:
Real timers, as for forward-needs-resolver-and-idle-forwarder, of which it is a duplicate (same lines, same mechanism).

One part is overstated: 'a call crossing k transits is lost with 1-(1-B)^k'. Every flood reaches every transit within milliseconds, so successive transits hold nearly the same set of pending floods, and a flood dropped upstream never loads the transits beyond it. The end-to-end loss is close to B at the busiest transit, not the independent-transit compound.

The new exchange/network.md §3.5 now says exactly this: 'A chain transit needs one as much as a hub: a leg written after the caller's A has gone has no edge left to release on'. It lists sizing as Open (§10). The load studies show NRES=2 is exactly enough on a 3-exchange chain, and NRES=1 loses at Engset(2 sources, 1 server).

findings.real_timing:
Every incoming flood at every leaf, at any timer scale. The cost is about 10.6 ms of forwarder and sweep time per flood, plus a meaningless n_nofwd count.

The consequences are smaller than stated:
- A classifier read has priority over the sweep (cls_issue before h_issue). It waits at most for the sweep's current read, about 9 frames (0.14 ms), not about 1 ms.
- The leaf's own origin waits at most about 10 ms (N_WANT, :848).
- A marker read can wait for its port's turn to line up with the sweep's free frame, up to about 9 ms.

All of these are negligible for service.
findings.evidence: fwd_mask = ~STRAP_N & ~(1<<cls_dir) (:505) is non-zero at a leaf. Unstrapped: leaf forwarder sweeps A 3, C 3; n_nofwd A 3, C 4; 32/32 PASS. The load studies (hub, transit, cap2) show nofwd_empty == seized_in at every leaf.

STRAP_N is used only in the forward decision (net_unit.v:505-506, :616-618), and the origin sweeps with h_mask 1111. So strapping a leaf's absent directions makes fwd_mask 0, at zero parts. Tested: leaf sweeps 3/3 -> 0/0, n_nofwd 0/0, tb_chain still 32/32 PASS. The one drawback is that the installer must remove the strap when a direction is added.

findings.evidence:
net_unit.v:882: `!claimed && tmr >= T_CLAIM` -> N_DROP, with tmr reset at b (f2). A good call drops its losing legs at the claim (:796-800, :831-837). The claim returns in ms: the hub study saw OCLAIM 1.6-1.8 ms after the resolver's R_LEG.

For the origin register, T_CLAIM (2 s) is about the time needed to dial h s anyway, so a doomed call costs that register about the same as a good one. The extra cost falls on the flood's links and resolvers.
findings.notes:
The mechanism is right, and the advice not to build transit refusal is right: it is unsafe, including at chain transits. The feedback magnitude (24% -> 32%) is arithmetic for an overload the register limit (C15) never lets the unit reach in this RTL. It would matter with register pools.

The T_CLAIM tap is a reasonable option, but T_CLAIM of 2 s is the new network.md §2 carrier allowance ('A's delay: anything'; round trip under 2 s). A shorter tap must also cover a second claim at the same owner waiting out the marker's S_WATCH (up to CLR, 256 ms) before cl_st frees. 500 ms covers that on copper and MF8. Untested.

verifier.root_cause:
Three causes, all in net_unit.v:
- **Forward admission is decided once.** A forward is admitted only at the classifier's hold write (net_unit.v:616-617, fst==F_IDLE && rs_free_any). Nothing queues it, retries it or falls back. Every forward, one leg included, holds one of NRES=2 resolvers from the forward to the claim or to the drop plus T_REL (:737-741, :681-708). The monitors are the same kind of limit: one of NMON=2 cells, or none (:612). These are fixed-pool sizing limits, and findings 1, 2 and 5 are all of this kind (1 and 2 are duplicates).
- **T_CLAIM is the only end for a flood nobody claims** (:882). This stretches doomed floods (finding 4), an amplifier of the first cause.
- **The unit does not know which directions exist**, so fwd_mask (:505) sends every leaf flood into a sweep that finds nothing (finding 3), a separate cause.
verifier.best_fix:
1. **Stuff the pools.** NRES=3 up to about 8-10 exchanges, 4 at a centre of about 20. NMON=3, and 4-5 beyond 20 exchanges. Both are parameters already. A resolver is about 4.5 packages, as old network.md sized it. Tested: NRES=3 on tb_fx sc4 at real timers forwards the third flood, and only a fourth is lost.
2. **Strap a leaf's absent directions (zero parts) to stop the leaf sweeps.** STRAP_N is used only by the forward decision, and the origin ignores it. Tested on tb_chain: leaf sweeps 3/3 -> 0/0, n_nofwd 0, 32/32 PASS. This replaces the auditor's '175 register.
3. **Optional: the transit agent's one-slot pending forward** (work/load/transit/fix/net_unit.v, about 3 packages). It closes the forwarder-busy loss, which is rare at real timers but common at scale 8. Tested: sc5d's second flood is forwarded 13.5 ms after its classification, sc4 is unchanged at 10/10, and tb_net passes 88/88. The bench's n_nofwd check still prints FAIL because the fix still counts at classification.
4. **Do not build transit claim-to-refuse**, not even at chain transits: the owner may be upstream and the refusal races its claim.
5. **Build the old doc's 'patch into the first direction found' only with the leg remembered**, for example a '174 per monitor cell. It is untested.
6. **A T_CLAIM tap of about 500 ms for copper/MF8 networks** is a reasonable, untested option. It must cover a second claim at the same owner waiting out S_WATCH (up to 256 ms).

  - tb_fx sc4: 10/10 PASS (runpf_fx_sc4.log).
  - tb_net: 88/88 PASS (runpf_net.log).
- **Leaf straps, tb_chain at scale 8:** unstrapped, leaf sweeps A 3 / C 3 and n_nofwd A 3 / C 4, 32/32 PASS (run_chain_counters.log). Strapped (A 1011, C 0111), sweeps 0/0 and n_nofwd 0/0, 32/32 PASS (run_chain_leafstrap.log).

verifier.summary:
All five mechanisms hold in the snapshot RTL. Both reproducers re-ran byte-identical to the auditors' logs, apart from walltime. They are capacity limits that fail gracefully: a silent cannot-complete at T_CLAIM, nothing stuck, never a wrong number. Most of it is now written down in the new exchange/network.md (§3.4, §3.5, §10 Open); the doc contradictions the findings quote are against the superseded network.md.

- **Findings 1 and 2 are one defect.** A forward needs a free resolver and an idle forwarder at the moment of classification. NRES=2 loses about 1.6-2.3% of floods per central transit at 8 exchanges and about 11% at 20; NRES=3 or 4 brings that to 0.1-0.4%.
  - The forwarder-busy half (sc5d) is real but needs a local origin sweep to coincide, about 1e-8 per second at real timers. At scale 8 it is an artefact.
  - Finding 2's '1-(1-B)^k over k transits' overstates the end-to-end loss, because every transit holds nearly the same pending floods.
- **Finding 5 (monitors)** is the same kind of pool limit on NMON, already a documented limit. About 0.6-0.9% at 8 exchanges, 5% at 20 with NMON=2.
- **Finding 4 (doomed floods)** is confirmed-overstated. The 2.4x hold is measured, but in this RTL the one-register limit (C15) throttles traffic long before links or unit pools run out.
- **Finding 3 (leaf sweeps)** is confirmed and low. Strapping a leaf's absent directions removes it at zero parts; tested on tb_chain.

Recommended fix: stuff NRES and NMON (parameters), strap the leaves, and optionally add the tested pending-forward slot. Two of the proposed fixes are unsafe: transit claim-to-refuse, and a patch-and-forget fallback that keeps no record of its leg.

Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C14-forward-resources/NOTES.md.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM + REALISM AND SEVERITY (independent skeptic, read-only; no simulation run)

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived this from the snapshot and the mechanism is exactly as stated. A forward is admitted only at the classifier's C_ACT write (net_unit.v:616-618). Only F_WRITE allocates a resolver (:737-741) and there is one forwarder, so a resolver that was free at classification is still free at F_WRITE. Nothing retries. Resolvers are freed only by R_LEG, R_GONE or rs_mine.

Release is not cascaded hop by hop. Every leg listens to its incoming port, so when the origin drops, M falls at every downstream incoming within milliseconds, and each port's fM falls one T_REL later, all in parallel. The '+0.26 s' holds at any depth.

One thing neither the auditors nor the verifier said: deciding once is a safety requirement, not an omission. A leg written after the caller's first break gives the downstream monitors a rise in the middle of a digit. They would count the tail of e as e, a wrong-number risk under monitor rule 1. Any retry must drop the seizure on M seen low and stay inside the guard's hop budget, so waiting seconds for a resolver can never be safe. Stuffing is the only remedy for the resolver half.

Forwarder-busy half, re-derived:
- Classifications are at least ~18.2 ms apart: C_HOLD exits at cls_ms > T_ARM+1 (:587), then a read at the port's next turn.
- A forward takes 10-11 ms of service.
- Only an origin sweep in front (F_WANT waits for hst idle and nst != N_WANT, :714) closes that gap.
- At the reference hub the rate is about 3e-9 per second; at 20 exchanges about 5e-8. This is negligible, as the verifier says.
- I found a second route: C_UNHOLD frees the classifier early, but F_HUNT ignores f_cancel until h_done (:720). It needs a seizure that dies inside 16 ms, so it is rarer still and not material.

Realism: the resolver half happens at real timers. On the docs' reference network (8 exchanges, 336 lines, 3 calls a line an hour, 30% leaving, holds of about 2.9 s), each hub sees about 0.23 E. With NRES=2 about 1.5% (Engset) to 2.3% (Erlang B) of floods go unforwarded: about 4-6 an hour at each hub, and about one cannot-complete per exchange per busy hour. At 20 exchanges it is about 11%.

The subscriber hears silence from the key until about 2 s after dialling b (by then usually dialling h s), then cannot-complete. There is never a wrong number, nothing sticks, and a retry usually succeeds.

Because each exchange has only one register, a transit never has more than one pending flood per source exchange. A 3-exchange chain therefore loses nothing, and a 3-leaf star loses about 1e-3. Medium is right for the design network with the RTL's default stuffing.

New doc error: exchange/network.md §10 says 'the one forwarder loses about the flood rate x 11 ms more'. That is the scale-8 behaviour. At real timers the doc's own §3.3 watch prevents it, and hub s1_burst and transit T9 at real timers saw 0 such losses.

This is the same root cause and the same lines as the first finding, so it should be kept only as its duplicate.

The one-leg forward does need its leg remembered, for two reasons:
- A local claim must drop the onward leg (:659-665). Without that, the leg keeps carrying the far caller's A down every downstream link for the length of the call.
- A leg written ~12 ms after the hold arms its fE only ~28 ms after the hold. If the incoming's M falls between the end of the classifier's watch (~18 ms) and then, only R_GONE can clear the leg; otherwise the channel sticks BUSY.

Two parts are overstated, as the verifier says:
- '1-(1-B)^k over k transits'. Every flood reaches every transit within milliseconds, so the pending sets are nearly the same floods, and the end-to-end loss is close to B at the busiest transit.
- 'The docs promise otherwise'. That is against the superseded network.md. The new §3.5 says 'A chain transit needs one as much as a hub', which is exactly the RTL.

fwd_mask (:505) is non-zero at a leaf, so every incoming flood runs a 10 ms sweep that finds nothing, and nf_empty is counted. The consequences are smaller than the auditors said:
- A classifier read waits at most one sweep step, about 0.14 ms, because cls_issue has priority over h_issue.
- A marker read can only select the port the sweep is naming at that moment (win blocks every other frame), so it waits up to about 9 ms.
- The leaf's own origin waits up to about 10 ms, and the guard counts from its seizure write, so the guard loses nothing.
- n_nofwd is a bench port, so the pollution is a bench matter.

This is closer to info than low; there is no service impact.

The verifier's zero-part fix is right. STRAP_N is used only in the forward decision, and the origin sweeps with h_mask 1111. The caveat is that if a link is later added in a strapped direction and the strap is forgotten, the new link carries only its two ends' calls. That shows up at commissioning; it is not silent in service. It is better than the '175 'directions present' register, which learns from sweeps and would miss a direction whose link came up since the last origin sweep.

The mechanism is right: an unclaimed flood ends only at T_CLAIM (:882), and the hub study measured a 4486 ms resolver hold against 1838 ms for a claimed flood at real timers.

The feedback gain is about (H_doom/H_ok - 1) x p, around 0.7 x p. At realistic blocking (p of 2% or less) occupancy rises only 1-2%. The auditors' 24% to 32% needs overload that the one-register limit (C15) never lets the unit reach.

The longest hold of all is one the finding lists but does not size: an accidental or faulty '1' holds every transit's resolver and every exchange's cell for T_KEY (5 s) plus T_REL, longer than a doomed T_CLAIM flood. A plausible fault makes this worse: a line that repeats hang-up, off-hook, short break about every 6 s occupies about one resolver per transit and one cell per exchange, network-wide, about 90% of the time. That halves NRES and NMON of 2 for everyone, and nothing reports it.

The verifier is right that refusal at a transit is unsafe. The T_CLAIM tap is a network-wide planning value like GUARD: it caps the carrier round trip, and it buys little.

The mechanism is right. A cell is given only if m_free1 (:612-615); the hold and the forward go ahead regardless. Because the held port stays BUSY, cls_seen never takes it again, so no late attach is possible, which rule 1 requires. The owner never claims, and the caller hears cannot-complete at T_CLAIM. It is graceful and never a wrong number.

I agree with the verdict and severity, but the verifier's load figures are too low in two ways.

(1) Numbering. A cell is held to b's ID (about 2.6 s, the same as a resolver) whenever e matches. The docs' own worked chain 22-25 shares e=2 everywhere (network.md §4.3: '2 is every monitor's e'), and the reference leaves share e by hub (21-23, 31-33). With a shared e, 8 exchanges put about 0.22 E on the cells, and NMON=2 loses about 1.3-1.9%, not 0.6-0.9%.

(2) A second path nobody listed: the ring strap doubles monitor use. A seizure on a strapped direction still gets a cell (:612 ignores STRAP_N), and the two strap ends receive each other's calls twice (network.md §7). C19-rings/run_r4both_b3_p1.log shows one flood holding both of Y's cells ('want 01', 'want 10'). In a triangle A-B-C with A-C strapped, A can see 3 concurrent seizures from 2 sources. A B-to-A call is lost whenever C's flood is in its cell window: about 1.6-3.1% at design load, where a 3-exchange chain loses 0. NMON=3 removes it.

Stale cells (C03) lower the effective NMON further.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
**Stuff NRES and NMON (parameters).** This is right, and it is the only safe remedy for the resolver half. Deciding once is required by monitor rule 1, so a retry that waits for a resolver can never be safe.
- Sizing: each exchange has one register, so a transit never holds more than one pending flood per source exchange. NRES of at least the number of exchanges whose floods reach it is lossless. The same holds for NMON, plus one for each strapped neighbour.
- In practice: 3 and 3 are lossless up to about 4 exchanges and give about 0.1-0.2% at about 8 exchanges; use 4 and 4 at a centre of about 20. Leaves need no resolvers once strapped.
- This bound breaks once registers are pooled (the C15 fix). It then becomes registers times sources.
- Cost: the verifier's '4.5 packages a resolver' is the old network.md figure for one shared '688 time-multiplexed over an 8 ms scan. The RTL's watch is parallel, 5 compares a resolver plus rs_mine. Built with its own '688s, a resolver is about 10 packages. At the new 1 ms pass a port-time is 64 master ticks, so a shared comparator doing about 28 compares at NRES=4 still fits, but it has to be drawn.

**Missing from the verifier's fix set: make the losses visible.** 'Held, not forwarded' and 'held, no cell' should become event words. The w_ev path and EV_NOTRUNK already exist, and counters.md §7 already asks for a transit-congestion code. It costs about two flags and two codes, and it is the only way to size the pools from live traffic. The findings' core complaint is 'silently'.

**Leaf strap.** This is correct and costs no parts. Remove the strap when a link is added.

**Pending-forward slot.** It is safe: it drops on M seen low, with PF_MAX 24 ms. But at real timers it saves about 1e-8 losses a second, and it lengthens that flood's hop to about 50 ms worst case, beyond the 22-30 ms slow hop that §6's guard must cover. Do not build it on the board; it only helps scale-8 benches.

**Transit claim-to-refuse.** Unsafe, for a broader reason than the verifier's: the origin takes the first M on any held trunk as the claim and drops every other direction (:796-800). A refusal from one branch kills a call whose owner is in another branch.

**Remembered-leg fallback.** At a chain transit it would let a forward proceed with either a resolver or a cell. It must also drop the leg on the cell's d_clr. It is partial at hubs and untested; stuffing is simpler.

**T_CLAIM tap.** Minor. It is network-wide like GUARD and caps the carrier round trip.

**Docs.**
- network.md §10's forwarder figure ('flood rate x 11 ms') is wrong at real timers.
- §7 and §10 should record that a strap end spends two cells per flood between the ends.
- §10's sizing should use the one-register Engset bound.
skeptics.summary:
All five mechanisms hold in the snapshot RTL, and I agree with the verifier on every verdict and severity:
- forward-needs-resolver-and-idle-forwarder: confirmed, medium.
- chain-forward-holds-resolver: confirmed, medium; a duplicate of the first.
- leaf-sweeps-for-nothing: confirmed, low.
- doomed-floods-hold-longest: confirmed-overstated, low.
- monitor-pool-exhaustion: confirmed, medium.

These are fixed-pool sizing limits that fail cleanly: a cannot-complete about 2 s after b, nothing stuck, never a wrong number. On the docs' reference 8-exchange network with the RTL's default NRES=NMON=2, that is roughly one extra cannot-complete per exchange per busy hour. It is zero on a 3-exchange chain, because one register per exchange caps pending floods at one per source.

What I add:
1. **Deciding once is required for safety.** A late leg would make downstream monitors count a truncated e, so stuffing is the only safe remedy for the resolver half. The pending slot is safe but buys about 1e-8 losses a second at real timers and lengthens the worst hop against the guard; do not build it on the board.
2. **The verifier's monitor load is too low for shared-e numbering.** The docs' own examples share e, which holds each cell to b.
3. **A missed path: ring-strap ends spend two cells per flood between the two ends.** C19's log shows one flood holding both of Y's cells. A strapped triangle with NMON=2 then loses about 2-3% of calls into its strap ends, where a chain loses none.
4. **The new network.md §10 overstates the forwarder loss.** 'Flood rate x 11 ms' is scale-8 behaviour; the §3.3 watch prevents it at real timers.
5. **The recommended fix has no observability.** It should add event words for 'not forwarded' and 'no cell'.
6. **Other points:**
   - The '4.5 packages a resolver' cost is the old-scan estimate.
   - Claim-to-refuse is unsafe more broadly than the verifier said: the origin drops every other branch on the first M.
   - A faulty line that keeps producing '1' would pin one resolver and one cell network-wide.

The second makes it worse: the origin keeps its register, and withholds caller<-trunk, until o_last (net_unit.v:410, :881; as specified in new network.md 4.1). This adds about 2.6 s per origin call, turns crossing calls into a double refusal, and delays the refusal tone to after s. Findings 1-3 share the first cause, with the second making them worse. All four findings hold, but the first is overstated. The one register refusing a claim that finds it busy is the documented rule, not an RTL defect. The real news is its size: incoming network calls are refused at about the register's occupancy, around 20% at 48 lines. The design's own traffic model (exch.py) never counted this, because it never takes a register at the owner on a claim.

I re-ran the crossing-call reproducer. At scale 8 it matches the auditor's log exactly. At real timers (conforming 10 pps dials, lifts 23 ms apart) both claims are refused, and each caller hears cannot-complete 1.82 s after the claim, only after dialling h s. The RTL matches the new network.md 4.1 ('connect at the last digit'). That contradicts old monitor.md 2 and common-control.md 2.3, and the new 4.2's 'heard through the path already up'.

The cheap fix is to connect at the claim (drop o_last at net_unit.v:881). It saves gates and gives the refusal at once. Of a crossing pair, at most one call now fails. Tested:

- tb_lfull is 40/40.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived it from the RTL and it holds. att_refuse (mini_marker.v:282) fires whenever r_busy is set outside WATCH: in S_YIELD, S_COLLECT, S_PROBE, S_READ-for-called and the first DRAIN tick. A claim waits only in S_READ-for-caller (r_busy is 0 there) and in WATCH. The origin's register stays in S_YIELD until N_DONE, and N_DONE is reachable only from N_WAITCL with o_last (net_unit.v:881). snapR's timestamps match that (claims at 2243.290 and 2320.290, both mk 6, both refused).

The severity is overstated, and medium is right:
- Refusing on a busy register is the documented rule (old mini-marker.md 312, monitor.md 2, common-control.md 2.3).
- The result is a clean cannot-complete, with no wrong number.
- The crossing case is not a separate driver. The realistic way to get crossing calls is two parties calling each other back after a dropped call. Then both called lines are off-hook anyway, so the double refusal loses nothing. S2's four free lines are ordinary occupancy.
- The ~22% needs 48 lines at 3 calls/h, which is a business calling rate. At a residential 1-1.5 calls/h it is about 8-11%. At 16 lines it is about 1 refusal per busy hour.

Three things neither the auditors nor the verifier counted make the figures somewhat worse:
(a) When one party clears, the other party, still off-hook, gets the register and dial tone. This is documented (old marker.md 186-187, mvp.md 108). It holds the register until hang-up plus CLR, or for NODIG's 10 s. It happens about once per answered call, and neither reg1.py nor exch.py counts it. I estimate +0.03-0.06 E, taking ~22% to ~25-27%.
(b) Callers redial after a refusal. A refused claim still claims (CLM), so its flood costs every link, monitor and resolver as much as a successful call. With persistent redial, attempts rise by about 1/(1-p).
(c) The model's fixed 0.8 s pause is the speed of a pulse keypad's sender. People on rotary dials pause longer, so the model's occupancy is optimistic for rotary phones.

The auditors call it graceful with nothing held. That is true except on the WATCH path: there a waiting claim is refused one tick late on a stale r_busy, and C01 shows that can latch CLM onto a released trunk for good. That is C01's defect, but C15's 'graceful' depends on C01 being fixed.

The auditor's 'network completion falls towards 0 under overload' is real during bursts. Local callers queue on their M and win every time the register frees. Claims never queue, so a busy exchange is unreachable from the network. Old network.md 5.1's bursty one-register row (callers wait 13 s at 99%) implies near-total claim refusal during a burst.

The loss is also silent to the operator. There is no event word for a refused claim: the RTL sends only 04 and 10, and counters.md 9.2 has none.

This is the same code path, correctly described: a claim that finds the register busy with anything is written 03 with BSY and CLM (mini_marker.v:320-327). That includes a local caller who has lifted and not yet dialled, since r_busy is set from the attach.

The claim handler serves one cell at a time (net_unit.v:331-340, 672-675). So of two claims in one tick, the second is refused whenever the first was taken.

The mechanism, its B = A/(1+A) figures and 'graceful, immediate at the owner' are all right, apart from the WATCH/C01 exception noted under the first finding. It duplicates one-register-claim-refusal.

Its mechanism is right. Its 16-19% is consistent with the model at 48 lines, and its point that monitor.md 2's 'hears it at once' does not hold is right: that is refusal-heard-after-hs.

Its proposed second register on the mini marker, reserved for claims, would work but is not cheap. It needs another pulse_reg (probe, pulse_rx, 16-bit store, timers) plus a second caller/called context through the one sequencer. It duplicates the first finding.

The caller is written to SILENCE at the key (mini_marker.v:428). caller<-trunk is written only at N_DONE (net_unit.v:818-822), which needs o_last. Nothing else writes the caller in between. In snapR the caller hears 03 1.82 s after the refusal, and in fixR 0.39 ms after the origin sees the claim (2244.171 to 2244.562).

What the subscriber gets: h s (about 2-3 s on a rotary dial) dialled into silence, then cannot-complete. That is common in real networks, so low severity is right.

It also has a capacity cost, counted under the first finding. The origin's register is held about 2.6 s longer, and the whole claimed path about as long again, since the caller keeps dialling before hearing the tone.

The RTL matches the new network.md 4.1. It contradicts old monitor.md 2 and common-control.md 2.3, and it makes new 4.2's 'heard through the path already up' misleading.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
FIX (1), CONNECT AT THE CLAIM (net_unit.v:881 `claimed && dmo==0`, o_last deleted), is correct, minimal and a gate saving on 74HC. I checked the diff myself:
- N_DONE is still reachable only from N_WAITCL. So glare inside the guard still waits for b, and the own-code and service-digit checks on e b still apply.
- The origin trunk still listens to the caller. The pulses of h s go down it unchanged after the register is freed.
- The caller's port carries BSY, so neither the marker nor the classifier re-takes it.
- The verifier's evidence stands: fixR/fix8 refusals A 1 B 0, B21 rings, tb_net 87/88 (only check 11's connect-at-last-digit assertion fails, by construction), tb_lfull 40/40.

It fixes refusal-heard-after-hs completely. It reduces, but does not remove, the capacity loss (model: 21.8% to 19.2%).

One nit: 'of a crossing pair at most one fails' is not strictly true on the fix. Each origin's register is freed only when the other end's claim or refusal comes back. So both are still refused when the two b digits are counted within about the claim's return delay of each other. From fixR's timestamps that is about ±1.2 ms on a direct link (monitor +1.0 ms, CLAIM word +0.29 ms, back at the origin +0.9 ms), growing a little per hop. That window is negligible.

The spec changes are wider than 4.1:
- network.md 4.1: the connect row, and 'silence from the key to the connect'.
- network.md 4.3: the worked example's 5828 'done, the register freed' becomes about 3311.
- network.md 5 (Glare): 'each origin connects at its caller's last digit' becomes 'at b'.
- network.md 4.2 is then true as written.
- The tb_net 11 check.

What else the fix should come with:
- Coordinate with C01's fix in the same att logic. att_refuse must not fire on the tick the marker has just issued r_release: gate it with !r_release, or take on the release tick. Otherwise a claim that waited out WATCH is still refused, and can latch a stuck CLAIM hold.
- A cheap event word 'claim refused, register busy' (DST the trunk). The refusal write already exists, and today the loss is invisible to the operator.
- Put the capacity figure in mini-marker.md 8 and network.md: refusal of incoming network calls is about the register's occupancy, about lines × calls/h × 6 s / 3600. This makes the mini marker with a unit a small-exchange build: at most about 5% refused means about 10 lines at 3 calls/h, or about 30 at 1 call/h. The old network.md 5.1 already says 'Fit three' registers for dial tone; the same argument applies to claims.
- exch.py Net should take the owner's register at the claim, and hold the remaining party's re-seizure.

A bounded claim wait gains about the ratio of the wait to the residual holding time, ~6% of refusals at 300 ms. It must stay well under the ~590 ms before the far caller's next break, or it risks a lost pulse and a silent wrong number. Not worth it.

Having the monitor cell collect h s and hand the marker a finished number would work, and the cell already has the probe, pulse_rx and steady output. But it needs a second caller/called context in the mini marker's one sequencer: moderate cost, a design decision for Joel. The real cure is a register pool, as the verifier says.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier on all four findings: first finding confirmed-overstated at medium; the two duplicates confirmed at medium; refusal-heard-after-hs confirmed at low.

From the snapshot RTL I re-derived:
- The one register refuses a claim in every state where it is held, except WATCH and the read of a caller candidate's word.
- The origin's register is held in S_YIELD until o_last.
- The caller sits on SILENCE until N_DONE.
The verifier's real-timer logs (snapR, fixR) agree to the tick.

It is a documented rule and a clean cannot-complete, so medium, not high. But it is systematic: about 8-22% of incoming network calls at 16-48 lines at 3 calls/h, roughly 9 refusals per busy hour at a 48-line exchange. The design's traffic model never counted it; I confirmed Net.claim/answered never takes the owner's register.

Things the auditors and verifier missed that make it somewhat worse:
- The off-hook party left behind at every call end gets the register and dial tone. This is documented behaviour but in no model; I estimate it takes ~22% to ~25-27%.
- Redials after a refusal each cost a full flood across the network.
- The model's 0.8 s pause is optimistic for rotary dials.
- A refused claim is invisible to the operator: no event word.
- 'Graceful, nothing held' holds only once C01 is fixed: a claim that waited out WATCH is refused one tick late on a stale r_busy and can latch a stuck CLAIM hold.

The crossing 'both refused' case is ordinary occupancy. In its realistic form, two parties calling each other back after a dropped call, both lines are busy anyway.

Connect-at-the-claim is the right fix: minimal, it removes gates, and it is sound because N_DONE still needs b. It completely fixes the late refusal tone. It also shrinks the crossing double refusal to a window of a few ms: one nit is that 'at most one fails' is not strictly true. It does not fix capacity. It needs doc edits in network.md 4.1, 4.3 and 5, plus the tb_net 11 check. It should be coordinated with C01's att fix and come with a 'claim refused' event word. The capacity figure should be recorded as a limit on the mini marker's size, with a register pool as the real cure.

My notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C15-skeptic-mechanism/NOTES.md.

verifier.root_cause: One root cause for both findings. With /NET low, mini_marker.v:337-345 (S_IDLE) sends every fresh M-and-not-BUSY port to a word read, and :365 (S_READ) sends a port whose word says trunk straight back to S_IDLE without remembering it. The marker has no equivalent of the unit's per-port st bit (net_unit.v:277, 283, 566-570). So an unheld flood trunk is read again every other pass. Each read keeps the marker in S_READ from the edge after T until mid-frame T+8 of the next pass (word_rx.v select and 8-frame collect), which means lines T+1..T+7 are never seen for as long as the trunk stays unheld. The triggers are: a classifier backlog; the T_REL window at the terminating exchange when the called party hangs up first (port.v:147,153: CLAIM keeps backward A up until B's fE falls, then far M stands another T_REL); and, under a fault, a far backward A stuck at 1, which makes it permanent.
verifier.best_fix:
This is finding 2's proposal. Give the marker its own per-port bit tk[p], meaning "its word said flood trunk, and M has stood since". It is set when a caller-candidate read returns rd_trunk and cleared by any probe sample of p with M low; S_IDLE skips ports whose bit is set. That is about 6 lines of RTL (work/verify/C16-marker-reread/rtl_fix/mini_marker.v, fix.patch). On the board it is a 64-stage delay line clocked at the frame edge, like the unit's st: eight '164, or one CD4031 or half a CD4517, plus a gate. A stale bit can only make the marker skip a port whose card is a flood trunk, which the marker never takes through S_IDLE anyway (claimed trunks come in through att), so the change is safe. The bit is set only on the trunk word, not on word 0, so a glitched zero read is still retried.

Finding 1's wording, "the unit's st delay line, shared on the tap", is wrong if taken literally. The unit sets st for LINES too (cls_seen at net_unit.v:283/570), so a line that lifted while the register was busy would be skipped by the marker until it hung up; tb_net scenario 12 is that case.

Doing nothing is also defensible under breadboard-first. The normal cost is at most about 256 ms of extra dial-tone delay on 7 lines. The argument for fixing it is fault containment: see case 4.

Tested at scale 8 on tb_c16 cases 1-4 and at real timers on case 1, then tb_mc +sc=2, then tb_net 88/88.

verifier.summary:
Both findings are real and come from one root cause: the mini marker keeps no per-port memory that a port's word said trunk (mini_marker.v:337-365). The auditors' numbers are overstated.

At real timers I measured a two-exchange bench based on tb_net scenario 2 (tb_c16). When the called party hangs up first, B11 stays BUSY for T_REL and then shows M with BUSY clear for exactly T_REL, 256 ms. During that window B's marker re-reads B11 128 times (the unit reads it 0 times, because st works), and a line at B11+7 waits 256.27 ms for dial tone instead of 2.27 ms. The blind zone is 7 ports, not 8: B11+8 got dial tone in 3.28 ms. The window is 256 ms, not about 0.5 s.

I found no sweep stretch at real timers. The auditor's own real-timer log shows 11 ms sweeps while the marker re-reads, the same as idle sweeps. The word_rx select rule explains why: during a sweep, win is 0 only at the sweep's own select, so the marker waits on the sweep rather than the other way round. At scale 8 the marker's share was 0-2 ms on 13-15 ms sweeps, and the rest of that stretch is the classifier's.

The burst trigger is bounded by the classifier, about 19 ms per queued seizure at real timers.

The "would last for ever" case is reachable with one plausible fault, a stuck-at-1 backward A on a live link or a far port wedged with CLAIM. The near trunk then stays M.!BUSY, and 7 innocent local lines get no dial tone for as long as the fault lasts. I measured that (case 4).

The per-port trunk bit (finding 2's fix) closes every case I tried and keeps tb_net at 88/88. Finding 1's "share the unit's st" would break waiting line callers. Severity is low in normal operation (at most 256 ms of dial-tone delay, re-reading stops whenever the register is busy, no lost or wrong calls), and medium only if the stuck-A fault is counted.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived the mechanism from mini_marker.v:337-365, word_rx.v:103-130 and probe.v:78-92, and it is as stated. The marker leaves S_IDLE on T's fresh sample, which is published at the edge from T to T+1. It selects T one pass later and is done at a_stb of frame T+8, so T+8's fresh sample, published at the next edge, is seen. The blind ports are T+1..T+7, the re-read cycle is 2 passes, and every other port is seen once every 2 ms. The consequences are overstated.

(1) Sweeps: net_unit.v:751-770 runs back-to-back 9-frame reads, so another reader's win==0 only at the sweep's own select frames. The marker therefore waits on the sweep, not the other way round. The auditor's run_real13_all.log shows this: mk=4 from 16907 to 16916 ms inside the 16906-16917 sweep, which lasts 11 ms like an idle one. A sweep can only lose a pass when a marker select lands in a gap: at the sweep's start, or after a classifier read cuts in.

(2) Classification: at most +1 pass per queued seizure, about 1 ms against about 19 ms (C_HOLD T_ARM+1 plus a read). It only adds marginally to C05's lateness.

(3) Window: at real timers each flood arrival is unheld for about 2-3 ms, or about 19 ms per seizure ahead of it in a backlog. Trunks sit in block 1 (11-17; single-channel trunks at 06-07 blind no lines), so only lines 20-26 are ever exposed. Any delay is tens of ms. On its own trigger this is info, not low; low is fine as the cluster's grade because finding 2 shares the root cause.

The verifier is right that the proposed fix as worded ('share the unit's st') is wrong. cls_seen (net_unit.v:360-361, 570) sets st for every M.!BUSY port the classifier reads, lines included, so a line that lifted while the register was busy would be skipped until it hung up (tb_net scenario 12).

The mechanism, the numbers and the window are as the verifier corrected them: 7 blind ports, not 8, and a window of T_REL, not about 0.5 s or 2xT_REL. I checked the window against port.v:147,153. At the terminating exchange B, B11's CLAIM holds backward A until its fE falls, T_REL after the called party hangs up. From then until B11's forward A drops, B11 is M.!BUSY for T_REL+2*link, whatever the number of hops. Transit incoming ports and origin trunks see only about 2*link.

Realism, normal case: about 12 called-first windows per busy hour at a 48-line exchange. On average about 4 exposed lines (of 20-26) per window. The chance of one of them lifting inside 256 ms is about 3e-4, so about 3e-3 affected lifts per busy hour, each delayed 0-256 ms. That is not noticeable to anyone.

Fault case: 'for ever' needs backward A stuck HIGH. That takes a driver fault or a short: an open conductor reads idle through the failsafe receivers (baseband.md 3.3), and a_tx is gated by link_up, so a cut cable is not this. The fault must also arise while the trunk is in a call. If it arises on an idle trunk the classifier holds it as C08's phantom seizure, which is BUSY and never re-read. When it does happen, 0-7 lines lose origination, depending on the trunk's position (11 blinds only 20; 17 blinds 20-26). Calls to those lines still complete (att and S_PROBE are unaffected). A blind line at T+j also escapes with probability j/64 each time the register is released, so it is dead only on a quiet exchange.

The verifier's 'far port wedged with CLAIM' in its reachable form (C01's late refusal) mostly ends as C01's phantom seizure instead. The backward-A dip between B11's release and the late CLAIM write clears st, and A's classifier then holds A11 BUSY. It reaches this loop only if that dip is shorter than a scan pass and is missed.

MISSED SECOND PATH: mini_marker.v:365 also returns word==0 (none/OOS) to S_IDLE unremembered. A plain line card's a12 is a strap to a row-c ground (cvsd_line_card.v:195), with the pull-up at the port (block.v:136, mainboard.v:106). An open a12 therefore reads 00 while the hook works: a bent finger, a cold joint, or a strap forgotten on a hand-built card. extensions.md also says an OOS port's lift is 'ignored'. Such a line off-hook, or with its receiver left off, makes the same endless loop. It blinds up to 7 LINES anywhere in blocks 2-7, and on a bench it shows up as a misleading 'dead neighbours' symptom. It is at least as plausible as a stuck-high A, and the verifier's fix does not close it. Severity stays low: no wrong or lost calls, only failed originations as collateral of a fault; medium only if fault containment is weighted heavily.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
The verifier's per-port tk bit is functionally correct for the trunk path and safe. A stale bit only makes the marker skip a port whose word said trunk, and att bypasses S_IDLE. It is tested on tb_c16 cases 1-4, tb_mc +sc=2 and tb_net (88/88). It is not the complete or cheapest fix:

(1) INCOMPLETE. The set is `if (rd_trunk)` only, so an OOS/word-00 port with M up (a line card whose a12 ground strap is open, left off-hook) still loops for ever. Set the bit on `rd_trunk || rd_word == 8'd0`, the same test S_READ already uses to go to S_IDLE. The objection that a 'glitched zero read is retried' is weak. A zero read from a working line means losing all eight pulled-down frames, and a wrongly set bit costs only that attempt, because it clears when the caller hangs up.

(2) HARDWARE WORDING. The set lands at rd_done, mid-frame T+8, not in T's own turn. A serial delay line (eight '164, or a CD4031 in recirculate mode) cannot be written there. It needs a pending flip-flop applied at T's next turn and ORed into the S_IDLE skip gate. The p_port==called '688 used by S_TAKE/S_PROBE already exists. So it is 'plus a flip-flop and two gates', not 'plus a gate'. The RTL models the bit as random access, unlike the unit's st, whose writes all happen at the head.

(3) PROPORTIONATE ALTERNATIVE for a low-severity defect on 74HC. A one-entry memory: one flip-flop meaning 'the port in `called` was refused (trunk or 00) and its M has stood since'. S_IDLE skips p_port==called while it is set. It clears on a fresh M-low sample of `called`, or when `called` is overwritten. It reuses the existing `called` latch and compare, costs about half a package, and covers every single-port case: the called-first window, a stuck-A fault, and an OOS line off-hook. Two refused ports at once fall back to today's behaviour, which only happens in bounded tens-of-ms backlogs.

(4) Testing: the fix was not re-run on tb_chain, tb_lnet, tb_lfull or tb_lchain; do that before merging.

Doing nothing is defensible for normal operation under breadboard-first. The case for fixing is fault containment and clear diagnosis.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier on both findings (confirmed-overstated, one root cause at mini_marker.v:337-365), re-derived independently from the RTL without running a simulation.

- **Blind zone:** T+1..T+7, with a 2-pass re-read cycle.
- **Window at real timers:** T_REL, 256 ms, and only at the terminating exchange when the called party hangs up first.
- **Unit:** no sweep stretch. During a sweep /HW is always occupied, so the marker waits on the sweep; the auditor's trace shows mk=4 held 9 ms inside an 11 ms sweep. The classifier loses at most one pass.

**Realism.** Trunks sit in block 1, so only lines 20-26 are ever exposed. That gives about 3e-3 affected lifts per busy hour, each delayed 0-256 ms, which no subscriber would notice. Finding 1's burst trigger is info on its own; the cluster's grade is low.

**Fault case.** The 'for ever' case needs backward A stuck high from a driver fault or a short. An open conductor reads idle, and a stuck A that starts on an idle trunk becomes C08's phantom seizure instead, which is never re-read. C01's CLAIM wedge usually also ends as a phantom seizure.

**Missed second path.** mini_marker.v:365 also returns word 00 (OOS) to S_IDLE with nothing remembered. A plain line card whose a12 ground strap is open reads 00 while its hook still works: a bent finger, a cold joint, or a strap left off a hand-built card. With the handset off, or the receiver left off, it loops for ever and blinds up to 7 LINES anywhere in blocks 2-7. The verifier's fix does not cover this, because it sets its bit on the trunk word only.

**Fix.**
- The fix is correct and safe for the trunk path.
- Set the bit on word 00 as well.
- On the board it also needs a pending flip-flop, because the set arrives 8 frames after T's turn.
- A cheaper one-entry memory would be enough: one flip-flop plus the existing `called` latch and its compare.
- Re-run tb_chain, tb_lnet, tb_lfull and tb_lchain on the fix before merging.

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers with conforming equipment, and confirmed there. The port's T_REL is an RC into a '14; the old marker.md s8 models it as +-20 %, and s7 says release >= 204 ms. CLR is an exact '4040 count on the crystal tick. So a port whose RC runs D ms short has a window of D + ~1.75 ms. Measured with the port 19 % short (T_REL 26 against CLR 32): 8 of 12 offsets at 1 ms spacing stuck, a 7.75 ms window. The '8 or 9 in the code' trigger is not reachable: a digit completes only on a make of ID, so the caller is off-hook and the port cannot have released. The guard's nogo also fires mid-break, not after a release.

The mechanism holds step by step.
