- pulse_reg reads M through its 1 ms probe (probe.v publishes at the end of the port's bit-time). pulse_rx.v:93 fires clear CLR ticks after the first changed sample, and gone follows one clk later (pulse_reg.v:244). Measured lag of r_gone behind the port's REL at CLR==T_REL is 1 or 2 ms, not the 0-1 ms the auditor gives: rel +247.999, gone +248.999; rel +246.999, gone +248.999.

The auditor's evidence does not reproduce. run_fix_s6.log (02:07) predates the current rtl_fix/*.v (mtime 02:08:59). It came from a one-sample claim-loss version that the auditor then debounced to 4 samples. My traced rerun of the current copy PASSES. The auditor's own run_fix2.log S6 passes too.

So one conforming event reaches C01's permanent stuck-CLAIM phantom consequence, which C01's own verifier confirmed. That event is a caller who, on a claimed network call, abandons mid-number with the hang-up about 9.74 s after the last digit (window ~3 ms, D+3 ms with RC spread). The consequence: a link channel dead at both ends, a monitor held for good at the neighbour, and at a transit a resolver plus a leg per link. If a short dip is missed (plesiochronous phase: p ~ dip/1 ms), the neighbour instead shows M=1 with BUSY=0 and st=1: the channel is dead, and the mini marker re-reads it every other pass, blind to the 8 ports after it. RATES (rough, stated assumptions: ~50-100 originations per busy hour, 3-5 % abandon at dial tone or mid-number, 1-3 %/s hang-up density near 10 s, ~3300 BH-equivalents a year).

- Trunk form: ~2e-5..1e-4 per exchange-BH, roughly 0.06-0.4 per exchange-year. It is permanent, silent and cumulative, so it will occur in service. That makes the cluster HIGH.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
FIX B, the r_hook gate on mini_marker's two timer-driven BSY writes, is the right fix. It is minimal and suits 74HC: r_hook is the register probe's '74 output already on the card, so the cost is two AND terms and no timer changes.

It is sound under any RC spread. A BSY word can only hurt a port that has already released, which needs T_REL ticks of M low. r_hook=1 means M was high at a probe sample at most ~1 ms ago. Line-card M is filtered to ms widths, and trunk M is a 1 kHz sample-and-hold of the far hook, so some port tick also saw that high and reset cm. The deferral always ends: on-hook leads to gone at CLR and the silence path; a make lets the word land off-hook, which is the designed cannot-complete. Residual hole: a re-lift shorter than T_ARM that lands inside [rel, gone). Hook bounce happens at the start of a hang-up, not ~T_REL later, so this is negligible.

FIX B also covers the far-end claimed-trunk form by construction: it is the same S_COLLECT branch, and r_hook is the trunk's relayed M. I did not run it (one run allowed). Next step: run work/verify/C17-skeptic/tb_c17f.v on RTL_fixB.list; I expect 0/8 stuck.

FIX B is INCOMPLETE for the tree:
(1) rtl/marker.v, the class marker in top_max, has the identical two branches with the same r_gone-only guard (:396-399 S_COLLECT r_nodig, :574-578 S_YIELD). top_max.v builds r_hook on the register card (:143, :179) but leaves it unused (:217). (2) Add the same gate to S_WATCH's r_nodig branch in both markers (mini_marker.v:542-548, marker.v:544-547). It is cheap; the trigger needs ~10 s of chatter.
(3) C01's att_refuse write (mini_marker.v:320-327) reaches the same stuck-CLAIM state from a different site and needs its own fix.

I agree the verifier is right to reject fix A (CLR a few ms under T_REL). Its margin must cover the RC and '14 threshold spread, and it opens a [CLR, T_REL) break class that frees a called port under a still-latched caller. I also agree with rejecting the auditor's bsy=r_hook variant: a guard abandon mid-break becomes dial tone.

findings.real_timing: The stated triggers do not reach the bug at any timer setting. A dropped origin trunk stays BUSY for T_REL (256 ms real) through its fE detector, so a claim from a ring's slower path (0.3-1 ms later, or even 33 ms later) is absorbed. Both of the auditor's triggers are absorbed: a ring skew over 1.5 ms, and a claim just after T_CLAIM. This matches tb_late DLY 10-33 and the hub G1/G2 runs. The only failure is the owner's CLAIM write landing on its own in-port after that port released itself, and before its cell's CLR. m_want is set only on a make (d_stb), so a claim can be that late only when cl_st is held by an earlier att (net_unit.v:671-674) that the marker neither takes nor refuses (mini_marker.v:273-282). With conforming equipment that is only S_WATCH, stretched to hang-up+CLR by a local caller who hangs up within SETTLE of a connect. The NODIG chatter case is a fault.

The auditor and the verifier missed a second path. The dropped copy need not come from a ring: any queued claim for another call works the same way if its far caller hangs up after b+ID. A tree network is enough, and it is just as rare.

The consequence needs refining. On the snapshot's only conforming route, WATCH exits with r_release registered while r_busy is still 1 on the next tick. So att_refuse fires (C01): claim 1, the live copy, is REFUSED (the call is lost, which is C01's harm), and claim 2, on the dead port, is TAKEN. The register then sees no M, and at gone (CLR) it writes the port free (S_COLLECT r_gone). The phantom is therefore transient, about CLR+T_REL. It is permanent, as in the verifier's tb_late, only when claim 1 is taken and claim 2 refused. That happens only with the bench's force on u_att, or after a C01 fix that takes at WATCH exit without a bound.

The window is about 1.3 ms nominal. It opens to about (CLR - T_REL_rc) when the port's RC runs short of the counted CLR, and closes when the RC runs long.

Rate: about 1e-6 to 1e-5 per exchange per busy hour. This takes a long WATCH (about 0.2/h), a claim arriving in a 1.3-25 ms slot, and a second queued claim.

Subscriber: nothing at the time. At worst, after a C01 fix, two trunks are lost for good. Unstrapped, there is also a steady-M phantom flood that holds a monitor and a resolver at each exchange it reaches (C08). Low is right.

I agree with the verifier's mechanism, its broader trigger and its corrected consequence, but not its severity (medium).

Mechanism: rs_mine (net_unit.v:366) sees only busy resolvers. w_res (:691-706) frees the resolver after patching the in-port to the leg carrying M; with one leg, the patch at :732-736 already did this at forward time. The owner's later w_claim (:656-668) writes in-port<-00+CLAIM. E falls, fE falls T_REL later, rel clears CLAIM, and the path unwinds. This is reproduced in run_pchain_snap.log: 2130.203 R_LEG on glare, 2389.999 claim, 2390.284 B11->0 clm1, 2422.999 self-release.

Trigger: broader than the auditor stated, and no false claim is needed. Glare anywhere in the owner's forward subtree is enough, because the glare M climbs through each transit's R_LEG and one-leg patch up to the owner's leg (C13 mechanism skeptic).

The auditor's 'two exchanges ring, one hears the caller' cannot happen. At real timers the in-port unwinds at about b+386 ms and the origin trunk at about b+642 ms, before h (b+720 ms at the earliest). Even with RC T_REL at +20% (about b+744 ms), no digit of h can complete: that needs make+ID, at b+908 ms or later.

This is the same event as C13 forward-glare-collapse (ii); count it once. Using the C13 realism arithmetic, glare is about 8e-5 per exchange per busy hour at design load, and about 0.1-0.15 of that has the owner upstream. That gives about 1e-6 per network call, and roughly 1 per 20-30 busy hours network-wide at twice the design load.

Subscriber: two callers get dead air after dialling, and both are left latched to released trunks. If a trunk is reused before they hang up, there is a latent one-way listen-in (C11), in under 1% of events. No wrong party is rung.

A rare failed call with a small privacy tail is low, not medium. The C13 realism skeptic also rated this same event low.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
F1. The verifier's M-gate (m_want[mk] && mp_m[mk] at net_unit.v:336) is correct and costs one AND per cell. Against back-to-back queued claims it is the most robust of the three options, because a copy whose forward M has fallen can never claim again. Its CLAIM therefore cannot land late, and neither can the marker's refusal of it. d_lbrk is not a substitute: combined with C01's CLR/2 = 128 ms WATCH bound, the second claim goes out about 128.5 ms after the drop. That is about 1.5 ms before d_lbrk (ID = 128) frees its cell. Its att can then wait up to another 128 ms, and the refusal (NOGO+CLAIM) lands about T_REL after the drop, on a released port: the same no-edge write, made by the marker.

The M-gate alone is also incomplete. It leaves the dropped copy's m_want standing until the counted CLR. If the port's RC T_REL runs below about 245 ms, the far end can free the same trunk and seize it again for a new call before that CLR. The gate then opens on the NEW seizure, and the stale cell claims it at seizure time. The new origin takes that as glare inside the guard, which counts as a claim. The owner's register then reads the new caller's e b as h s: a wrong number. This is argued, not run. It is extremely rare, since it also needs the long-WATCH coincidence, and the snapshot has it too (C03 stale-cell family). Adding the monclaim d_lbrk closes it: free a cell on a break of ID, one tap of the existing '4040. Dropping a wanting cell at its first break would also work.

The root is C01's unbounded wait in WATCH (mini_marker.v:282). It is the only conforming source of a claim lag near T_REL, and on the snapshot it also decides that the route is transient rather than permanent. The recommended set is:
- the M-gate;
- d_lbrk;
- C01's bounded wait, together with its rule that the marker refuses only while the claimed port's M is up.
As the verifier says, the auditor's origin-side mask is wrong: it leaves the owner's port holding CLAIM for good.

F2. The cell-free at w_res is safe for genuine claims: a non-owner transit's cell has already mismatched on e or b before any genuine downstream claim can arrive. It also closes the route where R_GONE leaves a stale cell, and it keeps tb_net at 88/88. At the owner, though, it hands the call to whatever raised the leg's M:
- glare gives strangers joined (the verifier's run_pchain_fix shows this);
- a false downstream claim, arriving while the owner's claim is held in WATCH, keeps h s at the false claimer. That is a wrong number which the snapshot's collapse happened to prevent.

So it must ship with C13's fix: the resolver ignores leg M younger than the guard (glare: count it and drop that leg), and the one-leg way back is deferred to R_LEG. With that fix in place, the owner's claim meets a still-busy resolver, and rs_mine drops every leg cleanly.

Hardware: instead of NMON new 6-bit comparators, the cells' existing probe '688s can do the match. At rs_in's scan turn, free the cells whose probe fires, using the resolver's existing rs_in==sp_port compare and a one-pass flag.
skeptics.summary:
F1 (late claim on a dropped origin trunk): I agree with the verifier on confirmed-overstated and low. The fE term in port.v:147 absorbs both of the auditor's triggers. The real failure needs the owner's CLAIM to land on its own in-port after that port released itself and before its cell's CLR. That needs a claim lag near T_REL, which with conforming equipment comes only from C01's unbounded wait in S_WATCH. The verifier also missed a second path: a queued claim for an unrelated call whose caller hangs up after b gives the same result, so a tree network is enough.

On the snapshot, the consequence along the conforming route is transient rather than permanent. C01's refusal at WATCH exit refuses the live claim 1 and takes the dead claim 2, and the register frees the dead port at gone. It becomes permanent only with the bench's force on u_att, or after a C01 fix that takes at exit without a bound. Rate: about 1e-6 to 1e-5 per exchange per busy hour.

On the fix, the M-gate is right, and it is better than d_lbrk against back-to-back claims under C01's 128 ms bound. It is not complete on its own: a stale want that meets a trunk seized again under RC-short T_REL can claim a new call, a rare wrong number. So d_lbrk and C01's bound should go with it.

F2 (late claim after resolve): I confirm the mechanism, the glare-driven broader trigger (anywhere in the owner's forward subtree) and the collapse outcome. The cell-free-at-w_res fix is sound, but it needs C13's leg-age gate and the deferred one-leg way back. Without them it turns glare into strangers joined, and a false claim held behind a WATCH into a wrong number.

No simulation was run. My notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C18-skeptic-mechanism/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: Needs a misconfiguration: a ring left without its STRAP_N jumper, which network.md §7 forbids ('the links without the strap must form a tree'). Forgetting the jumper at commissioning is plausible. Once the ring is unstrapped, the circulation and double claims happen on EVERY call at real timers. They are worse there than at scale 8, because the ~19 ms T_ARM watch spaces classifications past the ~11 ms forward, so there is no BUSY-FWDR stop (tb_ring4r: every copy forwarded). The late-copy wrong number is NOT reachable in a ring of about 8 with conforming dials. Each exchange forwards at most NRES=2 copies, and the clockwise and anticlockwise first-lap copies use both, so a copy dies about one hop into its second lap. The oldest copy is therefore about (N+1) hops x ~13 ms (+~2x19 ms serialisation) old. A 10 pps dial with 720 ms pauses breaks e >= ~580 ms after the seizure, so a late copy needs N >~ 40. The auditor's 'about 8' holds only for a caller breaking at the 128 ms guard edge (pauses ~270 ms, non-conforming).

findings.notes: Understated on two counts: it also doubles every incoming network call at the strapped end, and the cannot-complete race is demonstrated rather than only plausible, at real timers too. verifier.root_cause: One root cause behind both findings. A pulse flood carries no identity and no hop count, only C and A. So nothing can recognise a returning or duplicated flood, and loop and duplicate suppression rests entirely on the per-direction STRAP_N jumper being fitted at both ends of one link per cycle: net_unit.v:505 (fwd_mask), :616-618 (the forward gate). The origin seizes every direction regardless of the strap (net_unit.v:849, h_mask 4'b1111). Duplicates that do arrive are settled by two independent first-come races: the owner gives the register to the first cell to claim (net_unit.v:656, m_want1; mini_marker att) and the origin keeps the first M it samples (net_unit.v:794-804). Both are quantised by the 1 ms scan and the fabric. A missing strap (F1) or a strap at one end only (F2) turns this into circulation and double claims, and sometimes into a cannot-complete.
verifier.best_fix: A documentation fix plus a commissioning check. No RTL change: a flood with no identity cannot be made loop-safe in-band. Cost: zero parts. (1) Rewrite exchange/network.md §7's 'Strap both ends' reason to say what one end costs. The unstrapped end forwards the strapped end's own calls round the ring and forwards every call for the strapped end into the strapped link. So the strapped end's calls reach every exchange twice, every call to it arrives there twice, each is a double claim, and when the refused copy's claim reaches the origin first the call fails cannot-complete (never a wrong number). Also keep 'must form a tree' as a hard rule for F1. (2) Commissioning: one test call from and one to each end of every strapped link, and one call round each ring. Each call must give exactly one claim at the owner: no att_ack REFUSED after a TAKEN on the same call, and no seizure at the origin of its own flood. Rejected alternatives: (a) the auditor's strap-mismatch bit in the trunk word, which costs a word bit and still needs two jumpers; (b) stopping the origin seizing strapped directions, which fixes only X's own calls, not calls to X, and makes calls between the ends go the long way; (c) the auditor's 'refuse to forward late seizures of the same caller', which a transit cannot know. Tested: the documented both-ends configuration was run as the control and behaves (see fix_tested).
verifier.fix_tested: Doc fix, so no fixed RTL copy; the documented configuration (both ends strapped) was run as the control. tb_ring4 +define+BOTH, X->Y between the ends: 12/12 phase sets completed, the direct copy took the register and the origin kept it (run_r4both_b3_p1..p12.log). Hub obj_ringst with the same 8 directed calls: 8/8 OK with one claim per call, INVARIANT 50/50 (run_r2_bothstrap.log). Against that, one end only: tb_ring4 1 of 6 cannot-complete at s8 and the same phase set failing at real timers (run_r4one_b4_p5.log, run_r4real_b4_p5.log), and in the hub 14 claims for 8 calls (run_r1_onestrap.log).
verifier.summary:
Both findings are real, and both come from the same thing: STRAP_N is the only thing that breaks a loop, because a pulse flood carries no identity or hop count.

F1 (unstrapped ring) is confirmed but overstated. The circulation, the resource exhaustion and a double claim on every call were already reproduced on the snapshot by the hub load study (G1/G3). At real timers copies are forwarded even more freely. But copies die about one hop into their second lap, since NRES=2 is used up by the two first-lap copies. With conforming dials (first break of e at least ~580 ms after the seizure), the 'late copy, wrong number' needs about 40 or more exchanges in one unstrapped ring, not about 8. It is a configuration the document forbids.

F2 (jumper at one end only) is confirmed and understated. On a new 4-ring bench and on the hub bench with a one-end strap, the strapped end's calls reached every member twice and were double-claimed. Calls TO the strapped end were also double-claimed, which the finding missed. The 'refused copy wins, cannot-complete' outcome happened in 1 of 6 phase sets, at scale 8 and again at real timers with conforming dialling; it is never a wrong number. The documented both-ends configuration passed 12/12 and 8/8 with one claim per call.

The fix is to the document plus a commissioning check. §7 should say why one end is not enough (double delivery both ways, intermittent cannot-complete), and each strapped link should get one test call from and to each end. No RTL change is worth making.

Files are under /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C19-rings/: NOTES.md, tb_ring4.v, tb_ring4r.v, tb_hub1.sv, and the job*.sh scripts with their run_*.log files.

per_finding.reason:
I re-derived this from the snapshot, and the cited lines check out. A pulse flood carries only C and A, so there is no hop count and no origin identity. STRAP_N is the only loop breaker (net_unit.v:505, :616-618). A returning copy comes in on a port that is not `mine` and has its st bit clear, so it is classified as a fresh seizure (:283). The origin sweeps with h_mask 1111 (:849).

The late-copy wrong number is weaker than even the verifier says. With NMON=2, each ring member's two cells are taken by the clockwise and anticlockwise first-lap copies. They stay held until e ends, at least ~580 ms after the seizure. The second-lap copies that die one hop past the origin therefore find no free cell and go unwatched (:611-615). The oldest copy that is monitored is N-1 hops old at a ring member and N+1 hops old at a spoke of the origin. That is 0 to 2 hops more than the same exchanges would see strapped as a chain. At the origin itself, a miscounted returning copy can only match the origin's own code, and that register is busy, so the claim is refused. So the late-copy exposure is C05's guard reach, not a ring effect. At conforming 720 ms pauses it needs about 20 hops (slow 22-30 ms hops) to about 40 (typical 13 ms hops), never a ring of about 8.

What is real: every call is double-claimed, the equal-path race sometimes gives cannot-complete, and under load the extra copies use up the exchanges' resources. In hub G3 the unstrapped ring carried 0.11 E against 0.47 E strapped in G4. At light load the fault is quiet (G1: 5 of 5 OK), so a forgotten jumper can last until the busy hour. It is a configuration the document forbids ('must form a tree'). Low is right.

I traced a ring with L=X-Y strapped at X only. Every call from X reaches every member twice, because Y forwards X's L copy. Every call to X arrives at X twice, because Y forwards into L and X holds and claims on its strapped port. Calls from Y look exactly as they do with both ends strapped. X is the only origin whose own flood comes back. This matches the verifier's logs: tb_ring4 one-end 6/6 double claims, and the p5 failure at s8 and again at real timers (Z TAKEN on 11, REFUSED on 14, X keeps 74).

Three additions:
(1) The odds depend on geometry. The claims are ~0.4 ms apart, and each backward path adds about two uniform 0-1 ms quantisations: the transit fabric crossing and the origin's slot sample. So equidistant pairs fail roughly 10-25% of the time, which fits the verifier's 1 in 6. Pairs one hop apart in length fail a few percent, and pairs two or more hops apart almost never; hub 0/8 and the both-ends 12/12 are of that kind.
(2) Failures come in bursts. The outcome is set by the sites' scan phases, which drift only 1 ms every 25-250 s at 40-4 ppm offset, so an immediate redial often fails again.
(3) There is collateral damage the verifier missed. Each call from X fills both of every member's two cells until e ends, about 1 s. A flood for that member arriving in that window goes unwatched, so an unrelated caller gets cannot-complete.

I found no path to a wrong number. The dropped copy stays BUSY for T_REL through fE (port.v:148), so a late second claim is seen under BUSY and sets st. If claim 1 waits out S_WATCH (the C02 case), the origin still keeps copy 1, because its CLAIM M goes out before att. The outcome is cannot-complete. It needs a misconfiguration, which could also arise from a unit-card swap that loses the jumper. The failure is clean and a retry can succeed, so low is right.

skeptics.summary:
I agree with both of the verifier's verdicts and severities. There is one correction to the recommended fix.

F1, unstrapped ring: confirmed-overstated, low. The circulation, the double claim on every call and the collapse under load (hub G3 0.11 E against G4 0.47 E) are real. At light load the fault is quiet (G1: 5 of 5 OK), so it can go unnoticed. The late-copy wrong number is not a ring effect at all. With NMON=2 the second-lap copies find both cells held by the first-lap copies and go unwatched. The oldest monitored copy is therefore only 0 to 2 hops older than it would be in the same exchanges strapped as a chain. That makes it C05's guard reach, which needs about 20-40 hops at conforming dial pauses.

F2, jumper at one end only: confirmed-understated, low. I re-derived that calls from the strapped end X, and calls to X, are delivered twice and double-claimed. The verifier reproduced the refused-copy-wins cannot-complete at real timers.

Additions from this review:
- The failure rate depends on geometry: roughly 10-25% for owners at equal distance both ways round, near 0 when the two paths differ by two hops or more.
- Failures come in bursts, because the site scan phases drift slowly, so an immediate redial often fails too.
- Each X call fills both monitor cells at every member for about a second, so unrelated calls are lost as collateral.
- I found no wrong-number path. The dropped trunk stays BUSY for T_REL through fE, and in the C02 queue case the origin keeps the first CLAIM.

The fix is right as a document change plus a commissioning check, but the verifier's pass criterion ('exactly one claim at the owner') fails the documented both-ends design for calls between the two strapped ends; its own jobC_both logs show two claims in all 12 runs. The test must use calls to and from a third exchange at each end, and check that the origin never sees its own flood come back. It should be repeated after a unit card is replaced, since the jumper sits on that card. An optional double-claim event word would catch the fault in service. I ran no simulation.

Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C19-rings-skeptic/NOTES.md.

findings.real_timing: Not reachable at any timing. The overwrite at net_unit.v:659-663 is real code, but it needs two busy resolvers with the same rs_in. For that, port P must be classified again while the old resolver is still busy. cls_seen requires !sp_busy at P's visit (283-284), and that same visit sets R_GONE on the old resolver (688-689); if it is not R_NONE it is already acting. A second resolver on P only appears at F_WRITE, after a full 64-read sweep plus a confirm pass (~10 ms, 750-785, no early exit). w_res waits only behind one-shot pushers and room>=4, and the queue drains about 7 words/ms, so it cannot be held off for 10 ms. The marker cannot make P busy unseen either: both probes sample the same bit-time.

The auditor's worry about the jumper that free-runs SCLK off HCLK/4 is moot: HCLK/4 is 128 kHz, the same as SCLK, so the word time does not change.
findings.ran: tb_wait (work/verify/C20-misc/tb_wait.v): both ctl_queues as top_net fits them, plus net_unit.v:219-232 copied verbatim with WAIT as a run-time number. Marker word at tick 0, unit word at -4..600. WAIT = 640, 549, 548, 547, 546, 500. Log: work/verify/C20-misc/run_wait.log (10 s walltime).
findings.evidence: The marker's '244 is on for 547 ticks. At WAIT=640 the smallest gap is 94 ticks (auditor: 93), with no clash at any offset. It stays clash-free down to WAIT=546 (gap 0) and clashes at WAIT=500 (overlap 46 ticks). The worst offset is +2: the unit's push lands on the edge after the marker sampled /UREQ high. The residual point is real: ctl_write.v:80 hard-codes 16 bits, and net_unit's WAIT is missing from exch.vh's five-site 'WIDENS WITH `PW' list. At PW=9 a word is 23 bit-times, 739 ticks, which is more than 640. tb_net counts b_clash every tick (tb_net.v:157-160), but a small shortfall only lights when a unit push falls in the first (word - WAIT) ticks of a marker word, so tb_net 17's five tries could miss it.
findings.notes: Fix, no hardware cost: compute WAIT as a localparam from `CWW (for example (`CWW+1)*32 + 3 + margin), or add net_unit.v WAIT to exch.vh's WIDENS WITH `PW list. Not tested; it is a constant.

findings.real_timing: Only an assembly or jumper error can trigger it: a card at 00, or a port card with POS=0 on block 0. The spec already forbids it and says why: numbering.md:30 ('00 idle, never fitted') and :36-37 (every idle phone would ring). The auditor's local-trunk trigger is wrong: exchange-docs/local-trunk.md:213 ('Block 0 is never this group') and live numbering.md:43-44 forbid group trunks on block 0. In site_net, LTU[0] would also collide with the tone sources at 01 and 03 (site_net.v:95-99, 132-133).
findings.ran: tb_c20z (work/verify/C20-misc/tb_c20z.v), real timers. Exchanges A and X, baseband tie A11-X11, bench on A12. A phone is fitted at X00 and off-hook, and A20 dials 1 3 4 2 1. Log: work/verify/C20-misc/run_z.log.
findings.evidence: X21, idle with no call anywhere, was marked being-rung 50 ms out of 50. All of X's lines 20-27 read BUSY: every cleared latch listens to 00, so E=1 and fE holds BUSY (port.v:147). Idle X11 also listens to 00 and sends 00's M forward: A11 went BUSY at 590 ms, before A20 had keyed, as a phantom seizure that A holds and, going by h_ok=0, forwards. A20's flood then found no free trunk (origin states 2->8->0 at 730) and got cannot-complete. X's unit never claimed and X's register was never attached: no wrong number. The effect is a loud total outage of that exchange plus phantom seizures at its neighbours, not 'wrong numbers everywhere'. It would be seen at once in commissioning. The bench check 'no X line seized by the call' is badly worded on my part: those busy lines come from the fault's fE, not from the call.
findings.notes: Cheap guard: a $fatal in site_net or exch.v when PORT_FITTED[0] is set, or mask it. On the board the documented rule is enough; enforcing it in hardware would need a block-0-specific header.

findings.real_timing: Reachable at real timers with conforming parts and a conforming dial, on today's baseband and local trunks, not only on future carriers. The two ends' releases come from two different RC-and-'14 detectors in two exchanges (exchange/fabric.md:254-255; fabric.md §8 lists 'the detectors as RCs ... nothing has checked them' as Open). RTL counters are exact, but on the board a few percent of 256 ms outweighs the path margin. That margin depends on where the trunk sits in the stride-9 sweep: about 11-15 ms at A11 (step 8) and about 2 ms at the worst ports (steps 57-63: ports 02, 13, 24, 35, 46, 57, 70). The auditor's 0.13-0.29 ms leaves out the port's own bit-time wait and the E capture. MF8's 0.5 ms fall-late asymmetry fits inside the margin, contrary to the auditor. A pots tie's 5-10 ms break shortening (network.md:51) does not fit at late-sweep ports. The mirror case is lost too: if the far end frees first and seizes again, the near port shows M under BUSY, the st bit is set, and the seizure is never classified. It takes a hunt landing in the skew window right after a trunk frees. The lowest-first hunt tends to pick the trunk that just freed, and every call floods every link, so it happens under ordinary traffic.
findings.ran: tb_c20r (work/verify/C20-misc/tb_c20r.v, derived from C03's tb_c03r), real timers, snapshot RTL. A abandons a seizure of TA inside its guard, then Y's flood on A13 is forwarded onto TA as soon as TA frees. Runs: n11 full, TRELA 256 control (run_n11_full.log); s240 full, A's RC 6% short (run_s240_full.log); n70 scan with TA at port 070, the last port in the sweep, rs 244-252 (run_n70_scan.log); n70 scan with a 0.5 ms fall delay (run_n70_fd500.log); n11 scan (run_n11_scan.log, only rs=258 valid) and n11d debug (run_n11d_scan.log). All under work/verify/C20-misc/.
findings.evidence: Control, 256/256: TA and X11 free in the same ms (936), TA is seized again 13 ms later, X holds X11 as a fresh seizure, claims, and X22 rings (PASS 7/7). RC 6% short (TRELA 240): TA frees at +241 and is seized again at +254 while X11 is still held (busy=1). X never holds it fresh again, never claims, never attaches its register, and X22 is not rung (3 FAILs): the flood dialled to X is lost. X11 frees only 256 ms after that flood ends. Worst placement at exact counters: 2.285 ms from free to the new write, 3.89 ms margin at X with X's tick 0.68 ms ahead (the bench phase); an adverse phase takes about 1.7 ms off. With the 0.5 ms fall delay the margin is 3.06 ms: safe. C03's verifier got the same port-level loss with TRELA=200 on the monclaim fix (C03 run_r_fix200.log). Correction to my own scan: rs 254-257 in run_n11_scan.log are my bench artefact (the wait loop saw the old BUSY and dropped Y's M inside T_ARM, which triggered C_UNHOLD). I fixed the loop before the n70 runs.
findings.notes: The auditor's fix, a document line saying 'A fall and rise delays must match within 0.1 ms, or skip a port ~2 ms after it frees', does not close the hole: the RC tolerance alone is several ms. Seen by reading, not simulated, with the same root: the origin's N_DROP after the register's CLR, and a resolver's R_GONE drops, can write away a port that released early on a fast RC and has already been seized again. The sweep does not exclude d_held or rs_held ports (net_unit.v:759).

verifier.root_cause: There are three separate hygiene items and one real race. (1) net_unit.v:659-663 maps every rs_mine resolver onto the same slots, but two resolvers can never share rs_in. (2) net_unit.v:104's WAIT=640 is typed by hand rather than derived from `CWW and DIV (ctl_write.v:80 hard-codes 16 bits), and it is not in exch.vh's WIDENS WITH `PW list. (3) 'Port 00 never fitted' is a documented rule that nothing enforces. (4) The real defect: the two ends of a trunk release on two independent RC detectors, the near port's fE and the far port's fM (port.v:147, 176-193; fabric.md §5.2), and there is no release handshake. A hunt (net_unit.v:750-785) can seize a trunk again from whichever end frees first while the other end still holds the old seizure. The far port then stays BUSY with st set and is never classified (net_unit.v:283-284, 566-570). The RTL's exact counters hide this. It shares a root with C03's rc-tolerance-reseize.
verifier.best_fix: F1: none; at most a free bench assertion. F2: compute WAIT from `CWW, for example localparam WAIT = (`CWW+1)*32 + 3 + margin, or list net_unit WAIT among exch.vh's WIDENS WITH `PW sites. No hardware cost; the live spec's figure is already right. F3: a lint check or $fatal on PORT_FITTED[0] in site_net or exch.v, costing nothing; the board rule is already in numbering.md. F4 needs a design decision, not a document line. The complete, symmetric option is a hunt hold-off. The unit keeps two more bits per port on the st delay line ('BUSY seen this epoch' and 'last epoch', epoch G of about 64 ms, which must exceed the worst RC skew). The sweep then takes a port only if both bits are clear, so neither end can seize a trunk again until G to 2G after it freed. Cost: about two more chains of eight '164s plus gates, and a just-freed trunk rests 64-128 ms. It turns a stuck far-end hold into 'try the next trunk', but a direction with a single trunk still loses a flood arriving inside G. Other options: a tight detector tolerance (a comparator with a reference in place of the '14, about ±1%) covers only early-sweep ports. A far-end 'long break writes the hold away' rule (break of 128 ms or more, longer than any dial break) needs per-port timing that monitor cells give only while they are held. This should be designed together with C03's fixes, which C03's verifier found conflict with C04's. Not tested: the hold-off only shows its benefit with two trunks per direction, and tb_c20r has one.
verifier.fix_tested: Not tested: no finding came with an RTL fix. F1, F2 and F3 need a constant or a lint check. F4's options are design choices, listed in best_fix.
verifier.summary: The cluster holds four unrelated findings; only F4 matters. F1 (claim slot collision): not-a-bug. Two busy resolvers can never share rs_in, because the visit that lets a port be classified again also sets R_GONE, and a new resolver needs a 10 ms sweep. F2 (WAIT): confirmed-overstated, info. Measured: the marker's word is 547 ticks, the margin is 94 ticks (auditor: 93), it stays clash-free down to WAIT=546 and clashes at 500. The live bus.md already says 640 and lists it as Open, and the HCLK/4 jumper is the same 128 kHz. The real residual is that WAIT is not tied to `CWW (at PW=9 a word is 739 ticks). F3 (port 00): confirmed-overstated, low. The rule is in numbering.md, and the auditor's local-trunk trigger is itself forbidden (local-trunk.md:213). Simulated with a phone at X00 off-hook: every idle line rings and reads BUSY, every idle trunk sends a phantom seizure to its neighbour, and the caller gets cannot-complete. That is a loud outage, not wrong numbers. F4 (release margin): confirmed-understated, medium. The detectors are RCs, so the release skew between the two ends is their tolerance, not ±1 tick. At real timers with A's RC 6% short, a flood dialled to X was lost: X11 was still held when seized again, so there was no claim and X22 did not ring (run_s240_full.log). The 256/256 control passes. At exact counters the margin is 2-15 ms depending on sweep position, not 0.13-0.29 ms, and MF8's 0.5 ms asymmetry is safe while a pots tie's 5-10 ms is not. The auditor's document-only fix is insufficient; it shares a root with C03's rc-tolerance-reseize. One of my own scans (n11, rs 254-257) was a bench artefact; I found it, fixed it, and ran the n70 scans on the fixed bench. Notes, benches and logs are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C20-misc/ (NOTES.md, tb_c20r.v, tb_c20z.v, tb_wait.v, run_*.log). All obj dirs are removed.

skeptics.lens: MECHANISM + REALISM AND SEVERITY (skeptic review, read-only on the snapshot; no simulation run)

per_finding.reason: The code does overwrite: net_unit.v:659-663 maps every rs_mine resolver onto slots j2+1. The verifier's main argument holds. The resolver watch (681-690) and cls_seen (283-284) read the same sp_fresh/sp_busy sample of P, so R_GONE is set at or before the visit that classifies P again. A second resolver then needs a whole hunt, about 10 ms, and w_res frees the old resolver long before that. 'Not reachable at any timing' is too strong, though. There is a second path, through C09. When C_UNHOLD lands while fst==F_WRITE, F_WRITE ignores f_cancel (725). Because w_cls outranks w_fwd, R1 (rs_in=P) is created one tick after P was unheld. If w_fwd is held off for 1 ms or more (queue room below cnt_fwd, so 13 or more of 16 entries full), P's next visit can see P free and seized again before R1 exists. The new hold then keeps P BUSY at every later visit, R1 never gets R_GONE, and R2 for P follows. That takes a sub-ms coincidence, plus a multi-leg forward (C09 says a one-leg forward re-holds P BUSY for good, so P cannot be classified again), plus the far end seizing again within about 2 ms of abandoning. It is not reachable in practice, and C09's fix (honour f_cancel in F_WRITE) closes it. If it were reached, the effect would be worse than the auditor says. The stale R1 keeps legs up that carry the new caller's M, and a far M on an R1 leg would make R1 go R_LEG and write P onto that leg under R2's connection.

Derived again from ctl_queue.v:169-181 and ctl_write.v:69-113. The marker's s_req is at edge 0, ctl_write is busy over edges 1-546, and t returns to IDLE at 547. The unit's want_bus follows its push edge, it is granted at +640 and its oe is on at +641, which leaves a 94-tick gap (verifier: 94; auditor: 93). HCLK is the 512 kHz cell clock, so HCLK/4 is 128 kHz, the same rate as SCLK. A free-running SCLK adds at most one bit-time (32 ticks) of phase alignment, which still fits inside 94. The live bus.md:183-185 already gives 640 ticks and lists the wait as Open (:268). 1152 survives only in the retired exchange-docs/mini-marker.md:313 and decisions.md:285. The verifier's PW=9 residual is weaker than stated. At PW=9, ctl_write.v:80 still loads n=16, and ctl_queue's 15-bit entry has fixed fields (head[11:6], head[5:0]). exch.vh:7-11 says the fold and the 6-bit address are one decision. So WAIT would not be the first thing to break. It is still worth deriving it from `CWW/DIV.

The label and severity are right, and the auditor's 'wrong numbers everywhere' is overstated (run_z.log). The verifier states the scope too narrowly in three ways. (1) The transient. When 00 goes off-hook, every trunk X is holding (latch 00) gets E=1 and sends backward A (a_rx = e for a trunk, port.v:153; /ANS is tied low, so ON=0). The origin's claim watch (net_unit.v:795-804), or an upstream resolver's R_LEG (682-687), takes that as the claim and drops the other directions. At o_last it patches the caller to the trunk, and the caller hears 00's lane one-way. That is a silent misconnect, about one per incident. (2) The steady state is not just X out plus phantoms at the neighbours. The neighbours hold the phantom seizures, give each a monitor cell that is never freed (steady M: no digit and no 256 ms break), and forward them. Phantom floods therefore spread and use up monitors and resolvers at every exchange they reach, and incoming calls fail across the network while 00 stays off-hook. It clears when that phone hangs up and the network unwinds. (3) The trigger is wider than 'a card fitted at 00'. A shunt on JP1 POS reads 0 and open reads 1 (block-stack.md:332). A port card moved from slot 0 of another block into any block-0 socket keeps POS=0 and drives bit-time 00. That is an ordinary maintenance slip, not only an assembly error. It stays low because it is loud at X (every idle phone rings), self-announcing, and clears on hang-up. On the board, a debugger lamp for 'anything pulled /HA or /HB in bit-time 00' costs almost nothing. Masking the E capture at 00 would be wrong: e_cap would freeze, and a port cleared by fM with E still 1 would ring for ever.

The mechanism and sims hold (read: run_n11_full.log control PASS; run_s240_full.log shows X11 still held when A re-seizes TA, then no claim, no register and X22 not rung; run_n70_scan.log). The detectors are RC-and-'14 (fabric.md 5.2), and §8 lists them as unchecked. Additions: (a) The spread is far larger than the 6% simulated. The 74HC14's VT- spread alone (roughly 0.9-2.0 V at 4.5 V, quoted from memory) gives about 0.68x to 1.39x on an RC fall time, before capacitor tolerance. Two ports' T_REL can differ by up to about 180 ms, and typically by tens of ms, so the 2-15 ms margin at any sweep placement is small beside it. (b) There is an asymmetry nobody stated. The end that is still counting sticks only if its BUSY term does not cancel when M returns: the unit's hold latch (bsy) or fE. The fm&!m term cancels itself. On a dropped flood branch the far end is on the latch and the near end on fE, so both orders stick. At the end of a claimed call, exactly one order sticks. Every trunk release is therefore exposed, not only abandons. (c) Rate, for a tree of 10 exchanges carrying 500 floods/BH with sigma(T_REL) about 8%: roughly 1.7e-3 per release, about 7 events/BH across the network, about 0.7 per exchange-BH. About half cost the call, as a clean cannot-complete after T_CLAIM. The rate scales roughly as lambda squared, so it is rare at hobby load. For the lost branch itself, medium is right. It is also the race that enables C03 rc-tolerance-reseize (a wrong number, rated high), so the root fix is urgent. (d) The verifier saw a second path with the same root by reading; I think it is worse than F4 itself (reading only, not simulated). A resolver's leg L self-releases on its own fE before P frees on its fM, and this exchange's own sweep (759 ignores rs_held/d_held) takes L for the next flood. R_GONE then writes L to 00. This fires on the normal unwind of every unclaimed branch. The new holder keeps L in rs_held/d_held, and `mine` hides L from the classifier. A later far seizure of that channel shows M on L and is taken as the claim, so the new caller is patched one-way to a stranger's flood. That is a candidate separate finding, possibly high, and needs a bench. N_DROP after an abandon (r_gone at a digital 256 ms against the trunk's fE RC) has the same shape.

skeptics.fix_assessment:
F1: no fix needed. C09's fix (F_WRITE honours f_cancel and gates w_fwd with !f_cancel, one gate) removes the only path I found. If a model gate is wanted, the verifier is right that 'one rs_mine per tick' is not a fix. A correct one sets any extra rs_mine resolver to R_GONE instead of freeing it, so w_res drops its legs next; or add a bench assertion that no two busy resolvers share rs_in.
F2: derive WAIT from `CWW and DIV, and add it to exch.vh's WIDENS WITH `PW list, alongside ctl_write.v:80 (n=16) and ctl_queue's 15-bit entry, which are also PW=6-only. No hardware cost.
F3: keep the numbering rule and add the model lint/$fatal as the verifier says. On the board, the realistic trigger is a moved card still jumpered POS=0, which the rule does not prevent. A debugger lamp for any /HA or /HB pull in bit-time 00 is almost free and makes the fault announce itself. Do not mask the E capture at 00.
F4: the auditor's document line does not close the hole (agree with the verifier). A hunt hold-off is the right class of fix, but the verifier's 'G of about 64 ms' contradicts its own condition that G must exceed the worst RC skew. With 74HC14 threshold spread, G needs to be at least about 200 ms from the near port's free (a just-freed trunk rests 200-400 ms), and at least 256 minus T_REL_min so that C03's stale-cell re-seizure is closed as well. The verifier's version (two more 64-bit delay lines, about 16 '164s) works at that size.
A cheaper and more general option is at the card. A trunk card presents NONE on its word until both A directions have been low for G, with G above T_REL_max: about 400 ms from a counter, or about 600 ms nominal from an RC, reusing the card's existing power-up hold-off with a discharge whenever either A is high. It must never gate A itself. It covers the main race, the mirror race, the write-away family and carrier asymmetry such as the pots tie's 5-10 ms. The cost is about one gate package on a baseband card and per channel on MF8 and the local trunk, and it must be written into network.md §2's carrier contract.
Either way, add a one-gate digital complement: at H_CONFIRM (net_unit.v:779-782), drop a candidate when `mine` is true at its turn. That closes the R_GONE/N_DROP write-away family whatever the RCs do, and also stops the origin and a pending forward from taking the same free port.
C03's fixes (a) and (b) are still needed alongside, and all of this should be designed together with C03 and C04. None of these fixes was simulated.
skeptics.summary:
I agree with the verifier's verdicts and severities on all four findings. On mechanism and realism I have these corrections.
F1 (not-a-bug, info): the proof that nothing reaches it has a gap through C09 (F_WRITE ignores f_cancel). It is unreachable in practice and C09's fix closes it.
F2 (confirmed-overstated, info): I derived the 94-tick gap again. The PW=9 worry is moot, because ctl_write and ctl_queue also hard-code PW=6.
F3 (confirmed-overstated, low): the scope is wider than the verifier says. When 00 goes off-hook, floods X is holding are falsely claimed and patched one-way to the phone at 00. The phantom seizures then spread network-wide and use up monitor cells and resolvers. The realistic trigger is a card moved into block 0 still jumpered POS=0. It is still low, because it is loud and clears on hang-up.
F4 (confirmed-understated, medium): 74HC14 threshold spread makes the release skew between a trunk's two ends tens of ms, and up to about 180 ms, not 6%. The stuck state bites whenever the end still counting down is on its hold latch or fE, so every trunk release is exposed, not only abandons. That is roughly 0.7 events per exchange per busy hour at moderate load, and it scales with the square of traffic. The verifier's hold-off is the right idea but is sized too small (64 ms). A card-level word hold-off, plus a one-gate `mine` check in the confirm pass, is cheaper and more complete.
The write-away variant (R_GONE / N_DROP writing away a leg that was already seized again) has the same root. It fires on the normal unwind of every call's unclaimed branches and can end in a silent one-way misconnect. It should become its own finding and be tested on a bench.
No simulation was run. Notes are in /home/joel/telco/newimpl/build/flood/work/verify/C20-skeptic/NOTES.md.
